# desflow

> Realistic event streams from a SimPy simulation you can steer while it runs, written to Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL, Parquet, JSONL and Iceberg.

# Home

# desflow

**Realistic event streams from a simulation you can steer while it runs.**

Most test data generators write random rows. desflow writes the events of a working process: orders queue for packers, waits grow at busy times, and a backlog builds when orders arrive faster than the packers can pack them. The data comes from a [SimPy](https://simpy.readthedocs.io/) discrete-event simulation, so each change in it has a cause in the model, as in a real system. [Why desflow](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/about/why-desflow/index.md) explains why it was built and what it is for.

The three ways to write a model build one real-time run. Ingress connectors change its live parameters while it runs, and egress connectors write its events and telemetry:

The control dashboard of the [Kafka Digital Twin](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/examples/kafka/index.md) example changes simulation parameters during a run, and the telemetry shows the effect without a restart. The example's Quick Start runs the dashboard beside the simulation:

# Installation

# Installation

This page installs desflow and runs a first simulation that needs no containers.

## Install the Package

Install the core library with uv or pip:

```bash
# The desflow command
uv tool install desflow

# Or the library, in a uv project
uv add desflow
```

```bash
pip install desflow
```

desflow was called dynamic-des before 0.20.0. The package, the Python module and the command are now all named `desflow`. Code that imports `dynamic_des` and scripts that run `ddes` keep working with a warning until 0.30.0, and the [Changelog](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/about/changelog/index.md) says what to change.

Connectors and input fitting are optional extras. For example, `uv add "desflow[kafka,parquet]"` or `pip install "desflow[kafka,parquet]"`, and `uv tool install "desflow[kafka,parquet]"` for the `desflow` command:

| Extra       | Adds                                                                                                                                           |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `kafka`     | Kafka ingress and egress                                                                                                                       |
| `confluent` | Avro, JSON Schema and Protobuf with the Confluent Schema Registry (includes `kafka`)                                                           |
| `glue`      | Avro, JSON Schema and Protobuf with the AWS Glue Schema Registry (includes `kafka`)                                                            |
| `redis`     | Redis ingress and egress                                                                                                                       |
| `postgres`  | PostgreSQL ingress and egress                                                                                                                  |
| `parquet`   | Parquet and JSONL files on local disk, S3-compatible storage, Google Cloud Storage or Azure Blob Storage                                       |
| `iceberg`   | Apache Iceberg tables through a REST catalog, a SQL catalog on SQLite or PostgreSQL, or the Glue catalog                                       |
| `fit`       | scipy and matplotlib, for [input fitting](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/input-fitting/index.md) with `desflow fit` |
| `all`       | Every extra above                                                                                                                              |

On Python 3.15, the `kafka`, `confluent` and `glue` extras build aiokafka, and the `iceberg` extra builds pyiceberg and zstandard, from source, because those packages publish no wheel for 3.15 yet. A build from source needs a C compiler.

Run `desflow` on its own to list its commands. [Command Line](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/index.md) uses each command on one shop, the model of the `experiment` example, and links the full help of each.

## Run an Example

The local example models a shop that receives and packs customer orders. The simulation prints events and telemetry to the terminal. The example is written three ways: as a YAML blueprint, with the builder and with the low-level API. Each version runs in real time and ends on its own after 30 seconds. Pick the way you write models, then follow uv or pip:

**Quick Start**

`desflow examples get` downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

```bash
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get local --api yaml
cd local/yaml

# 3. Run it
desflow run local.yaml
```

```bash
# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get local --api yaml
cd local/yaml

# 3. Run it
desflow run local.yaml
```

**Quick Start**

`desflow examples get` downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

```bash
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get local --api builder
cd local/builder

# 3. Run it
uv run --no-project --with desflow local_example.py
```

```bash
# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get local --api builder
cd local/builder

# 3. Run it
python local_example.py
```

**Quick Start**

`desflow examples get` downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

```bash
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get local --api low-level
cd local/low-level

```

```bash
# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get local --api low-level
cd local/low-level

# 3. Run it
python local_example.py
```

`desflow examples` lists every example. Examples that need Kafka, a database or an object store start it with [odctl](https://github.com/jaehyeon-kim/odctl), and each example page shows how.

# What Is Discrete-Event Simulation?

If you have never used simulation, start here. No maths is needed. A simulation plays out "what would happen if" on a computer, one step at a time, instead of guessing from averages.

Think of a packing shop. Orders arrive about every 2 seconds, and a packer takes 1.5 seconds to pack one. Will orders queue in the busy hour? What if a second packer starts at 9:30, or a delivery brings twenty orders at once?

You could answer by watching the shop with a notebook. You would not write something down every second, because most seconds nothing changes. You would write only the moments when something happens: an order arrives, a packer starts on it, the order is packed. Each of those moments is an **event**, and the notebook is enough to tell you who waited and for how long.

A **discrete-event simulation** (DES) is that notebook, written by a computer. You describe the shop: how often orders come, how long packing takes, how many packers there are. The computer then plays out the events one after another, with random variation as in real life, and writes down what happens. Because it skips the moments when nothing changes, it plays out a day, or a year, in seconds. Change the description, add a packer or double the orders, and run it again to see the difference.

desflow does this for any system with arrivals, work and limited capacity: a factory, a warehouse, a shop, a support desk, a network. It also sends every event out as a record, to Kafka, a database or files, so the simulation becomes a source of realistic data. The [tutorial](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/first-simulation/index.md) builds the packing shop step by step, and this page explains the ideas it rests on.

______________________________________________________________________

## Events and the Event List

### In the Tutorial

The shop of [First Simulation](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/first-simulation/index.md) has one packer, orders about every 2 seconds and 1.5 seconds of packing. Its first records show the events:

- At 2.552 seconds order 1 arrives, finds the packer free and starts at once.
- At 2.696 seconds order 2 arrives and joins the queue, because the packer is busy.
- At 4.052 seconds, 1.5 seconds after it started, order 1 is packed, and order 2 starts in the same instant.

Order 2 waited 4.052 − 2.696 = 1.356 seconds. Nothing in the model says so: the wait comes from when the events fell.

### Why It Matters

A discrete-event simulation models a system as a series of events. Each event happens at an instant, and between two events nothing changes. The simulation therefore visits only the instants when events happen. It keeps a list of the events to come, in time order. It takes the earliest, moves its clock straight to that instant, and carries the event out. Carrying out an event usually schedules more: when a packer starts on an order, the simulation schedules the end of packing 1.5 seconds later.

Because the clock jumps, a simulated week with a few thousand events takes only the time needed to compute those events, not a week. Two events can fall at the same instant, as order 1 finishing and order 2 starting do. They run by priority and then in the order they were scheduled, as [Run Length](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/run-length/index.md) shows.

### How to Use It

You do not write the event list. desflow runs on [SimPy](https://simpy.readthedocs.io/), which keeps the event list and the clock. You describe the arrivals, the work and the resources, and desflow adds the parts of a simulation study that you would otherwise write yourself:

- **Statistics.** Waits, queue lengths and utilisation are collected for you, with a warm-up period left out. [Statistics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/statistics/index.md) explains them.
- **Replications.** `desflow run --replications` repeats a run with different seeds and gives each statistic with a 95% interval. [Replications](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/replications/index.md) explains it.
- **Experiments.** `desflow experiment` compares designs with the same random numbers, checks them against bounds and observed values, and writes a report. [Experiments](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/experiments/index.md) explains it.
- **Checks against queueing theory.** `desflow explain` works out each resource's utilisation and waits from the model alone, and `--verify` compares those figures with runs. [Command Line](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/#check-it-before-a-long-run) shows it.
- **Inputs from data.** `desflow fit` fits measured times to distributions, and `desflow dist` converts a distribution's parameters. [Input Fitting](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/input-fitting/index.md) explains it.

To see these events yourself, follow [First Simulation](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/first-simulation/index.md). It gives the shop's file in three forms, a YAML blueprint, a builder script and a low-level script, and how to install desflow and run each one. All three forms print the same records.

### What the Result Means

Read `sim_ts`, the simulation time of each record. It jumps from 2.552 to 2.696, then to 3.737, 4.02 and 4.052, because nothing happens in between. A run unpaced, with `factor: 0`, gives the same records in a fraction of a second. A run paced to the wall clock gives them in real time, which is how desflow feeds live data to a system that reads it.

______________________________________________________________________

## Entities, Resources and Queues

### In the Tutorial

The orders are the **entities**: the things that flow through the model. Each order arrives, needs a packer, holds the packer while it is packed, and leaves. The packers are a **resource**: something limited that an entity holds while it is served. When every packer is busy, the next order waits in the resource's **queue**.

An entity can carry **attributes**: facts about it that stay with it as it moves. [A Flow of Tasks](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/shop-logic/flow-of-tasks/index.md) marks each order as express or not when it arrives, and marks it as backordered when it was picked from an empty shelf. A rule reads an attribute as `attr.express`.

### Why It Matters

The time an entity spends in a model is of two kinds. An **activity** is a period of set length, such as the 1.5 seconds of packing. A **delay** is time spent waiting for something, such as a free packer, and the model does not set its length: it comes from the state of the shop. You describe the activities, and the simulation produces the delays. The wait in the queue is a delay, which is why it is a result and not an input.

Two models with the same average times can have very different waits, because a run of quick arrivals or one slow order holds everyone up. A simulation shows that directly, where an average cannot.

### How to Use It

A desflow model is built from these parts. An arrival starts entities, a service gives the length of an activity, a resource limits how many are served at once, and a task says what an entity does. [Model Parts](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/index.md) covers each one, [Arrivals and Services](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/arrivals-and-services/index.md) shows how to set an activity's length, and [Task Flow](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/task-flow/#attributes) shows how to set and read attributes.

### What the Result Means

The waits and queue lengths a run reports are delays, so they change when anything about the shop changes: the arrival rate, the packing times, their spread or the number of packers. [Queueing Basics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/index.md) explains how, and which results of queueing theory a model can be checked against.

______________________________________________________________________

## From Model to Records

### In the Tutorial

Each order in First Simulation publishes a `queued` event when it joins the queue, a `started` event when a packer takes it, and an `order_packed` event when it is packed. [Measuring a Run](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/measuring-a-run/index.md) adds telemetry: the queue length, the utilisation and the waits, published every 10 seconds.

### Why It Matters

A model on its own only moves its clock. What makes it useful here is what it publishes. A sink writes each record to a destination, such as a Kafka topic, a database table or an Iceberg table, so the simulation becomes a source of realistic data for whatever reads it.

Whether that data looks real depends on the model being **stable**. If work arrives faster than the resources can finish it, the queue grows without limit and every later event is delayed more. The records then show waits that grow all day, which no real shop would allow.

### How to Use It

Add a sink for each destination. [Streaming Out](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/running-live/streaming-out/index.md) writes the shop's events to files, and [Egress](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/egress/index.md) lists every sink. Before a long run, check that every resource's utilisation is below 1, as [Queues and Capacity](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/queues-and-capacity/index.md) shows.

### What the Result Means

Each record carries the simulation time, the entity's key and what happened. A reader can rebuild every order's path from them, as [Checking and Validating](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/checking-and-validating/#read-the-trace) does to check a model.

______________________________________________________________________

## Terminating or Steady-State

### In the Tutorial

The shop opens empty in the morning and closes at the end of the day. A question about one day, such as how many orders are still waiting at closing time, has a natural end: the day. A question about the busy hour, such as the mean wait when the shop is running at 1.8 orders a second, is about the shop after its empty start has stopped mattering.

### Why It Matters

[Banks et al.'s lecture notes on output analysis](https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/ece541/fa2016/OutputAnalysis.pdf) separate two kinds of study:

- A **[terminating](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#terminating-or-steady-state)** run has a natural end, and its results over that period are the answer.
- A **steady-state** study asks how the shop behaves in the long run. The start of each run is left out as a [warm-up](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#one-run-starts-empty), because an empty shop has shorter waits than a busy one.

The kind of study decides how long to run, whether to leave out the start, and how many runs to make.

### How to Use It

The same model can be run either way. A terminating run ends at the end of the day, and [End Conditions](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/end-conditions/index.md) shows how to close the doors and let the last orders finish. A steady-state study sets a warm-up, as [Trusting Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/trusting-results/index.md) does with its 2 minutes. [Run Length](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/run-length/index.md) shows how to set the end of a run.

### What the Result Means

A terminating result describes that period, with its empty start included. A steady-state result describes the shop once it is busy, and does not say what happens in the first minutes. [Output Analysis](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/index.md) explains how to get an interval for either.

______________________________________________________________________

- Ingalls, "Introduction to Simulation" (Winter Simulation Conference, 2001), read through [its published text](https://www.informs-sim.org/wsc01papers/002.PDF).
- [Banks et al.'s lecture notes on output analysis](https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/ece541/fa2016/OutputAnalysis.pdf).
- The explanations are our own.

# First Simulation

This tutorial models a shop that receives and packs customer orders: one packer, an order every 2 seconds on average, and 1.5 seconds of packing per order. It answers one question: **how long does an order wait with one packer?**

- **Decision:** how many packers the shop needs, which later pages decide.
- **Measures:** the wait of each order, from the moment it joins the queue to the moment packing starts.
- **Runs:** one run of the first 20 seconds, with the seed 42.
- **Assumptions:** orders arrive at random, and every order takes exactly the same time to pack.

## What You Will Learn

This page shows how to:

- describe a model as an arrival, a resource and a service time, in YAML, the builder or the low-level API;
- run it and read the event records it prints;
- read an order's wait from its `queued` and `started` events.

## What You Add

This page builds the first model of the shop: a simulation called `Shop` with an `orders` arrival, a `packers` resource with one unit, a `packing` service and a `pack_order` task, and a sink that prints each record. The following pages extend the same model, one idea per page.

Each step shows the code three ways, in tabs: a **YAML** blueprint, the **Builder** (`SimulationContext`) and the **Low-level** API (`DynamicRealtimeEnvironment` and SimPy processes). Choose the tab for your preferred API; all code tabs on the site switch to that API. The three build the same simulation and print the same records. [Writing a Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/index.md) explains how they relate.

Look at the order of the parts: orders arrive, wait in the packer queue and take the packer for 1.5 seconds. The simulation prints a record of each step to the console. The arrival loop and the task read their values from the registry. The steps below explain each of these parts.

## Describe the Shop

In discrete-event simulation (DES), an **entity** is a thing that moves through the model, here an order. A **resource** is what an entity needs and may have to wait for, here the packer. A **service** time is how long an entity holds the resource, and an **arrival** process sets when entities appear.

In desflow, these are parameters of one simulation. Its name, the `sim_id`, is `Shop` here. The shop has a resource called `packers` with one unit, a service called `packing`, and an arrival stream called `orders`.

```yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 1.0  # 1 simulated second takes 1 real second
  random_seed: 42  # the same arrival times on every run

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 1}

services:
  # Every order takes exactly 1.5 seconds to pack
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5}

arrivals:
  # One order every 2 seconds on average; each arrival spawns pack_order
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack_order}
```

```python
app = (
    # 1 simulated second = 1 real second; a seed gives the same arrivals every run
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    # Every order takes exactly 1.5 seconds to pack
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    # One order every 2 seconds on average
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
)
```

```python
PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=1)},
)
SEED = 42  # the same arrival times on every run
```

Packing is `constant`, so every order takes 1.5 seconds and only the arrivals are random. The gaps between orders are drawn from an `exponential` distribution with a mean of 2 seconds (30 orders a minute on average), `rate: 0.5`. The seed makes those draws the same on every run, so your trace matches the one below; [Randomness and Seeds](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/randomness-and-seeds/index.md) explains it.

The registry holds the model's live values: the settings that can change while the simulation runs. Each value has a path, such as `Shop.arrival.orders.rate` or `Shop.resources.packers.current_cap`. A scenario, or a message from outside the simulation, changes a value through its path, and the run goes on with the new value. [Live Changes](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/running-live/live-changes/index.md) does it on the shop, and [Live Parameters](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/live-parameters/index.md) explains how.

______________________________________________________________________

## Say What an Order Does

In DES terms an order **queues** for the packer, **seizes** it when it is free, is **delayed** for the service time, and **releases** the packer. desflow calls this a **task**. A task publishes three events: `queued` when the order joins the queue for the packer, `started` when the packer starts on it, and a finished event when packing ends. The value of the finished event is the task's payload.

```yaml
tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # The value of the finished event
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
```

`spawn: pack_order` on the arrival, in the step above, starts the task for every order.

```python
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    # Requests a packer, waits the packing time, releases the packer.
    # The returned dictionary is the value of the finished event.
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        # Waits for the next arrival and returns the new order, keyed orders-1, ...
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
        task_id += 1
```

`@app.task` publishes the three events and handles the packer for you. The arrival loop waits for each arrival and starts one `pack_order` for the order it returns.

```python
def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    """One order: wait for a packer, pack it, release the packer."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        service = env.registry.get_config(path_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(service))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    """Starts one pack_order for every arrival, keyed orders-1, orders-2, ..."""
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id))
        task_id += 1
```

These are SimPy constructs. `pack_order` is a **process**: a generator function that the environment runs, pausing at each `yield` until the event it yielded happens. `env.timeout(...)` is an event that happens after a delay. `packers.request()` is an event that happens when a packer is free, and leaving the `with` block releases the packer. `env.process(...)` starts a process. [SimPy and desflow](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/simpy/index.md) describes what desflow adds to them.

______________________________________________________________________

## Print the Records

A sink, called an egress, receives every record the simulation publishes. `ConsoleEgress` prints them; [Egress](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/egress/index.md) lists the others.

```yaml
egress:
  - type: Console
```

```python
app.add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
```

```python
SINKS = [ConsoleEgress()]  # passed to env.setup_egress in run below
```

Every event record carries the order's key, `orders-1` for the first order, so all the events of one order can be found together. `task` names the task, and `instance` counts the task's runs from 0. [Records and Telemetry](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/records-and-telemetry/index.md) describes every field.

## Run It

```yaml
run:
  until: 20
```

```python
if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(until=20)
```

```python
def run(until=20, factor=1.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor, strict=False)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress(SINKS)

    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    sampler = Sampler(seed=SEED)

    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()
```

Save the files from [Full Files](#full-files) in one folder and run the commands there. `desflow examples` downloads separate examples, not the files of these tutorial pages.

Start it from a terminal:

```bash
desflow run first_shop.yaml
```

```bash
python first_shop.py
```

```bash
python first_shop_low_level.py
```

At `factor: 1.0` one simulated second takes one real second. The run stops at simulation time 20 (`until: 20`), so it takes 20 real seconds. Each record is one line: `[EVT]` lines are events, and `[TEL]` lines are telemetry. The only telemetry here is `system.simulation.lag_seconds`, published once per simulation second, which says how far the run is behind the wall clock. These are the events of the first 6 seconds:

```text
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 2.552, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 2.552, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'started'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 2.696, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-2', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 1, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 3.737, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-3', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 2, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 4.02, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-4', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 3, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 4.052, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 4.052, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-2', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 1, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'started'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 5.552, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-2', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 1, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 5.552, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-3', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 2, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'started'}}
```

Read `sim_ts`, the simulation time of each record. It does not count up in small steps: it jumps from 2.552 to 2.696, then to 3.737, 4.02 and 4.052. The simulation clock moves straight to the time of the next event, because nothing changes between two events. At `factor: 0` the same run takes a fraction of a second, with the same records.

`--sample 5` shows the first records without waiting and without changing the file. It runs the blueprint unpaced, as fast as it can, prints its first 5 events to stdout as JSON lines (one record per line), and stops:

```bash
desflow run first_shop.yaml --sample 5
```

```text
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":2.552,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-1","task":"pack_order","instance":0,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","status":"queued"}}
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":2.552,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-1","task":"pack_order","instance":0,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","status":"started"}}
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":2.696,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-2","task":"pack_order","instance":1,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","status":"queued"}}
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":3.737,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-3","task":"pack_order","instance":2,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","status":"queued"}}
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":4.02,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-4","task":"pack_order","instance":3,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","status":"queued"}}
```

They are the first five events above, each printed as the whole record, with its `stream_type`. The run's log stays on stderr, so a pipe such as `| jq .key` reads only the records. [YAML Blueprints](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/blueprints/#preview-the-records) lists the other ways to run a blueprint.

`desflow` on its own lists every command, grouped by what it does, with examples. `desflow run --help` lists the options of `run`, also with examples. [Command Line](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/index.md) uses every command on one shop.

## What You Get and Why

How long does an order wait with one packer? It depends on how many orders are ahead of it, as the same records on a timeline show: each order waits (yellow) until the packer is free, then holds it for 1.5 seconds of packing (blue).

These records come from one run of the first 20 seconds, with the seed 42. `orders-1` finds the packer free, so its `queued` and `started` events have the same time. `orders-2` is the first order that has to wait: it is `queued` at 2.696 and `started` at 4.052, when `orders-1` finishes. **It waits 1.356 seconds.** `orders-3` arrives while `orders-2` is waiting and waits longer, 1.815 seconds, because two orders are ahead of it.

So with one packer, an order that arrives while the packer is busy waits until every order ahead of it has been packed. The wait depends on when orders happen to arrive, which is why the next pages measure it over many orders.

A discrete-event simulation keeps a list of future events, ordered by time. It takes the earliest one, moves the clock to its time, and runs what it triggers, which may add new events to the list: an arrival schedules the next arrival, and a start of packing schedules its end 1.5 seconds later. The trace above is that list, read in order. [What Is DES?](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/what-is-des/index.md) explains the event list in more detail.

## Key Takeaways

- A model has entities that arrive, resources they wait for, and service times that hold them. desflow calls the work an entity does a task.
- A task publishes `queued`, `started` and a finished event, and an order's wait is its `started` time minus its `queued` time.
- The simulation clock jumps from one event to the next, so a run gives the same records at any pace.

## Busy Hour Figures

The later pages of this tutorial and the concept pages run the busy hour with 3 packers in different ways, so they give different figures for its mean wait. A figure changes with the number of runs, the packing times, the [warm-up](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#one-run-starts-empty), the run length and the seeds. The table lists each figure, the pages that give it and how it was run. Every run is one hour at 1.8 orders a second unless the row says otherwise. Two terms in the table need a definition:

- "Measured times" are the 40 packing times measured at the bench, drawn as an `empirical` distribution.
- "Replications" have seeds spawned from 42. A run of 5, 10 or 20 replications uses the first 5, 10 or 20 of the 40 seeds.

| 2.93 ± 0.25   | [Fitting the Inputs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/fit-the-inputs/index.md)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | 40 replications, the triangular fitted to the measured times, 2-minute warm-up                                              |

The 1.35 and 1.38 seconds come from the same measured times. The two services draw the times in a different order, because each distribution draws from a random number stream named after its registry path, `service.empirical` or `service.packing` ([Randomness and Seeds](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/randomness-and-seeds/#add-returns) explains the streams).

## Full Files

Full files

The complete first shop, which the documentation tests run:

```yaml
# The First Simulation tutorial: the shop as a blueprint.
# Run it with: desflow run first_shop.yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 1.0  # 1 simulated second takes 1 real second
  random_seed: 42  # the same arrival times on every run

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 1}

services:
  # Every order takes exactly 1.5 seconds to pack
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5}

arrivals:
  # One order every 2 seconds on average; each arrival spawns pack_order
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # The value of the finished event
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

egress:
  - type: Console

run:
  until: 20
```

```python
"""The First Simulation tutorial: the shop, with the SimulationContext builder.

One packer, orders arriving about every 2 seconds, and 1.5 seconds of packing per
order. Every record is printed to the terminal.
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

app = (
    # 1 simulated second = 1 real second; a seed gives the same arrivals every run
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    # Every order takes exactly 1.5 seconds to pack
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    # One order every 2 seconds on average
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
)


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    # Requests a packer, waits the packing time, releases the packer.
    # The returned dictionary is the value of the finished event.
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        # Waits for the next arrival and returns the new order, keyed orders-1, ...
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
        task_id += 1


app.add_egress(ConsoleEgress())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(until=20)
```

```python
"""The First Simulation tutorial: the shop, on the low-level API.

One packer, orders arriving about every 2 seconds, and 1.5 seconds of packing per
order. Every record is printed to the terminal.
"""

import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=1)},
)
SEED = 42  # the same arrival times on every run


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    """One order: wait for a packer, pack it, release the packer."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        service = env.registry.get_config(path_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(service))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    """Starts one pack_order for every arrival, keyed orders-1, orders-2, ..."""
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id))
        task_id += 1


SINKS = [ConsoleEgress()]  # passed to env.setup_egress in run below


def run(until=20, factor=1.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor, strict=False)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress(SINKS)

    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    sampler = Sampler(seed=SEED)

    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()
```

# Queues and Capacity

In its busy hour the shop gets 1.8 orders a second, and packing still takes 1.5 seconds. One packer cannot keep up. This page asks: **how many packers keep the mean wait under 10 seconds?**

- **Decision:** the number of packers for the busy hour.
- **Measures:** the packers' [utilisation](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/#utilisation) and the mean wait.
- **Runs:** four runs of the hour, one for each number of packers, each with the seed 42.
- **Assumptions:** orders arrive at random at a steady rate, and every order takes the same time to pack.

## What You Will Learn

This page shows how to:

- work out a resource's utilisation before running the model;
- read the load, the stability and the bottleneck with `desflow explain`;
- choose the fewest packers that keep the mean wait short.

## What You Add

This page adds more orders, then more packers, and `desflow explain`, which works out the load from the model before it runs. The shop is the one from [First Simulation](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/first-simulation/index.md), with the arrival rate of the busy hour and the number of packers as a setting you change between runs.

______________________________________________________________________

## Work Out the Load

Before running anything, work out how busy the packers would be. **[Utilisation](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/#utilisation)** is the share of time a resource is busy:

> utilisation = arrival rate × mean service time ÷ number of units

The **load** is the part above the division: arrival rate × mean service time. Here it is 1.8 orders a second × 1.5 seconds = 2.7, so each second brings 2.7 seconds of packing, enough work for 2.7 packers. One packer would be busy 270% of the time, which is impossible: it falls further behind with every order.

- With utilisation below 1 a model is **stable**: the queue rises and falls, but stays bounded.
- At 1 or above it is not: the queue grows for as long as the run lasts, and every order waits longer than the one before.

The shop needs at least 3 packers, the fewest that bring utilisation below 1: 2.7 ÷ 3 = 0.9. [Queueing Basics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/index.md) explains utilisation, and why the queue grows without limit at 1 or above. Each resource in a model has its own utilisation. The one with the highest utilisation is the **[bottleneck](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/#flow-balance-and-the-bottleneck)**: it decides how long everything waits.

Here is the busy hour. The arrival rate is 1.8 orders a second, and `until` is one hour of simulation time:

```yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0  # unpaced: the hour runs in about a second
  random_seed: 42

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5 s}

arrivals:
  # The busy hour: 1.8 orders a second, more than one packer can pack
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 1.8, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

egress:
  - type: Console

run:
  until: 1 h
```

```python
app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)  # unpaced
app.add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
# The busy hour: 1.8 orders a second, more than one packer can pack. Each
# order starts the task pack_order.
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.8, spawn="pack_order")
```

```python
service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
# The busy hour: 1.8 orders a second, more than one packer can pack
arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=1.8)},
```

A blueprint accepts a duration with a unit wherever it takes a time, such as `until: 1 h` and `value: 1.5 s`, and reads a plain number as seconds. `factor: 0` runs the hour unpaced: as fast as the computer can, in about a second. Nobody needs to watch this run in real time.

______________________________________________________________________

## Explain the Load

`desflow explain` does this arithmetic from a YAML or builder model, without running it. It reads three numbers for each resource and works out the fourth:

- **λ** (lambda), the arrival rate: `rate: 1.8` of `arrivals.orders`;
- **μ** (mu), the service rate, one over the mean service time: `value: 1.5 s` of `services.packing` gives 1 ÷ 1.5 = 0.667 orders a second for each packer, one order every 1.5 seconds (40 a minute);
- **c**, the number of units: `current_cap` of `resources.packers`;
- **ρ** (rho), the utilisation: λ ÷ (c × μ).

Save the files from [Full Files](#full-files) in one folder and run the commands there.

```bash
desflow explain queues_and_capacity.yaml
```

The file is `queues_and_capacity.yaml` from [Full Files](#full-files). Its number of packers comes from the variable `PACKERS`, which [Run It With More Packers](#run-it-with-more-packers) sets. With `PACKERS` not set, the shop has one packer.

```python
def explain(packers: int) -> str:
    """The busy hour with `packers` packers, as `desflow explain` prints it."""
    return render_terminal(shop(packers).analyze())
```

`context.analyze()` returns the same analysis as an `Explanation`, and `render_terminal` prints it as the command does. `desflow explain` also loads a builder Python file that defines a `SimulationContext` at module level.

`desflow explain` does not support low-level models. It reads which arrival starts which task and which resource each task uses, and a low-level model does not declare those links: its SimPy code makes them as it runs.

For a YAML or builder model, it prints the graph from each arrival, the resources, the utilisation at each number of units the resource allows, and hints:

```text
Shop
`-- orders (arrival, rate 1.8/s)
    `-- spawn -> pack_order (task, rate 1.8/s)
        +-- uses packers (resource)
        `-- next (share 1) -> exit
Resources
+-------------------------------------------------------+
| resource |   λ |      μ | c |   ρ | Wq | L | status   |
|----------+-----+--------+---+-----+----+---+----------|
| packers  | 1.8 | 0.6667 | 1 | 2.7 |  - | - | UNSTABLE |
+-------------------------------------------------------+
packers by units
+-------------------------+
|  c |      ρ | status    |
|----+--------+-----------|
|  1 |    2.7 | UNSTABLE  |
|  2 |   1.35 | UNSTABLE  |
|  3 |    0.9 | CONGESTED |
|  4 |  0.675 | OK        |
|  5 |   0.54 | OK        |
|  6 |   0.45 | OK        |
|  7 | 0.3857 | OK        |
|  8 | 0.3375 | OK        |
|  9 |    0.3 | OK        |
| 10 |   0.27 | OK        |
+-------------------------+
Bottleneck: packers
Not estimated:
  wait at packers: unstable: the queue grows for as long as the run lasts
Hints for utilisation 0.85:
  packers with 4 units: utilisation 0.675, at most 0.85
  packers with 1 unit: utilisation 0.85 at a request every 1.76 seconds (34 a minute, 0.5667 a second)
```

The output has four parts:

- The tree shows each order starting `pack_order`, which uses `packers`, and the flow ending after it.
- The resources table gives λ (the arrival rate) 1.8 orders a second, μ (the rate one packer serves) 0.667 orders a second, c (the number of packers) 1 and utilisation ρ 2.7. The status is `CONGESTED` from utilisation 0.85 and `UNSTABLE` from 1, so it is `UNSTABLE`. The wait (`Wq`) and the number in the shop (`L`) are left blank, and the reason is printed below the tables: the queue grows for as long as the run lasts.
- The table by units covers 1 to 10 packers, up to `max_cap`. Three packers are stable but congested at utilisation 0.9.
- The first hint names 4 as the fewest packers at or below 0.85. The second hint keeps the current number of units. It gives the rate of requests into the resource at which utilisation reaches the target. With one packer, an arrival rate of 0.5667 orders a second, an order every 1.76 seconds (34 a minute), gives utilisation 0.85. In a network, that rate includes the requests that come back for rework, not only new arrivals.

## Run It With More Packers

The number of packers is the resource's `current_cap`. Each run sets it once:

```yaml
resources:
  # The number of packers comes from the PACKERS variable, 1 when it is not set
  packers:
    current_cap: ${PACKERS:-1}
    max_cap: 10
```

`${PACKERS:-1}` reads the environment variable `PACKERS`, and uses 1 when it is not set.

```python
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=packers, max_cap=10)
```

```python
resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=packers, max_cap=10)},
```

A `DynamicResource` with a `current_cap` of 3 behaves like a SimPy resource with three units: a request is granted as soon as any unit is free, so up to three orders are packed at once. [Resources](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/resources/index.md) describes how it is built and why.

`env.run(until=...)` runs [SimPy's event loop](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/simpy/#environment-and-the-event-list) until that time. `DynamicRealtimeEnvironment` is desflow's form of [SimPy's `RealtimeEnvironment`](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/simpy/#real-time-environment). A resource's capacity is its [number of units](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/simpy/#resources).

To read the mean wait, switch on the built-in statistics at the `typical` level, which keeps the mean wait of every task; [Measuring a Run](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/measuring-a-run/index.md) explains the levels.

```yaml
# The mean wait of pack_order, published once an hour and at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 1 h}
```

```python
# The mean wait of pack_order, kept by the run and read at the end
app.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
```

```python
# The mean wait of pack_order, kept by the environment and read at the end
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)
```

Now run the hour with 1, 2, 3 and 4 packers:

At the end, the run publishes the mean wait as `Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean`, among all its other records. `--stdout` prints the records as JSON lines, `grep` keeps the mean wait, and `tail -1` keeps its last reading:

```bash
# The mean wait with one to four packers
for n in 1 2 3 4; do
  PACKERS=$n desflow run queues_and_capacity.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'pack_order\.wait_mean"' | tail -1
done
```

```python
def mean_wait(packers: int) -> float:
    """Runs the busy hour with `packers` packers and returns the mean wait."""
    app = shop(packers)
    app.run(until=UNTIL)
    return app.env.stats.readings()["Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for packers in range(1, 5):
        print(f"packers {packers}: mean wait {mean_wait(packers):8.2f} s")
```

## Waits Near Full Use

With 2 packers, utilisation is 1.35. The queue grows all hour, so the mean wait depends mainly on how long the run was: run two hours and it roughly doubles. With 3 packers, utilisation is 0.9 and the wait settles. With 4 it is 0.675, and almost nobody waits.

A stable model can still wait a long time, because the wait grows much faster than utilisation near 1. Take one packer with exponential gaps and exponential service times: an M/M/1 queue, in the notation that [Queueing Basics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/#kendalls-notation) explains. Its mean wait in the queue is ρ ÷ (1 − ρ) × the mean service time, where ρ is the utilisation. At utilisation 0.95 the factor is 0.95 ÷ 0.05 = 19, and at 0.8 it is 0.8 ÷ 0.2 = 4, so the wait at 0.95 is about 5 times the wait at 0.8. The chart draws the formula for the shop's 1.5-second packing, with the function `desflow explain` uses:

Variable times make the wait longer still. Bursts of arrivals, or packing times that vary a lot, fill the queue while the average load is moderate, and the queue takes a long time to empty again. [Kingman's formula](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/#variation-lengthens-waits) gives the size of the effect for one server: it multiplies the M/M/1 wait by a factor for the spread of the gaps and of the service times. With exponential gaps and constant packing the factor is 0.5, so the shop's constant packing halves the wait. `desflow explain` uses Kingman's formula for a resource with one unit, and [Choosing Inputs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/choosing-inputs/index.md) measures the wait with constant, triangular, empirical and exponential packing times.

Little's Law checks a run's output. In a model that settles, the mean number of orders waiting is the arrival rate times the mean wait, Lq = λ × Wq, and the number in the shop is L = λ × (Wq + mean service time). `desflow explain` prints L beside Wq, and [Queueing Basics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/#littles-law) checks the law against runs of the shop.

______________________________________________________________________

## Networks and Bottlenecks

In a network, each task's rate comes from the tasks before it. This version of the shop checks every packed order with one checker, and sends one order in ten back to be packed again:

```yaml
arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 1.6, spawn: pack_order}

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5 s}
  checking: {dist: exponential, rate: 2.5}  # 0.4 s on average

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 4, max_cap: 10}
  checkers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
    next: check_order
  check_order:
    service: checking
    resource: checkers
    payload: {event_type: order_checked}
    # Nine in ten pass; the tenth is packed again
    next: {weights: {ship_order: 9, pack_order: 1}}
  ship_order:
    payload: {event_type: order_shipped}
```

```python
app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.6, spawn="pack_order")
app.add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
app.add_service("checking", dist="exponential", rate=2.5)  # 0.4 s on average
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=4, max_cap=10)
app.add_resource("checkers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4)

@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", next="check_order")
def pack_order(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

# Nine in ten pass; the tenth is packed again
@app.task(
    service_id="checking",
    resource_id="checkers",
    next={"weights": {"ship_order": 9, "pack_order": 1}},
)
def check_order(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_checked"}

@app.task()
def ship_order(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_shipped"}

# print(render_terminal(app.analyze())) prints what desflow explain prints
```

```python
NETWORK = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=1.6)},
    service={
        "packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5),
        # One check takes 0.4 s on average
        "checking": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=2.5),
    },
    resources={
        "packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=4, max_cap=10),
        "checkers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=4),
    },
)
# Each task's service and resource, and the task after it
STEPS = {
    "pack_order": ("packing", "packers", Router("check_order")),
    # Nine in ten pass; the tenth is packed again
    "check_order": (
        "checking",
        "checkers",
        Router({"weights": {"ship_order": 9, "pack_order": 1}}),
    ),
    "ship_order": (None, None, Router(None)),
}


def step(env, sampler, shop, name, entity, counters):
    """One task of an order, then the task its router chooses."""
    service, resource, router = STEPS[name]
    task_id = next(counters[name])
    if resource is None:
        env.stats.task_finished(name, task_id)
    else:
        env.stats.task_queued(name, task_id)
        with shop[resource].request() as request:
            yield request
            env.stats.task_started(name, task_id)
            config = env.registry.get_config(f"Shop.service.{service}")
            yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(config))
        env.stats.task_finished(name, task_id)
    following = router.choose(Upstream(task_id, entity, {}, {}), env)
    if following is None:
        env.stats.flow_finished("orders")
    else:
        env.process(step(env, sampler, shop, following, entity, counters))
```

`desflow explain` does not support low-level models. It reads which arrival starts which task and which resource each task uses, and a low-level model does not declare those links: its SimPy code makes them as it runs.

Every packed order is checked. Packing receives the new orders, 1.6 a second, and also the tenth of the checked orders that come back. Call the rate into packing x: then x = 1.6 + 0.1 × x, which gives x = 1.6 ÷ 0.9 = 1.778 orders a second. `desflow explain queues_network.yaml` solves this [flow balance](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/#flow-balance-and-the-bottleneck) for every task. This is its output without the hints at the end:

```text
Shop
`-- orders (arrival, rate 1.6/s)
    `-- spawn -> pack_order (task, rate 1.778/s)
        +-- uses packers (resource)
        `-- next (share 1) -> check_order (task, rate 1.778/s)
            +-- uses checkers (resource)
            +-- next (share 0.9) -> ship_order (task, rate 1.6/s)
            |   `-- next (share 1) -> exit
            `-- next (share 0.1) -> pack_order (again)
Resources
+----------------------------------------------------------+
| resource |     λ |      μ | c |      ρ | Wq | L | status |
|----------+-------+--------+---+--------+----+---+--------|
| packers  | 1.778 | 0.6667 | 4 | 0.6667 |  - | - | OK     |
| checkers | 1.778 |    2.5 | 1 | 0.7111 |  - | - | OK     |
+----------------------------------------------------------+
packers by units
+-------------------------+
|  c |      ρ | status    |
|----+--------+-----------|
|  1 |  2.667 | UNSTABLE  |
|  2 |  1.333 | UNSTABLE  |
|  3 | 0.8889 | CONGESTED |
|  4 | 0.6667 | OK        |
|  5 | 0.5333 | OK        |
|  6 | 0.4444 | OK        |
|  7 |  0.381 | OK        |
|  8 | 0.3333 | OK        |
|  9 | 0.2963 | OK        |
| 10 | 0.2667 | OK        |
+-------------------------+
checkers by units
+---------------------+
| c |      ρ | status |
|---+--------+--------|
| 1 | 0.7111 | OK     |
| 2 | 0.3556 | OK     |
| 3 |  0.237 | OK     |
| 4 | 0.1778 | OK     |
+---------------------+
Bottleneck: checkers
Not estimated:
  wait at packers: no closed formula for c > 1 with non-exponential times; run --verify to measure it
  wait at checkers: its input is not one arrival or a Poisson flow, which Kingman's formula needs; run --verify to measure it
```

The four packers are at utilisation 0.667 and the checker at 0.711, the higher of the two, so the checker is the bottleneck. In the table by units, 3 packers would be at utilisation 0.889, above the checker. So with 3 packers the packers are the bottleneck, and a fourth packer moves the bottleneck to the checker. Relieving a bottleneck makes the next busiest resource the new one. `desflow explain` estimates neither wait here, and says why: four packers with constant packing have no closed formula, and the checker's input is the packers' output, which is neither one arrival nor a [Poisson](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/#kendalls-notation) flow. `--verify`, in [Check Against Theory](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/analysis/check-against-theory/index.md), measures both.

______________________________________________________________________

## Tuning

To keep a resource stable, lower its utilisation or its variability:

- more units: a higher `current_cap`;
- faster service: a shorter service time;
- fewer arrivals: a lower `rate`;
- less variable gaps or service times, which shorten the wait at the same utilisation.

To test how a consumer of the records copes, do the opposite on purpose. From utilisation 0.85 a resource is congested, with long waits that come and go, and bursts make them longer. Above 1 it is overloaded: its queue, and the lag of everything after it, grows for as long as the overload lasts.

`--target` sets the utilisation the hints aim for, 0.85 by default. At 1 or above, the hints are for deliberate overload:

```bash
desflow explain queues_and_capacity.yaml --target 1.2
```

The end of its output, the hints:

```text
Hints for utilisation 1.2:
  packers with 2 units: utilisation 1.35, at least 1.2, for deliberate overload
  packers with 1 unit: utilisation 1.2 at a request every 1.25 seconds (48 a minute, 0.8 a second)
```

With 2 packers the shop runs at utilisation 1.35, above the target of 1.2. With 1 packer, an arrival rate of 0.8 orders a second, an order every 1.25 seconds (48 a minute), gives exactly 1.2.

A scenario step can raise the arrival rate while the model runs and push a resource past full use on purpose. [Changing Demand](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/changing-demand/index.md) runs such a rush, and its queue grows for as long as the rush lasts.

______________________________________________________________________

## What You Get and Why

How many packers keep the mean wait under 10 seconds? **3 packers**, as the mean wait for 1 to 4 packers shows:

With 3 packers the mean wait is 1.27 seconds, from [one run of the hour](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/first-simulation/#busy-hour-figures) with constant packing and the seed 42. With 2 packers it is over 400 seconds and still growing when the hour ends. The answer is the fewest packers that bring utilisation below 1. At utilisation 0.9 the wait stays under 10 seconds, because the shop's packing time is constant and 0.9 is not yet close enough to 1.

[Queueing Basics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/index.md) explains why the wait grows without limit as utilisation reaches 1, as the table shows for 1 and 2 packers. It also gives the formula for several packers sharing one queue. Each term of the utilisation is a live parameter, so a running model can be relieved, or overloaded on purpose, as [Live Parameters](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/live-parameters/index.md) shows. [Statistics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/statistics/index.md) describes how the mean wait is measured.

The formulas describe a queue that has settled. A run starts with no orders in the shop, so its early waits are shorter than the settled waits. A live change, such as a rush, makes the waits rise, and they take time to settle again. [Trusting Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/trusting-results/index.md) shows how to leave out a [warm-up](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#one-run-starts-empty) and how long to run.

## Key Takeaways

- Utilisation is the arrival rate times the mean service time, divided by the number of units. Below 1 the queue settles; at 1 or above it grows for as long as the run lasts.
- Near utilisation 1 the wait grows much faster than the utilisation, and variable times make it longer still.
- The resource with the highest utilisation is the bottleneck. Relieving it makes the next busiest resource the bottleneck.

______________________________________________________________________

Full files

```yaml
# The Queues and Capacity tutorial: the shop in its busy hour, as a blueprint.
# Run it once per number of packers, and read the mean wait from the last lines:
#   PACKERS=3 desflow run queues_and_capacity.yaml 2>&1 | grep wait_mean
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0  # unpaced: the hour runs in about a second
  random_seed: 42

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5 s}

arrivals:
  # The busy hour: 1.8 orders a second, more than one packer can pack
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 1.8, spawn: pack_order}

  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

egress:
  - type: Console

  until: 1 h

resources:
  # The number of packers comes from the PACKERS variable, 1 when it is not set
  packers:
    current_cap: ${PACKERS:-1}
    max_cap: 10

# The mean wait of pack_order, published once an hour and at the end
```
