```python
    return last / (sum(load**k / math.factorial(k) for k in range(units)) + last)


def mmc_wait(units: int, arrival_rate: float) -> float:
    """Mean wait in the queue of an M/M/c queue: Erlang C divided by (c / service - lambda)."""
    return erlang_c(units, arrival_rate * SERVICE) / (units / SERVICE - arrival_rate)


def kingman_wait(utilisation: float, arrival_cv: float, service_cv: float) -> float:
    """Kingman's formula for the mean wait in a one-server queue."""
    variability = (arrival_cv**2 + service_cv**2) / 2
    return utilisation / (1 - utilisation) * variability * SERVICE
```

```text
utilisation 0.5: mean wait M/M/1  1.50 s, M/D/1  0.75 s
utilisation 0.75: mean wait M/M/1  4.50 s, M/D/1  2.25 s
utilisation 0.9: mean wait M/M/1 13.50 s, M/D/1  6.75 s
utilisation 0.95: mean wait M/M/1 28.50 s, M/D/1 14.25 s
```

`desflow explain` gives the same figure for a one-packer model: for the shop of First Simulation, M/D/1 at utilisation 0.75, its `Wq` column reads 2.25 seconds.

### What the Result Means

Near full use, the wait depends strongly on the exact arrival rate. Before trusting a wait at a utilisation of 0.9 or more, check how good the estimate of the rate is, as Parameter Sweeps does. A run near full use also needs to be long before its mean wait settles, as [Output Analysis](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/index.md) explains.

______________________________________________________________________

## Several Packers

### In the Tutorial

The busy hour has three packers with constant packing at utilisation 0.9. Ten long runs of it give a mean wait of 2.05 seconds, as [Check a Formula Against the Shop](#check-a-formula-against-the-shop) shows. One packer with constant packing at the same utilisation would make orders wait 6.75 seconds on average, by the M/D/1 formula above. Three packers sharing one queue wait far less at the same utilisation.

### Why It Matters

With several packers sharing one queue, an order waits only when every packer is busy. For exponential gaps and service times (M/M/c), the share of orders that find every packer busy is the **Erlang C** formula. The mean wait in the queue is that share divided by (c ÷ the mean service time − the arrival rate). The `erlang_c` and `mmc_wait` functions above compute it.

### How to Use It

Compare designs at the same utilisation with the formulas. With a mean packing time of 1.5 seconds, one packer at utilisation 0.8 gives a mean wait of 6 seconds. Three packers at utilisation 0.8 give about 1.6 seconds:

```text
one packer at utilisation 0.8: mean wait 6.0 s
three packers at utilisation 0.8: mean wait 1.62 s
```

### What the Result Means

Pooling packers into one queue shortens the wait at the same load. A design question such as "one fast packer or three slower ones" needs the wait, not only the utilisation. The formula covers exponential times only, so the shop's own runs answer it for other times.

______________________________________________________________________

## Variation Lengthens Waits

### In the Tutorial

[Choosing Inputs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/choosing-inputs/index.md) runs the busy hour with four candidate packing times, all with a mean of 1.5 seconds. The mean waits are 1.27 seconds with constant times, 1.28 with triangular, 1.35 with the measured times and 2.37 with exponential. The same mean with a wider spread gives a longer wait.

### Why It Matters

**Kingman's formula** gives an approximate mean wait for one server with any distributions. It measures the spread of each input by its **coefficient of variation**, the standard deviation divided by the mean, called variation for short. The variation is 1 for an exponential distribution and 0 for a constant one. The mean wait is the product of three parts:

- utilisation ÷ (1 − utilisation), which grows quickly as utilisation nears 1;
- (arrival variation² + service variation²) ÷ 2, the effect of the spread;
- the mean service time.

With exponential gaps (variation 1) and constant service (variation 0), the middle part is 0.5. The formula then gives half the M/M/1 wait, which is the M/D/1 result above. Variation in the gaps counts as much as variation in the packing times. When both variations are 0, the formula gives no wait at all.

### How to Use It

The `kingman_wait` function above computes it. Use it to judge how much the choice of an input distribution matters before you fit one. Choosing Inputs shows how to compare the candidates by running each.

### What the Result Means

A model whose inputs are replaced by their averages has no variation, so it shows no queue while utilisation is below 1. Its waits are too short. [Common Mistakes](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/common-mistakes/index.md) lists this among the errors that distort a result.

______________________________________________________________________

## Flow Balance and the Bottleneck

### In the Tutorial

[Queues and Capacity](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/queues-and-capacity/#networks-and-bottlenecks) adds a checker to the shop. Orders arrive at 1.6 a second, every packed order is checked, and a tenth of the checked orders go back to packing. Four packers take 1.5 seconds an order, and one checker takes 0.4 seconds on average.

### Why It Matters

In a network of tasks, work reaches a task in two ways: as new work, and as work routed to it from other tasks. The rate into a task is the sum of the two. This is **flow balance**. For packing, the rate is 1.6 + 0.1 × the rate into packing. Solving for it gives 1.6 ÷ (1 − 0.1) = 1.6 ÷ 0.9 = 1.778 orders a second. Every packed order goes to the checker, so the checker receives the same 1.778.

Each resource's utilisation follows from its rate. The four packers have 1.778 × 1.5 ÷ 4 = 0.667. The checker has 1.778 × 0.4 = 0.711. The resource with the highest utilisation is the **bottleneck**, here the checker. It is the first to reach full use when demand grows, and adding units anywhere else does not raise the most the shop can handle.

### How to Use It

Work out the rate into each task, then each resource's utilisation:

```python
# Orders arrive at 1.6 a second, and a tenth of the checked orders go back to packing,
# so the rate into packing solves: rate = 1.6 + 0.1 x rate.
flow_rate = 1.6 / (1 - 0.1)
packers = flow_rate * 1.5 / 4  # four packers, 1.5 seconds an order
checker = flow_rate * 0.4  # one checker, 0.4 seconds an order on average
print(f"rate into packing and into checking: {flow_rate:.3f} orders a second")
print(f"utilisation: packers {packers:.3f}, checker {checker:.3f}")
```

`desflow explain` does the same from the model and names the bottleneck:

```bash
desflow explain queues_network.yaml
```

It ends its resource tables with `Bottleneck: checkers`.

```python
from queues_and_capacity import network

explanation = network().analyze()
print(f"desflow explain names the bottleneck: {explanation.bottleneck}")
```

`desflow explain` does not support low-level models. Explain the [YAML or builder form](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/queues-and-capacity/#networks-and-bottlenecks) of the network.

```text
rate into packing and into checking: 1.778 orders a second
utilisation: packers 0.667, checker 0.711
desflow explain names the bottleneck: checkers
```

### What the Result Means

Add capacity at the bottleneck first. Here a second checker lowers the checker's utilisation to 0.356, while a fifth packer leaves the checker at 0.711 and the shop no faster. Rework raises the load on every task it passes through, so a model without it underestimates every utilisation.

______________________________________________________________________

## Check a Formula Against the Shop

### In the Tutorial

The busy hour with exponential packing times is M/M/3 at utilisation 0.9. The Erlang C formula gives a mean wait of 4.083 seconds. Ten one-hour runs of the shop measure 4.784 ± 1.301 seconds, so the formula lies within the interval of the runs.

### Why It Matters

A formula and a run that agree check each other. The formula shows that the model is built as intended, and the runs show that the formula applies. A model that disagrees with a formula on a case the formula covers has a fault in its logic or its statistics.

### How to Use It

`desflow explain --verify` runs the model and compares each measure with the analysis:

```bash
PACKING=exponential desflow explain choosing_inputs.yaml --verify --replications 10
```

```text
Verify: 10 runs to 3600 s, seed 42
+---------------------------------------------------------------------+
| node       | measure      | analysis | measured |        ± | result |
|------------+--------------+----------+----------+----------+--------|
| packers    | utilization  |      0.9 |   0.9066 | 0.008966 | agrees |
| packers    | queue_length |    7.349 |    8.659 |    2.396 | agrees |
| pack_order | wait         |    4.083 |    4.784 |    1.301 | agrees |
| orders     | throughput   |      1.8 |    1.805 |  0.01634 | agrees |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

This shop takes the gaps and the packing times as exponential or constant by choice:

```python
def shop(arrival: dict, service: dict, packers: int) -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop with the given arrival gaps and packing times, and `packers` packers."""
    app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
    app.add_arrival("orders", **arrival)
    app.add_service("packing", **service)
    app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=packers, max_cap=10)
    app.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


# Exponential gaps and times are the M of Kendall's notation, constant ones the D
def exponential(mean: float) -> dict:
    return {"dist": "exponential", "rate": 1 / mean}


def constant(mean: float) -> dict:
    return {"dist": "constant", "value": mean}
```

This function runs ten [replications](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#replications), each leaving out its first 2,000 seconds, and returns the mean wait with its 95% [half-width](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#interval-and-half-width):

```python
def measured_wait(arrival: dict, service: dict, packers: int, until: int):
    """Mean wait over 10 runs, with its 95% half-width; each run leaves out its first 2,000 s."""
    result = replicate(
        lambda: shop(arrival, service, packers),
        10,
        seed=42,
        until=until,
        warmup=2000,
        measures=["tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"],
    )
    row = result.summary[0]
    return row["mean"], row["half_width"]
```

`--verify` does not support low-level models. `replicate` runs a `LowLevelModel` the same way, as [Replications](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/replications/index.md) shows, and its mean and half-width compare with a formula as in the Builder tab.

The Builder tab's checks compare each formula with the runs, and pass when the formula lies within the interval:

```python
for rho, figures in ((0.5, (1.50, 1.47, 0.06)), (0.75, (4.50, 4.46, 0.33))):
    arrival = exponential(SERVICE / rho)
    check(
        f"M/M/1 at utilisation {rho}",
        mm1_wait(rho),
        measured_wait(arrival, exponential(SERVICE), 1, 20_000),
        figures,
    )
check(
    "M/M/3 at utilisation 0.8",
    mmc_wait(3, 1.6),
    measured_wait(exponential(1 / 1.6), exponential(SERVICE), 3, 30_000),
    (1.62, 1.64, 0.06),
)
arrival = exponential(SERVICE / 0.75)
check(
    "M/D/1 at utilisation 0.75, Kingman",
    kingman_wait(0.75, 1, 0),
    measured_wait(arrival, constant(SERVICE), 1, 20_000),
    (2.25, 2.23, 0.14),
)
```

```text
M/M/1 at utilisation 0.5: formula 1.50 s, mean of 10 runs 1.47 ± 0.06 s
M/M/1 at utilisation 0.75: formula 4.50 s, mean of 10 runs 4.46 ± 0.33 s
M/M/3 at utilisation 0.8: formula 1.62 s, mean of 10 runs 1.64 ± 0.06 s
M/D/1 at utilisation 0.75, Kingman: formula 2.25 s, mean of 10 runs 2.23 ± 0.14 s
```

The busy hour itself is M/D/3, which has no exact formula. For one packer, constant service halves the M/M/1 wait. This check compares the M/D/3 runs with half the M/M/3 wait, as an approximation:

```python
# The busy hour is M/D/3: exponential gaps (M), constant service (D), three packers.
# The runs are compared with half the M/M/3 wait at this load.
check(
    "M/D/3 at utilisation 0.9, half the M/M/3 wait",
    mmc_wait(3, 1.8) / 2,
    measured_wait(exponential(1 / 1.8), constant(SERVICE), 3, 20_000),
    (2.04, 2.05, 0.13),
)
```

```text
M/D/3 at utilisation 0.9, half the M/M/3 wait: formula 2.04 s, mean of 10 runs 2.05 ± 0.13 s
```

These are [10 runs of 20,000 seconds](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/first-simulation/#busy-hour-figures), each without its first 2,000 seconds, not one-hour runs.

Kingman's formula is an approximation, and this check shows where it is not exact. Constant gaps of 2 seconds with exponential service (D/M/1) at utilisation 0.75:

```python
mean, half_width = measured_wait(
    constant(SERVICE / 0.75), exponential(SERVICE), 1, 20_000
)
kingman = kingman_wait(0.75, 0, 1)
print(
    f"D/M/1 at utilisation 0.75: Kingman {kingman:.2f} s, mean of 10 runs {mean:.2f} ± {half_width:.2f} s"
)
```

```text
D/M/1 at utilisation 0.75: Kingman 2.25 s, mean of 10 runs 1.78 ± 0.09 s
```

### What the Result Means

Where a formula is exact, as for M/M/1 and M/M/c, it lies within the interval of the runs. Half the M/M/3 wait is close for the M/D/3 busy hour. Kingman's formula lies outside the interval for D/M/1: it is accurate near full use and for the cases above, and a rough guide elsewhere. A check that fails on a case the formula covers points to a fault in the model. A check that fails outside the formula's cases says only that the formula does not apply.

______________________________________________________________________

## Key Takeaways

- Write the model in Kendall's notation first, to know which formulas apply.
- Work out utilisation for every resource before a run. At 1 or above, the answer is more capacity.
- Check a run's statistics with Little's law before trusting any result.
- Expect long waits near full use, and longer ones when gaps or packing times vary.
- Find the bottleneck with flow balance, and add capacity there first.
- Check the model against a formula on the cases the formula covers. The simulation answers the cases it cannot: several resources, priorities, breakdowns and changing demand.

______________________________________________________________________

## Sources

- Wikipedia: [Kendall's notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendall%27s_notation), [Little's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little%27s_law), [Kingman's formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingman%27s_formula), the [Erlang C formula](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erlang_(unit)#Erlang_C_formula>) and the [Jackson network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_network).
- The explanations and the checks are our own.

# A Simulation Study

Building a model is one step of a simulation study, and often not the largest. This page walks through the whole study, from the question to the report, with the packing shop as the example. Each step says what to produce and names the tutorial page that does it for the shop. [The Complete Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/complete-model/index.md) runs every step in order.

The steps follow Law's seven-step approach. Two steps are checks: [Check the Assumptions](#check-the-assumptions) checks the conceptual model, and [Build and Check the Model](#build-and-check-the-model) checks the programmed model. When either check fails, the study goes back to [Ask One Question](#ask-one-question) and [Conceptual Model and Data](#conceptual-model-and-data), because the question or the conceptual model may need to change.

Law notes that programming the model is only 25 to 50 percent of the work of a sound study, despite the common view of simulation as a programming exercise.

______________________________________________________________________

## What You Will Learn

- how to write a question that a study can answer;
- what a conceptual model holds, and how to choose the inputs;
- how AIC and the KS test score a fitted distribution;
- how the assumptions and the model are checked;
- how an experiment answers the question;
- what a report of the study states.

______________________________________________________________________

## Ask One Question

### In the Tutorial

The shop's question is: **how many packers keep the mean wait under 10 seconds in the busy hour?** The measures are the mean wait of an order and how busy the packers are. The question also fixes the period (the busy hour), the system (the packing area, not the whole warehouse) and who decides (the shop manager).

### Why It Matters

A study with no well-defined objective cannot say when it is finished, and Law lists this first among the pitfalls. Without a specific question the right level of model detail cannot be set either: every part of the warehouse could be modelled, and nothing says which parts matter.

### How to Use It

Write the question and its measures down before building anything. Name the measure as a statistic the model publishes, such as `tasks.pack_order.wait_mean`, and the value that decides the answer, such as 10 seconds. An experiment file can state the question and check the decision rule, as [Comparing Designs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/comparing-designs/index.md) does.

### What the Result Means

[Queues and Capacity](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/queues-and-capacity/index.md) answers the question: 3 packers. [Trusting Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/trusting-results/index.md) measures the mean wait of an order with 3 packers: 2.32 ± 0.20 seconds, the mean of 40 [replications](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#replications) with the half-width of its [95% interval](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#interval-and-half-width). Those runs use the measured packing times and a 2-minute [warm-up](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#one-run-starts-empty), and [other pages run the hour in other ways](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/first-simulation/#busy-hour-figures). The whole interval is far below 10 seconds, so the answer holds at this precision.

______________________________________________________________________

## Conceptual Model and Data

### In the Tutorial

The shop's **conceptual model** says what the model includes, the assumptions it makes and the data it needs:

- Orders arrive one at a time, at a rate that does not change during the hour.
- A packer takes the next order from one queue, in order, and packs it.
- Packing takes 1.5 seconds on average. The first model uses a constant 1.5 seconds, and [Choosing Inputs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/choosing-inputs/index.md) replaces it with the times measured at the bench.
- Pickers, stock and delivery are outside the model.

### Why It Matters

Law calls this the assumptions document. It is what the people who know the shop check, and what the model is checked against. It also decides how much detail goes in. Law warns against building one model element for each element of the real system: more detail costs run time, can miss the deadline and can hide the factors that matter.

Each input is an estimate until it is measured. For the shop these are the arrival rate and the packing time.

### How to Use It

Collect what is known about the system and write the document before writing code. Take the data from the real system where it exists, choose a distribution for each input, and test how much the choice matters. [Choosing Inputs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/choosing-inputs/index.md) compares the candidate distributions, and [Fitting the Inputs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/fit-the-inputs/index.md) fits them to measured times. Add detail only when it can change the decision. [Model Parts](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/index.md) lists the parts a model can have.

### What the Result Means

A model with an input nobody has measured is still usable, as long as the study tests how far the answer depends on it. [Parameter Sweeps](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/parameter-sweeps/index.md) does this for the arrival rate: with three packers the wait depends strongly on the rate, and with four it does not.

______________________________________________________________________

## AIC and the KS Test

### In the Tutorial

Fitting a distribution to measured times gives a candidate from each family, such as a gamma or a lognormal, and two scores say how well each candidate matches the data. For the shop's 40 packing times, [Fitting the Inputs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/fit-the-inputs/#fit-the-packing-times) gives the triangular an AIC of 56.68 and the gamma 56.79.

### Why It Matters

The two scores measure different things:

- **AIC**, Akaike's information criterion, scores how likely the data is under the fitted family, with a penalty for each parameter the fit chose: 2k − 2 × the log-likelihood, where k is the number of parameters. Lower is better.
- **KS**, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, is the largest gap between the share of the data below a value and the share the family puts below it. Its **p-value** is the chance of a gap at least that large if the data came from the family.

### How to Use It

`desflow fit` fits each family to a column of measured values and prints both scores, as Fitting the Inputs shows. Compare the AIC of two families on the same data: only the difference means anything. Use the KS p-value to rule a family out: a small p-value, such as below 0.05, is a reason to reject it.

### What the Result Means

By a common guideline, an AIC difference below 2 does not tell two fits apart, so the triangular and the gamma fit the shop's times equally well. When the family was fitted to the same data, the KS p-value is approximate and tends to be too high. A good score therefore does not settle the choice. Run the model with each close candidate and check whether the answer changes, as Fitting the Inputs does.

______________________________________________________________________

## Check the Assumptions

### In the Tutorial

Ask the shop manager whether arrivals really are steady in the busy hour, and whether a packer ever does anything else. If orders come in a rush at the start of the hour, the first assumption is wrong, and [Changing Demand](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/changing-demand/index.md) shows the model that follows.

### Why It Matters

Law calls this step a structured walk-through. It finds wrong assumptions before code depends on them. It also makes the results more credible to the people who will act on them, because they have checked what the model assumes.

### How to Use It

Walk the people who know the system through the assumptions document, one line at a time. Record each assumption they confirm, and change the document where they correct it. An experiment file keeps the agreed assumptions, the source of each input and the limits of the model, as [The Complete Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/complete-model/#build-the-report) does.

### What the Result Means

An assumption the owner of the system confirms can go into the model. One they correct sends the study back to the conceptual model, before any code is written.

______________________________________________________________________

## Build and Check the Model

### In the Tutorial

The shop's model is built in [First Simulation](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/first-simulation/index.md) and extended in the tutorials that follow it. [Checking a Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/checking-a-model/index.md) checks it: it traces fixed inputs, pushes the inputs to extremes, compares the model with queueing theory and with the real shop, and tests its sensitivity.

### Why It Matters

A model can run without errors and still be wrong. The checks are of two kinds, which [Checking and Validating](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/checking-and-validating/index.md) describes. **Verification** checks that the program does what the conceptual model says. **Validation** checks that the model is a good enough picture of the shop for the question.

### How to Use It

Verify by reading the trace, working a case by hand, and comparing the statistics with each other. `desflow explain --verify` compares the model with the queueing formulas where they apply. Validate by comparing the model's results with the real shop's where there is data, and by testing its sensitivity to the inputs. [Queueing Basics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/index.md) gives the formulas that check the queue.

### What the Result Means

A model that passes the checks is fit for the question it was checked against, not for every question. A failed check sends the study back to the conceptual model or to the code.

______________________________________________________________________

## Run the Experiments

### In the Tutorial

[Comparing Designs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/comparing-designs/index.md) compares three packers with four. Over 20 replications of each design with the same seeds, a fourth packer cuts the busy hour's mean wait by 2.21 ± 0.31 seconds (the mean difference and the half-width of its 95% interval).

### Why It Matters

An experiment is a set of runs designed to answer the question. One run of each design can show a difference that comes from the random numbers alone. Several replications, with the same seeds for each design, give an interval for the difference.

### How to Use It

Decide the run length, the warm-up and the number of replications, then run each design and compute an interval for each measure. [Output Analysis](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/index.md) explains these choices, and [Trusting Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/trusting-results/index.md) makes them for the shop. `desflow experiment` runs the designs and the checks from one file.

### What the Result Means

The interval for the difference, 2.21 ± 0.31 seconds, lies wholly above 0, so the fourth packer shortens the wait at this precision. Whether 2.21 seconds is worth a packer is the shop manager's decision, not the model's.

______________________________________________________________________

## Report the Result

### In the Tutorial

[The Complete Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/complete-model/index.md) ends with `report.md`. It states the comparisons and the checks, the observed comparison, the assumptions, where each input came from, and the limits of the model.

### Why It Matters

A reader who was not part of the study acts on the report alone. The report must let that reader judge how far to trust the answer, and repeat the study.

### How to Use It

State the answer to the question first, then the evidence for it. Say what the model includes and leaves out, what the inputs were and where they came from, how the model was checked, and how precise each result is. `desflow report` writes the report from an experiment's results. [Readiness and Reporting](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/readiness-and-reporting/index.md) lists what to include, and [Common Mistakes](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/common-mistakes/index.md) lists the errors that make a study wrong.

### What the Result Means

A study often repeats. A result that surprises is a reason to check the model again, and a changed question is a reason to change the model. The steps are an order of work, not a one-way path.

______________________________________________________________________

## Key Takeaways

- Write one question, its measures and the value that decides it, before building anything.
- Write the assumptions down, and have the people who know the system check them.
- Choose each input from data where it exists, and test how much the choice matters.
- Verify the program and validate the model before trusting a result.
- Answer the question with intervals from replications, and report the answer first, with its limits.

______________________________________________________________________

## Sources

- Law, "How to Conduct a Successful Simulation Study" (Winter Simulation Conference, 2003), which gives the seven-step approach. We read the paper in full.
- Wikipedia: the [Akaike information criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akaike_information_criterion) and the [Kolmogorov-Smirnov test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov%E2%80%93Smirnov_test).
- The wording and the shop example are our own.

# Checking and Validating

A model that runs is not a model that is right. This page explains how to check a model in two ways that need different evidence: **verification** asks whether the program does what the model on paper says, and **validation** asks whether that model is a good enough picture of the real system for the question. Both are done on the way through a [simulation study](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/a-simulation-study/index.md), and neither is finished by one test. [Checking a Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/checking-a-model/index.md) applies every check on this page to the shop. The page's own one-packer cases come from [checking_and_validating.py](https://github.com/jaehyeon-kim/desflow/blob/v0.27.0/docs/snippets/pages/checking_and_validating.py), which asserts each number.

______________________________________________________________________

## What You Will Learn

- the difference between verification and validation;
- how to read a trace and work a case by hand;
- which statistics must agree with each other, and which formulas a run must match;
- how to compare a model with the real system, and what to do when they disagree;
- how sensitivity analysis shows whether an estimate is good enough.

______________________________________________________________________

## Verification and Validation

### In the Tutorial

The model on paper says the shop's arrivals, packing times and number of packers. The program is the `SimulationContext`, the blueprint or the low-level code that runs them. The real shop is the packing area with its own records. Verification compares the program with the model on paper. Validation compares the program's results with the real shop.

### Why It Matters

Banks et al., as the [lecture notes](https://courses.ie.bilkent.edu.tr/ie324/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2016/09/Validation.pdf) give it, put the difference briefly: verification is building the model correctly, and validation is building the correct model. A model can pass one and fail the other. A program can follow the model on paper exactly, while the model leaves out the thing that makes the real shop slow. A model can also describe the shop well and have a fault in its code.

### How to Use It

Name each check by what it compares. The trace, a case worked by hand, the statistics against each other and a formula are verification. A comparison with the real shop and sensitivity analysis are validation. Law adds **credibility**: a model is credible when the people who will use its results accept them, and walking them through the assumptions earns it.

### What the Result Means

Checking a Model passes every verification check and finds one disagreement with the shop's observed values. Verification alone would have called the model ready. The study must explain the disagreement before it trusts the model for the decision.

______________________________________________________________________

## Read the Trace

### In the Tutorial

The records of a desflow run are a trace: the record of each event in time order. In [First Simulation](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/first-simulation/index.md), order 2 arrives at 2.696 seconds and joins the queue, and starts at 4.052 seconds, the instant order 1 is packed.

### Why It Matters

The [lecture notes](https://courses.ie.bilkent.edu.tr/ie324/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2016/09/Validation.pdf) on Banks et al. list three ways to find errors in a program: a trace, a look at whether the output is reasonable under a variety of input settings, and a check of the model by someone else. The trace is the cheapest of the three.

### How to Use It

Run a few orders and follow one by hand. It should arrive, wait while every packer is busy, start when a packer is free, and finish after its packing time. [Streaming Out](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/running-live/streaming-out/#find-one-orders-records) shows how to pick one order's records out of a long run.

### What the Result Means

An order that starts while every packer is busy, or finishes before its packing time, is a fault in the program. A trace that follows the rules shows only that the cases in it are right, so the next checks test the rest.

______________________________________________________________________

## Work a Case by Hand

### In the Tutorial

[Checking a Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/checking-a-model/#trace-fixed-inputs) runs three packers for 10 seconds, with an order every second and 4 seconds to pack each. Worked by hand, 4 orders finish, 5 are still in the shop, the mean wait is 5 ÷ 7 = 0.714 seconds, the packers are busy 80% of the time and the queue averages 0.8 orders. The run reports the same numbers.

### Why It Matters

Constant gaps and constant packing times make every number exact, so a difference is a fault, not chance. Cases at the extremes test the logic further: with demand above capacity, the queue must grow for as long as the run lasts, and a model that cannot show this has a fault.

### How to Use It

Replace every random input with a constant, run for a short time, and compare each statistic with the answer worked on paper:

```yaml
# Three packers; an order arrives every second and takes 4 seconds to pack
resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 3, max_cap: 10}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: constant, value: 1, spawn: pack_order}

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 4}
```

`desflow run checking_a_model.yaml` prints the 20 records of the run, which are its trace, then the statistics at 10 seconds.

```python
def fixed_shop() -> SimulationContext:
    """Three packers, an order every second and 4 seconds to pack each, for 10 s."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=3, max_cap=10)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="constant", value=1)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=4)
        .with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
    )
```

```python
# Three packers; an order arrives every second and takes 4 seconds to pack
FIXED = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=4)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=3, max_cap=10)},
)
```

Then run the extremes, where the answer is known without the model. Four cases with one packer and 1.5 seconds of packing, over an hour:

- One order every 3 seconds: orders arrive at 3, 6 and on to 3,597 seconds, so 1,199 arrive. Each is packed before the next arrives, so none waits, and the packer works 1,199 × 1.5 seconds of the 3,600, which is 49.96%.
- One order every second: the packer needs 1.5 seconds for each, so it never keeps up. 3,599 orders arrive, 2,399 finish, and 1,200 are in the shop at the end.
- One order every 10,000 seconds: no order arrives in the hour, so none starts and none finishes.
- One order a second with 100 packers: a packer is always free, so no order waits.

### What the Result Means

A run that matches every case worked by hand has the logic of the model on paper. Checking a Model also runs the busy hour at its extremes over 20 replications: one packer finishes 2,318 orders on average against the most possible, 2,320, and ten packers are busy 27.08% of the time against 27% by hand. A difference in any of these cases must be found before any experiment.

______________________________________________________________________

## Check the Statistics Against Each Other

### In the Tutorial

[Measuring a Run](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/measuring-a-run/index.md) reports the queue length, the arrival count and the mean wait of the busy hour separately. By [Little's law](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/#littles-law) they must agree: 2.406 orders in the queue on average, against 1.736 orders a second × 1.3817 seconds = 2.399.

### Why It Matters

Some relations hold for every model that settles, so they test the statistics without any hand calculation. A run measures each statistic separately, so if they disagree, one of them is wrong.

### How to Use It

Compare the average queue with the arrival rate times the mean wait, as [Queueing Basics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/#littles-law) shows in each form of the model. Check that the counts in [Statistics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/statistics/index.md) add up: when no order balks or reneges, the orders started over the whole run are those finished plus those still in the shop. In Measuring a Run, 6,261 started, 6,250 finished and 11 are still in the shop.

### What the Result Means

Agreement shows the statistics are consistent with each other. It does not show the model is right for the shop: a model with the wrong packing times would agree just as well. Little's law is also weaker for a queue that never settles. Checking a Model finds it roughly holds with one packer, but that queue's mean depends on how long the run lasts.

______________________________________________________________________

## Check Against a Formula

### In the Tutorial

Checking a Model runs `desflow explain --verify` on the busy hour of Trusting Results, ten times. The utilisation of 0.9 and the throughput of 1.8 orders a second agree with the runs: 0.9034 and 1.807. The wait has no formula for three packers with measured packing times, so it is not compared.

### Why It Matters

For a simple case there is a formula. One packer with exponential gaps and service times at [utilisation](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/#utilisation) 0.75 has a mean wait of 4.5 seconds when the service time averages 1.5 seconds. A run of the model, repeated with several seeds, must produce an interval that contains it. A formula tests the part of the model it covers. It cannot test priorities, breakdowns or changing demand, which is why those are the parts to check by hand and against the real shop.

### How to Use It

`desflow explain` applies the formulas to a model without running it. It gives each resource's utilisation, and the mean wait where a formula applies. `desflow explain --verify` then runs the model and compares what the runs measure with those values. Where the formulas do not hold, it gives no value, makes no comparison and says why. [Queueing Basics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/#check-a-formula-against-the-shop) shows the command in each form, and [Check Against Theory](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/analysis/check-against-theory/#when-the-formulas-do-not-apply) states the rule and how to read a difference.

### What the Result Means

This is verification, not validation. It checks that the program agrees with the queueing formulas, and that the model's rates, units and service times are consistent with each other. It does not show that the model is close enough to the real shop.

______________________________________________________________________

## Compare With the Real Shop

### In the Tutorial

Checking a Model compares the model with values observed in the shop over 58 minutes of a busy hour: a mean wait of 2.6 seconds and a utilisation of 91%. The values are illustrative. The wait lies inside the model's 95% interval over 20 replications, 2.16 to 2.80 seconds. The utilisation lies outside its interval, 89.70% to 90.96%.

### Why It Matters

Validation needs evidence from the real system. Law suggests comparing the model's results with the existing system's where there is one, along with a walk-through of the assumptions by the people who know the system, and sensitivity analysis. The [lecture notes](https://courses.ie.bilkent.edu.tr/ie324/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2016/09/Validation.pdf) on Banks et al. describe calibration as a loop: compare the model with the real system, adjust it, compare again. They also give three steps:

1. Build a model with high face validity: one that looks right to the people who know the system.
1. Validate the model's assumptions.
1. Compare input-output behaviour with the real system's data.

### How to Use It

Give the model the inputs of a real period and compare its measures with what happened. An experiment places each observed value beside the model's interval, as [Experiment Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/experiment-results/#compare-with-observed-values) describes. Check the inputs as well as the outputs: [Choosing Inputs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/choosing-inputs/index.md) and [Fitting the Inputs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/fit-the-inputs/index.md) cover the inputs, and [Local Replay](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/local-replay/index.md) runs a model on the arrivals of a real trace.

### What the Result Means

The results need to agree closely enough for the decision, not exactly. A value outside its interval is a disagreement that the study must explain before it trusts the model. The interval covers only the model's spread from run to run, not the error in the shop's own measurement. When the real system does not exist yet, as for a proposed design, there is nothing to compare with, and validity rests on the assumptions and on sensitivity analysis.

______________________________________________________________________

## Test the Sensitivity

### In the Tutorial

[Parameter Sweeps](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/parameter-sweeps/index.md) changes the shop's arrival rate around its estimate of 1.8 orders a second. With three packers, a rate 6% above the estimate more than doubles the mean wait, from 2.48 to 5.55 seconds, each the [mean of 20 replications after a 2-minute warm-up](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/first-simulation/#busy-hour-figures). With four packers, the mean wait is at most 0.35 seconds at every rate in the sweep.

### Why It Matters

A model has inputs that are estimates. **Sensitivity analysis** changes them and sees whether the answer changes. It shows which estimates the decision depends on, and so which ones need more data.

### How to Use It

Sweep each uncertain input over the range it could take, and run every design at each value with the same seeds. `desflow experiment` runs a sweep from one file, as Parameter Sweeps shows.

### What the Result Means

If a 6% change in the arrival rate changes the decision, the estimate needs more work. If the decision stays the same, the estimate is good enough. For the shop the choice of four packers holds for any demand in the range, while the three-packer wait cannot be predicted well without a better estimate of the rate.

______________________________________________________________________

## Key Takeaways

- Verification checks that the program does what the model on paper says. Validation checks that the model is close enough to the real system for the decision.
- Check as you build: after each part is added, run a case with a known answer.
- Before the experiments, check the statistics against each other and against a formula where one exists.
- Before the results are used, compare with the real system, or say that no comparison was possible.
- Write the checks as tests, as Checking a Model does, so they run again after every change. [Readiness and Reporting](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/readiness-and-reporting/index.md) lists what a model needs before its results are trusted, and [Common Mistakes](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/common-mistakes/index.md) lists the errors these checks find.

______________________________________________________________________

## Sources

- Banks et al., *Discrete-Event System Simulation*, chapter 10, read through [lecture notes on it](https://courses.ie.bilkent.edu.tr/ie324/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2016/09/Validation.pdf): verification and validation, the trace, the reasonableness checks, review by someone else, calibration and the three-step approach.
- Law, "How to Conduct a Successful Simulation Study" (Winter Simulation Conference, 2003), read through [the paper](https://www.informs-sim.org/wsc03papers/009.pdf): credibility and the comparison with the existing system.
- The checks with Little's law, with a formula and with fixed gaps, the extreme-condition tests, the explanations and the shop examples are our own.

# Output Analysis

A simulation run gives numbers, and a number from one run is a sample, not the answer. Output analysis is the work of turning runs into an answer with a stated precision. This page explains the ideas with the busy hour of the shop. [Trusting Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/trusting-results/index.md) and [Comparing Designs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/comparing-designs/index.md) apply them and show the commands.

______________________________________________________________________

## What You Will Learn

- whether a question is terminating or steady state, and what each needs;
- why a run's empty start biases its mean, and how to choose a warm-up;
- why one run is not enough, and what replications give;
- how a 95% interval and its half-width are built;
- how many replications a study needs;
- which orders a reading covers;
- why designs are compared with the same random numbers.

______________________________________________________________________

## Terminating or Steady State

### In the Tutorial

[End Conditions](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/end-conditions/index.md) treats the shop as terminating: orders stop at 3,600 seconds, and the question is what happens to the work still in the shop. The busy hour of [Trusting Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/trusting-results/index.md) is treated as steady state, because the question is what the shop's waits usually are.

### Why It Matters

A **terminating** run ends at a time or an event the system has by nature, and starts from conditions the system really has. A shop that opens empty and closes at the end of the day is terminating: the day's answer is the answer. A **steady-state** study asks how a system behaves in the long run, after the effect of its starting conditions has gone. The two need different handling of the start of the run and of its length.

### How to Use It

Decide which question the study asks, before choosing a run length:

- **Terminating:** the start is part of the answer. Run the real opening state, run to the real closing event, and use replications to measure the spread.
- **Steady state:** the start is a distortion. Leave out a warm-up, and run long enough that the rest represents the long run.

### What the Result Means

The same model can be either, because the choice depends on the question and on the system, not on the model. A terminating result describes the period with its start. A steady-state result describes the shop once it has settled, and says nothing about its first minutes.

______________________________________________________________________

## One Run Starts Empty

### In the Tutorial

Trusting Results plots the busy hour from its start. The mean wait so far climbs from 0.46 seconds to about 1.5 seconds in the first two minutes, because the first orders found free packers. After that it moves up and down with no trend.

### Why It Matters

The first orders of a run find every packer free, so their waits are shorter than the waits of the hour as a whole. The mean wait of a run is therefore biased low by its start. When the question is the long run, as for the busy hour, this distortion is called **initialisation bias**. A **warm-up** is a time at the start of a run whose observations are left out.

### How to Use It

Choose the warm-up from evidence, not from habit, in two steps:

1. Plot a running statistic from the start of the run, such as the queue length or the mean wait so far, and note when it stops climbing. Law's paper shows a plot made with Welch's method for this, in which the warm-up is the time after which the average has levelled off, and advises choosing it conservatively.
1. Compare a few candidate warm-ups. Run the same replications after each, and check whether a longer warm-up moves the mean by more than its [half-width](#interval-and-half-width). A candidate passes when it does not.

Then keep the shortest candidate that passes the comparison and covers the climb in the plot. Set it on the run:

```yaml
# Records and statistics start after the first 2 minutes; 0 keeps everything
warmup: ${WARMUP:-2 min}
```

```python
# Records and statistics start after the first 2 minutes; None keeps everything
SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42, warmup=warmup)
```

```python
# Records and statistics start after the first 2 minutes; None keeps everything
WARMUP = 120.0  # seconds, passed to setup_egress in run below
```

In the low-level API the warm-up is an argument of `env.setup_egress`, because the sinks are what leave the records out, as [Trusting Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/trusting-results/#plot-the-start) shows.

The warm-up resets every statistic once at that time, as [Run Length](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/run-length/index.md) and [Statistics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/statistics/index.md) describe.

### What the Result Means

[Trusting Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/trusting-results/#compare-warm-ups) compares warm-ups of 1, 2 and 4 minutes over five seeds. The longer ones move the mean by 0.011 and 0.036 seconds, far less than the half-width of 0.47 seconds, so all pass, and 2 minutes covers the climb. In the run with the seed 42, the warm-up changes the mean wait only from 1.382 to 1.381 seconds: an hour is long enough that its first minutes hardly count. A shorter run, or one that starts far from the usual state, needs the warm-up much more. A warm-up is not a fix for a model that never settles: if [utilisation](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/#utilisation) is 1 or more, there is no steady state for a warm-up to find.

______________________________________________________________________

## Replications

### In the Tutorial

In the busy hour, with the measured packing times and a 2-minute warm-up, 40 replications give a mean wait of 2.32 ± 0.20 seconds: the mean of the 40 values, with the half-width of its 95% interval. The mean waits of the 40 replications range from 1.45 to 4.39 seconds. The [one run with the seed 42](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/first-simulation/#busy-hour-figures) measured 1.38 seconds, lower than any of them.

### Why It Matters

The waits of orders in one run follow each other: after a busy period, many orders in a row wait long. They are not independent samples, so the usual formula for the spread of an average, which assumes independent samples, gives an interval that is too narrow. Law lists this as a pitfall, along with treating one run as the truth.

### How to Use It

A **replication** is a run of the same model with its own random stream. It gives one independent value of each statistic. Run several, and take the mean of their values as the estimate:

```bash
# 40 runs: the mean wait and the packers' utilisation, each with its interval
desflow run trusting_results.yaml --replications 40 --measure tasks.pack_order.wait_mean --measure resources.packers.utilization_avg
```

```python
MEASURES = ["tasks.pack_order.wait_mean", "resources.packers.utilization_avg"]


def replications(n=40):
    """Runs the busy hour n times, each after the warm-up, with seeds spawned from 42."""
    return replicate(shop, n, seed=42, until="1 h", measures=MEASURES)
```

```python
MEASURES = ["tasks.pack_order.wait_mean", "resources.packers.utilization_avg"]


def model(env, sampler):
    """The busy hour in a given environment: replicate sets the statistics."""
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers))


def replications(n=40):
    """Runs the busy hour n times, each after the warm-up, with seeds spawned from 42."""
    shop = LowLevelModel(model, sim_id="Shop")
    return replicate(shop, n, seed=42, until=3600, warmup=WARMUP, measures=MEASURES)
```

`LowLevelModel` names the function that builds the model in an environment it is given, and the warm-up is an argument of `replicate`, because a replication has no sinks.

[Replications](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/replications/index.md) describes every option. The seeds are spawned from one seed, so the set repeats exactly. [Randomness and Seeds](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/randomness-and-seeds/index.md) explains the streams.

### What the Result Means

One run would have given a confident and wrong answer: 1.38 seconds, against 2.32 ± 0.20 over 40 replications. The [interval](#interval-and-half-width) says how precise the estimate is.

______________________________________________________________________

## Interval and Half-width

### In the Tutorial

Over 40 replications of the busy hour, the mean wait is 2.32 ± 0.20 seconds. The interval runs from 2.12 to 2.52 seconds, and 0.20 seconds is its **half-width**.

### Why It Matters

A **95% interval**, in full a 95% confidence interval, is the mean of n replications plus or minus a half-width of t × s ÷ √n, where:

- s is the standard deviation of the n values.
- s ÷ √n is the **standard error**, an estimate of how far the mean itself varies from one set of replications to the next.
- t is the **Student t quantile** for n − 1 degrees of freedom, one less than the number of replications. t is about 2.1 for 20 replications and 2.0 for 40, and larger for fewer, because s is then a rougher estimate.

### How to Use It

Every replication command prints the mean and the half-width of each measure. `--level` changes the confidence level: `--level 0.9` on the command line, or `level=0.9` in `replicate`. Choose the level before the runs, with the precision the decision needs.

### What the Result Means

Over many studies, about 95% of the intervals built this way contain the true mean. A 90% interval from the same 40 runs is narrower, ± 0.16 seconds, but misses the true mean more often: 1 study in 10 instead of 1 in 20.

______________________________________________________________________

## How Many Replications

### In the Tutorial

Trusting Results asks for a half-width within 10% of the mean. Utilisation meets it with 5 replications. The mean wait first meets it at 40: its half-width is 21.2% of the mean after 5 replications, 11.0% after 10, 13.0% after 20 and 8.4% after 40.

### Why It Matters

There is no fixed number that is enough, such as 30. Waits vary far more from run to run than how busy the packers are, so each output needs its own number of replications, and the study needs enough for the least precise output the decision uses.

### How to Use It

Decide the precision each output needs, then run until the least precise output has it. The half-width shrinks with √n, so a half-width k times smaller needs about k² times as many replications. A first set of a few replications suggests how many are needed: 10 replications gave 11.0%, so 10% needs about 10 × (11.0 ÷ 10)² ≈ 12.

### What the Result Means

That estimate is a guide, not a promise: 20 replications gave 13.0%, because the half-width of the first set is itself an estimate. Add replications, then read the half-width again. A longer run is the other way to gain precision. It reduces the effect of the start, but its mean is still one sample.

______________________________________________________________________

## Which Orders a Reading Covers

### In the Tutorial

In [End Conditions](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/end-conditions/index.md), the fixed horizon ends at 3,600 seconds with 2,436 orders started, 2,398 finished and 38 in the shop. With a drain, the run ends at 3,656.4 seconds with all 2,436 finished.

### Why It Matters

A mean is over some orders, and two runs of the same hour can cover different orders. At a fixed horizon, some orders have started and not finished, and the mean wait covers those that started. With a drain, every order admitted finishes, at the cost of running past the hour.

### How to Use It

Report the counts beside the means. The warm-up adds a third group: orders that were in the shop when the warm-up ended. An order that started before the warm-up ended and finished after it counts as finished, and its whole wait counts in the wait and service times. It does not count as started. [Statistics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/statistics/index.md) has the table of which orders each count covers.

### What the Result Means

Two means over different groups of orders are not comparable. A reader needs the counts to tell whether a difference between two results comes from the shop or from which orders each reading covers.

______________________________________________________________________

## Comparing Designs

### In the Tutorial

[Comparing Designs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/comparing-designs/index.md) runs three packers and four with the same 20 seeds. A fourth packer cuts the busy hour's mean wait by 2.21 ± 0.31 seconds.

### Why It Matters

Run each design with the same seeds, so that each pair of runs meets the same arrivals and the same service times, and take the difference seed by seed. This is a **paired comparison**, and the shared random numbers are called **common random numbers**. The random variation that the two runs of a pair share cancels in their difference. The interval of the differences is therefore narrower than the interval an unpaired comparison of the same runs gives. Law names comparing designs without a sound statistical approach as a pitfall.

### How to Use It

An experiment pairs its designs by seed and reports the difference with its interval, as Comparing Designs shows. The check below shows the effect on 40 runs of the busy hour with 3 packers, 20 packing in 1.5 seconds and 20 packing in 1.45 seconds, with the same 20 seeds. It builds two intervals for the difference of the mean waits from the same runs: one paired by seed, and one that treats the designs as independent.

```bash
desflow experiment comparing_designs_experiment.yaml
```

The experiment runs every design with the same seeds and reports each difference paired by seed. It does not build the unpaired interval, which the Builder tab computes for the comparison.

```python
def waits(service: float, n: int = 20) -> list[float]:
    """The mean wait of each replication; the same seed gives the same seeds to every design."""
    runs = replicate(lambda: shop(service), n, seed=42, until=3600, measures=[WAIT])
    return runs.values[WAIT]


def paired_and_unpaired(slow: list[float], fast: list[float]):
    """Half-widths of the difference of the means: paired by seed, and as if independent."""
    n = len(slow)
    paired = interval([a - b for a, b in zip(slow, fast)])
    # Welch's interval: the two designs' variances add, and the degrees of freedom shrink
    va, vb = statistics.variance(slow) / n, statistics.variance(fast) / n
    df = (va + vb) ** 2 / (va**2 / (n - 1) + vb**2 / (n - 1))
    unpaired = t_quantile(0.975, df) * math.sqrt(va + vb)
    return paired, unpaired
```

`replicate` takes a `LowLevelModel` in place of the builder function, as the Replications section above shows. The two functions then work on its values unchanged.

### What the Result Means

With the seeds spawned from 42, the mean wait of the 20 runs packing in 1.5 seconds is 0.69 seconds longer than that of the 20 runs packing in 1.45 seconds. The paired interval is ± 0.12 seconds and the unpaired one is ± 0.29 seconds, so pairing more than halves the interval here. [Common Mistakes](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/common-mistakes/#comparing-designs-with-one-run-each) runs the same two designs with other seeds and without pairing, so its means differ from these.

Pairing helps only when the designs use the random numbers in the same way. desflow gives each distribution a stream of its own, so adding a step to one design does not shift the numbers the shared steps draw. The comparison report lists any stream that only one design used, because draws from such a stream are not paired. Check that list before trusting a paired interval.

______________________________________________________________________

## Key Takeaways

- Decide first whether the question is terminating or steady state.
- For a steady-state question, choose the warm-up from a plot and a comparison of candidates, and report the evidence.
- Answer with replications, not one run, and give each output as a mean with its half-width.
- Choose the precision each output needs, and run until the least precise output has it.
- Say which orders each count covers.
- Compare designs with the same seeds, and check the list of unpaired streams. [Readiness and Reporting](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/readiness-and-reporting/index.md) lists what a report must contain.

______________________________________________________________________

## Sources

- Banks et al., *Discrete-Event System Simulation*, chapter 11, on output analysis for a single model, read through [lecture notes on it](https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/ece541/fa2016/OutputAnalysis.pdf). The notes give the interval across replications the same form as the one above.
- Law, "Twenty-Three Critical Pitfalls in Simulation Modeling and How to Avoid Them" (Winter Simulation Conference, 2024), read through [its published text](https://informs-sim.org/wsc24papers/inv198.pdf): the output-analysis pitfalls and Welch's method.
- The explanations are our own.

# Readiness and Reporting

A model is ready when someone who was not part of the study can see what it answers, how far to trust the answer, and how to repeat it. This page explains what that takes, with the shop's study in [The Complete Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/complete-model/index.md) as the example. It points to three published checklists written for simulation studies, and shows which parts desflow does for you and which parts only you can write.

______________________________________________________________________

## What You Will Learn

- why readiness is a statement about a decision, not about a model;
- what the three levels of the Model Readiness Checklist ask for;
- what a report needs, by the STRESS-DES checklist;
- what to share so that others can run the model, by the STARS framework;
- which items desflow records for you, and which only you can write.

______________________________________________________________________

## Ready for What

### In the Tutorial

The shop model is ready to say how many packers the busy hour needs: its inputs came from data, its checks passed, its results carry an interval, and a reader can repeat the runs. It is not ready to say anything about a holiday week, whatever its code looks like.

### Why It Matters

A model is built and checked for one question. The checks of [Checking and Validating](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/checking-and-validating/index.md) show it fits that question, with the inputs and the range of conditions it was checked under. Outside them, nothing has been checked.

### How to Use It

Write down the question the model is ready for, as [A Simulation Study](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/a-simulation-study/#ask-one-question) does, and state the limits of its use. An experiment file keeps them with the runs: The Complete Model lists "One busy hour only; the rest of the day is not modelled" among its limits, and `report.md` prints them.

### What the Result Means

A reader who wants to use the model for another question can see at once that it was not built for it. That question needs its own checks before the model answers it.

______________________________________________________________________

## Model Readiness Checklist

### In the Tutorial

The shop's study meets most of the first level below. Its replications and warm-up come from [Trusting Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/trusting-results/index.md), its seeds are fixed, its core logic is checked in [Checking a Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/checking-a-model/index.md), and it is compared with values observed in the shop. The review of the process with the people who know it is the walk-through of [Check the Assumptions](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/a-simulation-study/#check-the-assumptions), which no tool does.

### Why It Matters

The open book [HSMA: the little book of DES](https://des.hsma.co.uk/) has a chapter, [Model Readiness Checklist](https://des.hsma.co.uk/model_checklist.html), that sorts what a model needs into three levels, by the size of the decision:

- **Bronze** is the level for small to medium decisions within one organisation. It asks for views of the model running, checks of the core logic, enough [replications](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#replications) and a [warm-up](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#one-run-starts-empty), a fixed seed, a comparison with the real system, a review of the process with the people who know it, and documentation.
- **Silver** is the level for larger or costlier decisions, or for models used across several areas. It adds a formal reporting checklist such as STRESS-DES, documented code, a code review, automated tests, an open licence, version control and a sensitivity analysis.
- **Gold** is the level for models that will be reused, adapted or published. It adds:
  - a documentation site and a changelog;
  - identifiers for the authors and an archive of the code;
  - an online environment to run the model in, parallel runs, a web app and an animation;
  - formal methods for the warm-up and the number of replications;
  - tests against historical data.

### How to Use It

Choose the level from the decision, then go through its items. Some items cost nothing in desflow, and some need you:

| Item                                  | In desflow                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A fixed seed and independent streams  | `random_seed` fixes a run, and `replicate` makes one integer seed for each replication from one seed and records them, so the same call gives the same results and any replication can be repeated alone. See [Replications](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/replications/index.md) |
| Enough replications, with an interval | `replicate` gives the mean and the [half-width of the 95% interval](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#interval-and-half-width). [How many](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#how-many-replications) is your decision                    |
| The designs and the inputs on record  | An experiment records the compiled parameters of each design and writes its summary, its comparisons, its checks and a `report.md`. See [Experiments](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/experiments/index.md)                                                                         |
| A comparison with the real system     | An experiment can read an observed file and compare it with the model. See [Experiment Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/experiment-results/index.md). Which data to use is your decision                                                                                    |
| A view of the model running           | Every event and reading is a record, which you can read or send to a sink. See [Egress, Batching and Delivery](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/egress/index.md)                                                                                                    |
| Core logic checked                    | Yours: [Checking and Validating](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/checking-and-validating/index.md) shows the cases to work by hand                                                                                                                                                      |
| Assumptions, data sources and limits  | Yours: they go in the experiment file and the report, and no tool decides them                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

### What the Result Means

A level is met when every item of it is done, not most. An item left out goes into the report as a limit, so that the reader knows which check the model has not had.

______________________________________________________________________

## Reporting a Study

### In the Tutorial

The Complete Model's `report.md` gives the question, the model and its versions, the assumptions, each input with its fitted parameters and where it came from, the run settings, the counts, the results, the comparisons, the checks and the observed comparison, then the limits and any input with no source. Its Comparisons section answers the question with each difference and its interval: a fourth packer cuts the packing wait by 1.77 seconds, with a half-width of 0.16 seconds.

### Why It Matters

A reader acts on the report alone. The reporting checklist STRESS-DES lists what that reader will ask. It has 20 items in six groups: objectives, logic, data, experimentation, implementation and code access. It is by Monks, Currie, Onggo, Robinson, Kunc and Taylor, and the book gives it in its chapter [STRESS-DES Reporting](https://des.hsma.co.uk/stress_des.html).

### How to Use It

Answer each group in one short paragraph of the report, in this order, after the answer and its interval:

- **Objectives:** the question and the measures, as in [Ask One Question](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/a-simulation-study/#ask-one-question).
- **Logic:** the conceptual model, with its assumptions and what it leaves out.
- **Data:** where each input came from, and how it was fitted or chosen.
- **Experimentation:** the run length, the warm-up, the number of replications and the designs compared.
- **Implementation:** the software and its version, and the random number streams.
- **Code access:** where the code, the data and the seeds are kept.

### What the Result Means

`report.md` answers the objectives, the data and the experimentation from the experiment file, and gives the software versions. The logic beyond the listed assumptions, how the model was checked, and where the code is kept are yours to add. [Common Mistakes](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/common-mistakes/index.md) lists what to look for before you send the report.

______________________________________________________________________

## Sharing the Model

### In the Tutorial

Each tutorial page ends with Full Files: every file its runs need, so a reader can repeat them. desflow itself is under the MIT licence and installs from PyPI with a stated version.

### Why It Matters

The framework STARS, by Monks, Harper and Mustafee, says what to share so that others can run and reuse a model. The book gives it in [The STARS Framework](https://des.hsma.co.uk/stars.html). A model that only its author can run cannot be checked by anyone else.

### How to Use It

STARS separates essential parts from optional ones:

- **Essential:** an open licence; a list of the software the model needs, with its versions; free and open software; a minimum of documentation; an identifier for each author; a citation file; a code repository; and an archive that gives the code a permanent identifier.
- **Optional:** fuller documentation, a hosted documentation site, an online environment to run the model in, an interface, and a hosted web app.

Keep the blueprint or the Python files, the experiment file and the observed data in one repository, with the desflow version they ran on.

### What the Result Means

A model shared with its essential parts can be run again by a reader, with the same seeds and the same results. That is the strongest evidence a report can give.

______________________________________________________________________

## Key Takeaways

- Ready is a statement about one decision: write down the question and the limits of the model's use.
- Choose the readiness level from the size of the decision, and meet every item of it.
- desflow records the seeds, the intervals, the designs, the inputs and the comparisons. The assumptions, the checks and the limits are yours to write.
- Report the answer first, with its interval, then the six groups of STRESS-DES.
- Share the model with an open licence, its software versions and its files.

______________________________________________________________________

## Sources

- The open book [HSMA: the little book of DES](https://des.hsma.co.uk/), its chapters [Model Readiness Checklist](https://des.hsma.co.uk/model_checklist.html), [STRESS-DES Reporting](https://des.hsma.co.uk/stress_des.html) and [The STARS Framework](https://des.hsma.co.uk/stars.html). The chapters are under the CC BY-NC-SA licence, so none of their text is copied here. We read the three and link them, and the lists above are our own summaries.
- Monks, Currie, Onggo, Robinson, Kunc and Taylor, "Strengthening the reporting of empirical simulation studies: Introducing the STRESS guidelines" ([Journal of Simulation, 2019](https://doi.org/10.1080/17477778.2018.1442155)).
- Monks, Harper and Mustafee, "Towards sharing tools and artefacts for reusable simulations in healthcare" ([Journal of Simulation, 2024](https://doi.org/10.1080/17477778.2024.2347882)).

# Common Mistakes

Most wrong simulation results come from a short list of mistakes, and most of them are made before the first run. This page explains eight, in the order they happen in a study. Each one shows what the mistake does to the packing shop, why, how to avoid it, and what the result looks like once it is avoided. The checks behind the figures are in [common_mistakes.py](https://github.com/jaehyeon-kim/desflow/blob/v0.27.0/docs/snippets/pages/common_mistakes.py), which runs each one with the builder and asserts each number the page quotes.

______________________________________________________________________

## What You Will Learn

- why a study needs one question, and a model only the detail that question needs;
- what replacing an input by its mean, or choosing a distribution by habit, does to the waits;
- why one run, or one run of each design, is not an answer;
- why a steady-state question needs a warm-up;
- why the orders of one run cannot give an interval.

______________________________________________________________________

## No Clear Question

### In the Tutorial

A shop model built to "see what happens" could include the pickers, the stock, the couriers and the breaks. Nothing says which of them matter, so nothing says when the model is finished.

### Why It Matters

A model with no question grows, and its results cannot be judged, because there is no measure to judge them by.

### How to Use It

Write one question before you write the model, with the measure that answers it, such as "how many packers keep the mean wait of the busy hour under 10 seconds?". [A Simulation Study](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/a-simulation-study/#ask-one-question) shows how to write it.

### What the Result Means

With the question written, each part of the model can be judged by whether it changes the answer. The shop's question needs the packers and the orders, and not the couriers.

______________________________________________________________________

## Copying the Real System in Full

### In the Tutorial

The busy-hour question depends on the arrivals, the packing times and the number of packers. The pickers, the stock and delivery are outside the shop's first model, and [A Flow of Tasks](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/shop-logic/flow-of-tasks/index.md) adds picking only when a question needs it.

### Why It Matters

A model with every detail of the real shop takes long to build, is hard to check, and needs data for each detail that nobody collected. More detail can also hide the factors that matter.

### How to Use It

Ask of each part: would the answer change if it were different? If not, leave it out. [A Simulation Study](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/a-simulation-study/#conceptual-model-and-data) writes this down as the conceptual model, and lets the question decide how much detail goes in.

### What the Result Means

A small model that answers the question is easier to check and to explain. A part added later, when a new question needs it, is checked on its own.

______________________________________________________________________

## Replacing a Distribution by Its Mean

### In the Tutorial
