Packing takes 1.5 seconds on average and an order arrives every 2.0 seconds on average, so it is tempting to put those two numbers in as constants. With one packer, constant gaps and constant packing times, the mean wait over 10 [replications](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#replications) is 0.00 seconds. With exponential gaps of the same mean and the same packing time, it is 2.45 seconds over the same 10 replications.

### Why It Matters

Real orders do not come at even gaps, and that variation is what makes a queue. With constant inputs, each order arrives after the last one is packed, so no order ever waits. [Kingman's formula](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/#variation-lengthens-waits) shows the same: with no variation in the gaps or the packing times, the wait is zero.

### How to Use It

Use the distribution you measured, not its mean. [Choosing Inputs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/choosing-inputs/index.md) compares candidate distributions for the packing time, and [Fitting the Inputs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/fit-the-inputs/index.md) fits them to measured times.

### What the Result Means

A model whose waits are near zero while utilisation is high has probably lost its variation. In Choosing Inputs, the same mean packing time gives a mean wait from 1.27 seconds with constant times to 2.37 seconds with exponential ones.

______________________________________________________________________

## Choosing a Normal or Uniform by Habit

### In the Tutorial

A normal distribution with a mean of 1.5 seconds and a standard deviation of 1.0 is a tempting packing time. About 6.7% of 100,000 draws from it are below zero.

### Why It Matters

A time cannot be negative. The model would have to clip the negative draws, which changes the mean, or fail. A uniform distribution has the opposite problem: it gives every value between its ends the same weight, which real times seldom have.

### How to Use It

Fit a distribution to the data, and let a goodness-of-fit check and a plot say which family it is. [Input Fitting](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/input-fitting/index.md) does this, and [Fitting the Inputs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/fit-the-inputs/index.md) works an example. [A Simulation Study](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/a-simulation-study/#aic-and-the-ks-test) explains the scores.

### What the Result Means

With no data, a triangular distribution of the least, most likely and greatest values is a usual stand-in. Law's pitfall 18 warns against using one when data could be collected, because the greatest value is hard to choose and the long right tail of real times matters. Collect the data if you can.

______________________________________________________________________

## Taking One Run as the Answer

### In the Tutorial

Run the busy hour with three packers 10 times with different seeds. The mean wait of a run ranges from 1.52 seconds, 28% below the mean, to 2.75 seconds, 30% above it, and the mean of the 10 is 2.11 seconds.

### Why It Matters

One run is one sample. A report that gave one run alone could be that far off, and it would carry no sign of how far.

### How to Use It

Run replications and report the mean with an interval. [Output Analysis](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#replications) explains replications and how many to use, and [Trusting Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/trusting-results/index.md) runs them for the shop.

### What the Result Means

The pages of this site give several figures for the busy hour's mean wait, because each runs it in a different way. [Busy Hour Figures](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/first-simulation/#busy-hour-figures) lists each figure and how it was run.

______________________________________________________________________

## No Warm-up for a Steady State

### In the Tutorial

Take one packer and an order about every 1.58 seconds on average. With 1.5 seconds of packing, the packer is busy 1.5 ÷ 1.58 = 95% of the time. Forty runs of 30 minutes from an empty shop give a mean wait of 11.4 ± 2.1 seconds. The formula for the long-run wait of this shop (M/D/1) gives 14.25 seconds, above the whole interval.

### Why It Matters

A run starts with an empty shop, so the first orders find no queue, and the mean of a short run is biased low. The effect is largest when the shop is nearly full, because the queue then takes longest to reach its usual length.

### How to Use It

For a steady-state question, leave out a warm-up and run long enough. [Output Analysis](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#one-run-starts-empty) explains how to choose the warm-up, and shows the setting in each form of the model.

### What the Result Means

Forty runs of 20,000 seconds that each leave out their first 4,000 seconds give 14.2 ± 1.3 seconds. The interval now contains 14.25 seconds, so the bias is gone. Terminating questions do not need a warm-up, because the empty start is part of the question.

______________________________________________________________________

## Comparing Designs With One Run Each

### In the Tutorial

Packing in 1.45 seconds instead of 1.5 is a real improvement. Over 20 runs of each, with seeds spawned from 1 for the slower design and from 2 for the faster one, the mean wait is 1.99 seconds for the slower design and 1.51 seconds for the faster. Match the runs in order, first with first: in 4 of the 20 matches, the slower design's run had a mean wait at or below the faster design's run.

### Why It Matters

In those 4 matches, one run of each design would have said the change did not help. The difference between two single runs is mostly the difference between their random numbers.

### How to Use It

Compare designs with the same number of replications each and an interval on the difference. Use [common random numbers](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#comparing-designs) to reduce the random variation in the difference. [Comparing Designs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/comparing-designs/index.md) does this on the shop.

### What the Result Means

These runs are not paired, so they are not the runs of the paired comparison in Output Analysis, which runs both designs with the seeds spawned from 42. With pairing, the interval of the difference there is ± 0.12 seconds against ± 0.29 seconds without it.

______________________________________________________________________

## Treating One Run's Statistics as Independent

### In the Tutorial

In the busy hour, an order that waits long is usually followed by another that waits long, because the second waited in the same queue, behind the first.

### Why It Matters

The mean wait of one run is a mean of values that depend on each other. The usual interval formula assumes independent values, so an interval built from the orders of one run is too narrow.

### How to Use It

Build the interval from the replications, each of which is independent of the others. [Output Analysis](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#interval-and-half-width) shows how.

### What the Result Means

An interval from replications says how far the mean may be from the true one. An interval from one run's orders claims a precision the run does not have. [Checking and Validating](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/checking-and-validating/index.md) lists the checks that catch the other mistakes before a result is reported.

______________________________________________________________________

## Key Takeaways

- Write one question, and model only what its answer depends on.
- Use measured distributions, not their means, and not a normal or uniform by habit.
- Answer with replications and an interval, never with one run.
- Leave out a warm-up for a steady-state question.
- Compare designs with the same seeds and an interval on the difference.

______________________________________________________________________

## Sources

- Law, "Twenty-Three Critical Pitfalls in Simulation Modeling and How to Avoid Them" (Winter Simulation Conference, 2024), which we read. The list follows its pitfalls.
- The examples are our own runs.

# How desflow Works

This page shows how desflow is built: the parts that run a model, why each one exists, and how a run moves through them. Each part links to the How It Works section that describes it in full.

One run moves through the parts of desflow like this:

Whichever way a model is written, it builds one environment, and one run goes the same way from there. The environment holds the registry of live parameters, and the resources, stores and containers follow it. Ingress connectors change registry values from outside while the run goes on. Tasks and other processes publish events and telemetry, and egress connectors write them to their sinks on a thread of their own. The registry paths, the [records](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/records-and-telemetry/index.md), the batching and the connectors are therefore the same in all three ways.

______________________________________________________________________

## What It Is

desflow is built on [SimPy](https://simpy.readthedocs.io/). SimPy gives the event list, the clock, processes and resources, and desflow keeps all of them. SimPy leaves seven things to the modeller, and each part of desflow adds one of them:

| Left to the modeller in SimPy                                                                       | What desflow adds                                                                      | Read                                                                                                                    |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| the code around a model: a class of parameters, an entity class, a model class and a loop over runs | three ways to write a model, each built on the one below                               | [Writing a Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/index.md)                               |
| one pacing `factor`, fixed when the environment is made                                             | one environment that runs history at full speed, then switches to the wall clock       | [Time and Pacing](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/#how-it-works)                          |
| random times, drawn by the model's own code                                                         | ten checked distributions, each with a random stream of its own                        | [Arrivals and Services](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/arrivals-and-services/#how-it-works)  |
| parameters that only the model's code changes                                                       | a registry of named paths that connectors, scenarios and processes change during a run | [Live Parameters](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/live-parameters/#how-it-works) |
| resources, stores and containers that keep the capacity they were made with                         | resources, stores and containers whose capacity follows the registry                   | [Resources](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/resources/#how-it-works)                                      |
| output, which the model prints or logs                                                              | records of a fixed shape, written to sinks on a thread of their own                    | [Egress](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/egress/#how-it-works)                   |
| statistics, replications and confidence intervals                                                   | statistics collected during the run, replications, experiments and `explain`           | [Built-in Statistics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/statistics/#how-it-works)                   |

[Coming from SimPy](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/simpy/coming-from-simpy/#what-desflow-changes) compares each change with plain SimPy.

______________________________________________________________________

## How It Works

Each part is described in full on its own page. In short:

| Part                             | How it works                                                                                                                                                                                                                | Read                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Writing a model                  | A YAML blueprint, the builder and the low-level API are layers. `from_yaml` makes the calls a builder script makes, and the builder's `run()` makes the calls a low-level script writes by hand.                            | [YAML Blueprints](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/blueprints/#how-it-works), [What `run()` Does](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/tasks-and-processes/#what-run-does)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Environment and pacing           | `DynamicRealtimeEnvironment` is SimPy's `RealtimeEnvironment` with the registry, the connectors and the statistics added. It runs without waiting at `factor: 0` and switches to real time at `go_live_at`.                 | [Time and Pacing](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/#how-it-works)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Random times                     | A distribution reads its parameters at each draw, so a change applies from the next draw. Each one has its own random stream, made from the run's seed and its registry path.                                               | [Arrivals and Services](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/arrivals-and-services/#how-it-works)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Registry                         | Every live value sits under a dot path, such as `Shop.service.packing.mean`. Each update is checked before it is stored.                                                                                                    | [Live Parameters](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/live-parameters/#how-it-works)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Resources, stores and containers | Each waits on its registry path, so its capacity changes during a run. A resource that shrinks lets its busy units finish.                                                                                                  | [Resources](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/resources/#how-it-works), [Stores and Containers](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/stores-and-containers/#how-it-works)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Threads, ingress and egress      | The SimPy thread runs the model. Ingress and egress run their connectors on threads of their own, each on an asyncio loop, so a network wait never stalls a simulation step.                                                | [Time and Pacing](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/#how-it-works), which also compares these queues with the waiting lines of the model; [Ingress](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/ingress/#how-it-works), [Egress](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/egress/#how-it-works), [Write a Connector](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/records-and-kafka/write-a-connector/index.md) |
| Measurement and explain          | One statistics object collects readings while the run goes on. Replications run the model again for each seed and give a Student t interval. `desflow explain` applies queueing formulas to the model before anything runs. | [Built-in Statistics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/statistics/#how-it-works), [Replications](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/replications/#how-it-works), [Experiments](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/experiments/#how-it-works), [Command Line](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/#how-it-works)                                                                                                                     |

# Writing a Model

desflow has three ways to write a simulation: a YAML blueprint, the builder API and the low-level API. This page says how they relate and which to choose. If you are new to desflow, start with [First Simulation](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/first-simulation/index.md), which shows the same model in all three APIs side by side. Return here to look up a specific component.

______________________________________________________________________

## What It Is

The three are layers, not alternatives. Each layer writes the one below it for you:

- **YAML blueprint:** a file. `SimulationContext.from_yaml`, which `desflow run` calls, reads it and makes the same builder calls a Python script would make, so the result is an ordinary `SimulationContext`.
- **Builder API:** `SimulationContext` collects resources, distributions, tasks and connectors through its methods and decorators. Its `run()` compiles them into a `SimParameter`, builds the environment, registers the parameters and starts the processes.
- **Low-level API:** you write that last step by hand: a `SimParameter`, a `DynamicRealtimeEnvironment` that registers it, and SimPy processes that use the environment's resources and publish records.

Because each layer ends in the one below, the layers mix: a blueprint can reference Python written for the builder with `!python`, and a builder process can use the environment directly.

______________________________________________________________________

## How to Use It

|                          | YAML Blueprint                                                                                           | Builder API                                                                                            | Low-level API                                                        |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Entry point**          | `desflow run` or `SimulationContext.from_yaml`                                                           | `SimulationContext`                                                                                    | `DynamicRealtimeEnvironment`                                         |
| **What you write**       | the simulation, declared in a file; Python only for logic YAML cannot express, referenced with `!python` | what the system looks like, with decorators for each task's steps                                      | how every event and resource operates, step by step                  |
| **What it does for you** | everything the builder does, and no Python to run                                                        | publishing each task's events, requesting resources, sampling times, routing between tasks, statistics | nothing: you queue, start, time out and release yourself             |
| **Typical use**          | changing rates, capacities, connectors and timed experiments between runs without editing code           | models whose logic is most of the program, and configuration built in code, for example from a loop    | what the builder does not do, such as resources created during a run |

### Which to Choose

- **YAML blueprint** when the configuration is what changes between runs: a new arrival rate, another packer, a different broker, a scripted experiment. A file is easy to review and to diff, a run is one command, and a blueprint has a scenario of timed changes on the simulation clock built in. Logic that YAML cannot express goes in a Python module beside the file, as [Call Python from YAML](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/tools/yaml-advanced/index.md) shows.
- **Builder API** when most of the program is logic and you want it in one Python file, or when you build the configuration in code.
- **Low-level API** when you need what the builder does not do, or full control of every event.

[YAML Blueprints](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/blueprints/index.md), [Builder API](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/builder-api/index.md) and [Low-level API](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/low-level-api/index.md), the next three pages, describe each way in full.

______________________________________________________________________

## How It Works

Whichever way a model is written, it builds the same environment, and one run goes the same way from there. [How desflow Works](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/how-desflow-works/index.md) shows that run and each part it passes through.

# YAML Blueprints

A YAML blueprint is a simulation written as a file. This page shows how to run one, how a file is read and checked, how to change settings per environment, and where an error points. [YAML Keys](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/yaml-keys/index.md) lists every key a blueprint accepts.

______________________________________________________________________

## What It Is

A blueprint holds, as data, the builder calls that a Python script would make. Each section becomes the builder call of the same name: `resources` is `add_resource`, `tasks` is `@app.task`, `stats` is `with_stats`, and so on. There is no second way of building: `SimulationContext.from_yaml` makes those calls, in the order a script would, and returns an ordinary `SimulationContext`. A blueprint and a script that make the same calls produce the same simulation, and the tests check that the YAML, builder and low-level versions of every example publish the same records.

Use Python for logic that YAML cannot express. Reference it with `!python`, as [Call Python from YAML](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/tools/yaml-advanced/index.md) shows.

______________________________________________________________________

## How to Use It

### Run a Blueprint

Run it from a shell with the `desflow` command, which the package installs. These lines use the local example:

```bash
desflow examples get local --api yaml    # downloads local/yaml/local.yaml
cd local/yaml
desflow run local.yaml                   # runs until run.until
desflow run local.yaml --until 10min     # overrides run.until
desflow run local.yaml --seed 7          # overrides simulation.random_seed
desflow examples                         # lists the other examples
desflow --version
```

`--until` takes seconds or a duration such as `10 min`, `2 hours` or `1 week`. The command logs at INFO level. `ConsoleEgress`, in its default `log` format, writes each batch at that level, so its output is visible. A run with no seed logs the seed it drew, with the command that repeats it. An invalid file prints its errors and exits with code 1.

Or run it from Python:

```python
from desflow import SimulationContext

app = SimulationContext.from_yaml("local.yaml")
app.run()  # calls run.before, then runs until run.until
```

`run()` calls the blueprint's `run.before` functions first, and uses `run.until` when no `until` is passed. The builder methods and decorators still work on the context `from_yaml` returns.

`load_context` loads a blueprint or a builder Python file by the same path, so a script that takes either kind of file needs no check of its own:

```python
from desflow import load_context

# A blueprint, or a builder Python file that defines a SimulationContext at
# module level, from its folder: the one loader desflow run and explain use
app = load_context(".", "local.yaml")
```

### Preview the Records

`desflow run FILE` builds the blueprint and runs it with its own sinks until `--until`, `run.until` or Ctrl+C. It takes a YAML file only. A Python builder file runs with `python FILE`. Two options print the records instead of sending them to the file's sinks:

| Command                       | Behaviour                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `desflow run FILE --sample N` | Prints the first `N` events, then stops. `N` is 1 or more. The run is unpaced: `factor` is set to 0 and `go_live_at` is cleared. `logical_start_time` and `random_seed` are kept, so timestamps and values look as they would in the real run. Ingress entries and `run.before` are skipped. Telemetry records print between the events but are not counted, and `system.simulation.lag_seconds` is not printed. |
| `desflow run FILE --stdout`   | Prints every record of a normal run except the `system.simulation.lag_seconds` readings, which describe the wall clock, not the model. `factor`, `go_live_at`, `logical_start_time` and ingress are kept; `run.before` is skipped.                                                                                                                                                                               |

Both replace every egress entry with one `Console` of `format: json`, and a second one for labels when the file has a `when: labels` entry. A JSON console writes each record as one JSON line on stdout. The run's log stays on stderr, so `desflow run FILE --sample 10 | jq .value` reads only the records.

A preview checks the whole file, but not the connectors it leaves out:

- The structure, keys and names of the whole file are validated.
- `run.before` is skipped, because its functions prepare the real sinks, such as creating topics. A warning on stderr says so when the file has any.
- The connectors a preview replaces or skips are not built, so only their `type` is checked. Their `config` is checked only by a run that builds them, such as `desflow run FILE` without these options.

| Combination                                           | Result                                                                                                                                             |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--sample` with `--stdout`                            | Allowed. `--stdout` adds nothing.                                                                                                                  |
| `--sample` with `--until`, or a file with `run.until` | The run ends at whichever comes first. When `until` comes first, stderr says `sample ended at until with k of N events`.                           |
| `--sample` on a file with `go_live_at`                | A backfill-then-live file prints its first history events. `when: history` and `when: live` have no effect, because their entries are replaced.    |
| `--sample` on a file that publishes no events         | It runs until `until` or Ctrl+C, printing telemetry.                                                                                               |
| `--stdout` on a file with several egress entries      | One console prints each record once. Per-entry `batch_size` and `flush_interval` are dropped with the entries, and the `batching` section applies. |
| `--sample` or `--stdout` with `--replications`        | Usage error, exit code 2: both print one run.                                                                                                      |
| `--sample 0`                                          | Usage error, exit code 2.                                                                                                                          |

[Command Line](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/index.md) lists every command and option.

### Times and Durations

A time in a blueprint is a number of seconds or a duration such as `90 s`, `10 min`, `2 hours` or `1 week`: `run.until`, a scenario step's `at`, `simulation.warmup`, a stats `interval`, and every time-valued distribution parameter. `rate` is the exception: it is a number per second.

`logical_start_time` and `go_live_at` are instants: `now`, a signed duration from now such as `-1d` or `-10m`, or an ISO datetime such as `2026-01-01T00:00:00`. Both are read against one moment, when the file is loaded, so `-10m` and `now` are exactly ten minutes apart. `now`, the relative forms and an ISO datetime without an offset are read in `simulation.timezone`, UTC by default, as [Clocks and Pacing](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/clocks-and-pacing/#time-zone) describes.

### Settings per Environment

`${VAR}` in a value is replaced with the environment variable, so one file can serve several environments. `${VAR:-default}` uses the default when the variable is unset or empty, as in a shell, and `$${` writes a literal `${`. An unquoted value is read as YAML reads it after the replacement, so `factor: ${SIM_FACTOR:-0}` is the number 0. A quoted value stays a string. An unset variable with no default stops the load, and the error names its line.

```yaml
# Settings that change per environment, read from environment variables.
# Run it with: SIM_FACTOR=1 desflow run environment.yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: ${SIM_ID:-Shop}
  # An unquoted value is read after the replacement, so this is the number 0
  factor: ${SIM_FACTOR:-0}
  # Read against the moment the file is loaded: a day of history up to now
  logical_start_time: -1d
  # Under simulation: timestamps written in Melbourne time, with its offset; the
  # start and now are read in it. UTC by default
  timezone: ${SIM_TIMEZONE:-Australia/Melbourne}
  # Under simulation: how far the run is behind the wall clock, every 10 s; by
  # default off at factor 0 and every second otherwise, and 0 turns it off
  lag_interval: 10 s
  # Under simulation: raise RuntimeError when a paced step is more than factor
  # seconds behind the wall clock; false by default, and never checked at factor 0
  strict: true

egress:
  - type: Console

resources:
  # Quoted, because ${...} inside {...} would end the mapping early; the check
  # turns the text into a number
  packers: {current_cap: "${PACKERS:-2}", max_cap: 5}

run:
  # A duration, such as 1 week, or a number of seconds
  until: ${RUN_FOR:-1 hour}
```

The [Parquet example](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/examples/parquet/index.md) switches from the local disk to S3 with five variables, and [Queues and Capacity](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/queues-and-capacity/index.md) runs one file with several numbers of packers.

### Include a File

`!include path` puts a mapping from another YAML file in place, such as the settings `desflow fit` writes: `packing: !include fitted/packing.yaml`. The path is relative to the file that names it. `!include {file: path, spawn: pack}` adds keys to the file's mapping, such as the task an arrival spawns. The file is read with the same loader, so `${VAR}`, `!python` and `!include` work in it. A file that includes itself, directly or through another file, is refused. [Input Fitting](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/input-fitting/#load-the-settings) shows it.

### Run on Your Own Environment

`simulation.environment` runs the model on your own subclass of `DynamicRealtimeEnvironment`, named with `!python`, as `SimulationContext(environment=...)` does in Python, for example `environment: !python my_model.TracingEnvironment`.

A subclass that overrides `__init__` takes `**kwargs` and passes them on, because desflow builds it with the arguments it builds its own environment with. One that overrides `schedule` or `step` calls `super()`. When a script steps outside `run()`, `step` runs once per model event. Inside `run()`, it runs once per event, desflow's own events included.

In a blueprint, the class is named under `simulation`. `CountingEnvironment` in `endings_logic.py` counts the events the run processes:

```yaml
# Run on a subclass of DynamicRealtimeEnvironment, from endings_logic.py beside the file
environment: !python endings_logic.CountingEnvironment
```

### Check as You Type

`desflow schema` prints the JSON Schema of a blueprint, and the same file is published on this site, so an editor can complete keys and mark a misspelt key or a value of the wrong kind as you type. [Set Up Your Editor](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/tools/set-up-your-editor/index.md) shows the setting, and [YAML Keys](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/yaml-keys/index.md) lists every key.

______________________________________________________________________

## How It Works

`from_yaml` makes the builder calls for you, so a blueprint gets everything [the builder does](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/builder-api/#how-it-works), and it checks the whole file before anything runs. A file is read and checked in five steps, and any step that fails stops the load with a `BlueprintError` before anything runs:

1. **Read the file.** `read_document` reads it with a subclass of `yaml.SafeLoader`. `${VAR}` is replaced while each scalar is read, `!python module.attribute` imports the module and returns the attribute, `!include path` reads a mapping from another YAML file relative to this one, and every key's line is kept in a source map. Every other node is built as `yaml.safe_load` would build it.
1. **Check every field.** The document is validated against the `Blueprint` model. Unknown keys are refused, so a misspelt key is reported rather than ignored. Every distribution is built as the builder would build it, so a parameter out of range, or one the family does not take, is refused here. Every relative time is read against one `now`. A `spawn` `after` and a `fire` `after` must be above 0. `simulation.environment` must be a subclass of `DynamicRealtimeEnvironment`. All validation errors are reported at once.
1. **Check the names.** Each name in the file must exist and fit where it is used:
   - Every service, resource, store, container and next task that a task names exists.
   - Every task's `spawn` and `on:` spawn names a task that does not share an arrival's name.
   - A `subscribe` names a task or a signal.
   - An `on:` fire names a signal, and an `on:` interrupt names a task.
   - An `on:` `fire ... from` names a signal or a task. The task must run on the same entity as the `on:` list. For a task's list, that is the entity of the task that holds the list. For a signal's list, it is the entity of a task that fires the signal.
   - Every `level.<name>` in an expression names a store or a container, and every `users.<name>` and `queue.<name>` names a resource.
   - A store and a container do not share a name.
   - A task's `priority` needs a resource with `queue: priority`.
   - Resources and stores have whole-number capacities.
   - An `on:` fire with `urgent` or `after` names a signal with `once: true`.
   - `simulation.environment` names a subclass of `DynamicRealtimeEnvironment`.
1. **Build the context.** The builder calls are made in the order a script would make them: the simulation, ingress, egress, batching, stats, resources, stores, containers, variables, services, arrivals, tasks, arrival loops, processes, telemetry and the scenario.
1. **Check the paths.** The parameters are registered into a scratch registry, with the code that the run uses. Every scenario `path`, and every `registry["..."]` that an expression reads, is then checked against the paths the run will have. Every scenario `value` must convert to the type its path holds.

______________________________________________________________________

## Stability and Limits

An error at any step is mapped back to its line through the source map:

```yaml
# A blueprint with a mistake, for the YAML Blueprints page: pack_order has a priority,
# but its resource serves its queue in the default order, fifo.
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 2}

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5 s}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    priority: 0
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
```

```python
try:
    SimulationContext.from_yaml("blueprint_error.yaml")
except BlueprintError as error:
    print(f"Error: {error}")  # what desflow run prints, before exiting with code 1
```

```text
Error: blueprint_error.yaml:20: task 'pack_order' has a priority, but resource 'packers' does not set queue: priority; set it, or remove the priority
```

A blueprint covers configuration, including several resources per task (`resource: [picker, bench]` and `keep`), preemption (`preempt: true`) and breakdowns (`breakdown:`). These stay in Python:

- **Values computed per entity.** A mapping payload is a constant, apart from three values added for each entity: the task id that `id_field` adds, the attributes that `attributes` adds, and the item a `get` took, which `item_field` adds. Random choices, derived fields and state carried between events are a Python payload or process, as [Call Python from YAML](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/tools/yaml-advanced/index.md) shows. A task's `priority` and a `get` or `put` amount can be an expression. `next` rules read attributes, payload fields, levels, registry values, the item a `get` took (`item.<field>`), the wait's branches (`wait.<branch>.done`) and signals (`signal.<name>.count`), as [Task Flow](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/task-flow/index.md) describes.
- **Entity keys.** A blueprint uses the default key, `<arrival>-<n>`. A key function is builder only.
- **Batching.** Collecting several entities into one is a process in Python.
- **One simulation per file.** A blueprint has one `sim_id`. `!include` puts a mapping from another file in place, such as fitted settings, but not a second simulation.

### Security

A blueprint with no `!python` references is read entirely by `yaml.SafeLoader`, and loading it imports only the connector modules its `type` entries name. An `!include` reads another YAML file the same way and imports nothing itself. A file that references Python, directly or in a file it includes, runs the imports it names. Such a file needs the same trust as a Python script: run blueprints only from people whose scripts you would run. [Call Python from YAML](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/tools/yaml-advanced/#security) explains.

# Builder API

This page writes a whole simulation as one Python file with the builder, `SimulationContext`: a shop that packs orders with boxes from stock, prints a label, and leaves the parcel for a courier. It builds on [Writing a Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/index.md), which places the builder between a blueprint and the low-level API, and on [Tasks and Processes](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/tasks-and-processes/index.md), which describes what a task does.

______________________________________________________________________

## What It Is

The builder works in two phases. You describe the simulation with its methods and decorators, and nothing runs. `run()` then builds the environment and the connectors and starts the clock:

Until `run()` builds the environment, the runtime helpers `context.spawn`, `context.call`, `context.signal`, `context.get_resource`, `context.get_store`, `context.get_container` and `context.env` raise `RuntimeError`. Loops, tasks and processes run only after that, so the helpers belong inside them.

______________________________________________________________________

## How to Use It

### Create the Context

The context names the simulation and sets its clock: `factor` for the pacing, `random_seed` for the draws, `logical_start_time` for the timestamps. It also takes `go_live_at` and `warmup`, which [Time and Pacing](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/index.md) describes.

```python
app = SimulationContext(
    sim_id="Shop",
    factor=0.0,  # 0.0 unpaced, 1.0 real time
    random_seed=42,  # the same draws on every run
    logical_start_time=datetime(2026, 10, 1, 9, 0),  # what simulation time 0 is
)
```

### Declare Resources, Stores and Containers

A task holds a resource while it works. A container holds an amount and a store holds items, and tasks take from and add to both. `add_variable` registers any other live value. [Resources](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/resources/index.md) and [Stores and Containers](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/stores-and-containers/index.md) describe each.

```python
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=2, max_cap=5)  # 2 packers now, room for 5
app.add_container("boxes", current_cap=200, max_cap=200, level=100)  # an amount
app.add_store("parcels", current_cap=20, max_cap=50)  # items, waiting for a courier
app.add_variable("conveyor_speed", 1.5)  # any other live value
```

### Add Distributions

Each service is a distribution, given its parameters by keyword. Each arrival is a distribution too, and [Start Them from Arrivals](#start-them-from-arrivals) adds it with the task it starts. A parameter out of range, or one the family does not take, raises `ValueError` here, before the run. [Arrivals and Services](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/arrivals-and-services/index.md) lists the ten families.

```python
app.add_service("packing", dist="triangular", low=1, mode=2, high=4)
app.add_service("labelling", dist="constant", value=0.5)
```

### Write the Tasks

`@app.task` turns a function into a task: it publishes `queued`, waits for its resource and its `get`, publishes `started`, waits the service time, adds its `put`, and publishes what the function returns as the finished event. `next` names the task that follows, and the function receives `upstream`, `entity` or `item` when it declares them. [Task Flow](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/task-flow/index.md) covers rules and weights.

```python
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    get={"container": "boxes", "amount": 1},  # one box, once it has a packer
    next="print_label",  # the task that follows
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    # The value of the finished event: exactly this dictionary
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.task(service_id="labelling", put={"store": "parcels"})  # a timed step
def print_label(task_id: int, upstream):
    # upstream is what pack_order handed on; the payload becomes the parcel
    return {"event_type": "label_printed", "packed_by": upstream.task_id}


@app.task(get={"store": "parcels"})
def collect(task_id: int, item):
    return {"event_type": "parcel_collected", "label": item["event_type"]}
```

### Start Them from Arrivals

`add_arrival` with `spawn=` is the builder form of YAML's `spawn`: each arrival starts the named task for its entity, keyed `orders-1`, `orders-2` and so on. The record's `instance` comes from the task's one counter, which `next` and other arrivals share, so no two runs of the task share an id. A `spawn` that names a task never added is refused when `run()` checks the model.

```python
# An order every 2 s on average, keyed orders-1, ..., each starting pack_order
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5, spawn="pack_order")
app.add_arrival("couriers", dist="constant", value=10, spawn="collect")  # every 10 s
```

`@app.arrival_loop` runs a generator of your own that waits with `context.wait_for_arrival` and starts tasks with `context.spawn`. A loop is needed only when it does more than start one task, such as choosing the task from the entity's attributes. [Tasks and Processes](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/tasks-and-processes/#arrivals-start-tasks) shows a loop that does what `spawn=` does, written by hand.

### Measure the Run

`with_stats` switches on the built-in statistics, published as telemetry. [Statistics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/statistics/index.md) lists the levels.

```python
app.with_stats("typical", interval=30)  # readings, counts, waits, every 30 s
```

### Add a Process

`add_process` is for anything that is not a task. It calls a generator with the context when the run starts. Here the process is a speed that drifts.

```python
def speed_drift(context: SimulationContext, step: float):
    """Raises the conveyor speed a little every 10 simulation seconds."""
    path = "Shop.variables.conveyor_speed"
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(10.0)
        speed = context.env.registry.get(path).value
        context.env.registry.update(path, speed + step)


app.add_process(speed_drift, step=0.1)
```

### Attach the Connectors

`add_ingress` brings parameter changes in, and `add_egress` writes records out, each with its own batching if it needs it. [Ingress](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/ingress/index.md) and [Egress](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/egress/index.md) list the connectors.

```python
app.add_ingress(LocalIngress(schedule=[(5.0, "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 3)]))
app.add_egress(ConsoleEgress(), batch_size=100, flush_interval=1.0)
app.with_batching(batch_size=1_000, flush_interval=5.0)  # defaults for other sinks
```

`LocalIngress` counts its delays in wall-clock seconds, so the change to 3 packers is due 5 seconds after the run starts. This unpaced run ends in under a second, so the change never lands. At `factor=1.0`, it lands 5 seconds into the run. For a change at an exact simulation time, use a scenario step, `add_step(at, path=..., value=...)` or `add_scenario(steps)`, which [Live Parameters](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/live-parameters/#script-an-experiment) describes. A process that waits and then updates the registry, as `speed_drift` above does, also works.

`compile_parameters()` returns the `SimParameter` that `run()` will register. Call it to check the registry paths before a run:

```python
paths = app.compile_parameters()  # the SimParameter that run() registers
```

### Run It

```python
if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    app.run(until="2 min")
```

`ConsoleEgress` writes each batch of records in one INFO log call, one line per record, so the script switches logging on before it runs. Only the first line of a batch carries the logging format's prefix, such as the time and the level. The other lines are bare. The first events of the run:

```text
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 2.552, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 2.552, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'started'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 2.696, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-2', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 1, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 2.696, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-2', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 1, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'started'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 3.737, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-3', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 2, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 4.02, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-4', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 3, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 4.632, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-2', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 1, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 4.632, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-2', 'task': 'print_label', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.labelling', 'status': 'started'}}
```

______________________________________________________________________

## How It Works

`run()` takes the steps a [low-level script](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/low-level-api/index.md) writes by hand, in the same order, which [What `run()` Does](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/tasks-and-processes/#what-run-does) lists. It adds these:

- **A seed for every run.** It makes `Sampler(seed=random_seed)`, and draws and logs a seed when there is none.
- **Resources, stores and containers.** One for each `add_resource`, `add_store` and `add_container`, which `context.get_resource`, `get_store` and `get_container` return. `add_resource` takes a `type`, a subclass of `ResourceBase` to build the resource from ([Custom Resource Types](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/resources/custom-resource-types/#custom-resource-types)). `add_store` and `add_container` take a `type` too, a subclass of `StoreBase` or `ContainerBase` ([Custom Store and Container Types](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/stores-and-containers/#custom-store-and-container-types)). A store or container with no `current_cap` and no `max_cap` has no limit.
- **Tasks.** `@app.task` publishes `queued`, `started` and the finished event with the entity key, task and instance, reports each step to the statistics, takes and adds stock, and routes to the next task with a `Router`.
- **Entities.** `context.wait_for_arrival` returns an `Entity` with its key and attributes.
- **Names with the `sim_id`.** `context.publish(name, value)` puts the `sim_id` in front of the name. The low-level `env.publish_telemetry` uses the name as given.

______________________________________________________________________

## Stability and Limits

A mistake stops the script before the clock starts. A method raises `ValueError` when it is called with a value it cannot take:

- an `environment` that is not a subclass of `DynamicRealtimeEnvironment`;
- a `fire` action with `urgent` or `after` on a signal that is not `once=True` (raised at `start()`);
- a negative `after`;
- a distribution parameter out of range, or one its family does not take;
- an unknown queue order;
- a `current_cap` or `max_cap` that is not a whole number or infinity, or a `max_cap` below 1 given with no `current_cap`;
- a `type` that is not a subclass of `ResourceBase`;
- a negative `queue_limit`, or one on a `type` with a `PutQueue` of its own;
- a task with a resource but no service, or a priority without a resource;
- an unknown `on_interrupt`;
- a second task with the same name;
- a `spawn` with an `after` of 0 or less;
- a `fire` action given both `value` and `from`.

`run()` then checks what each task names, before the clock or any connector starts. It raises `ValueError` for:

- a resource, service, store, container, signal or task that was not added;
- a priority on a resource that does not queue by priority;
- two tasks that acquire resources in opposite orders;
- a spawned task that shares an arrival's name;
- a `fire` action's `from` that names both a signal and a task, or neither;
- a `level.<name>`, `users.<name>`, `queue.<name>`, `signal.<name>`, `wait.<branch>` or `registry["..."]` that an expression reads but that does not exist.

The builder's limits are those of its tasks and its resources:

- **Resources are fixed when the run starts.** `run()` creates every resource, store and container before the clock starts, and has no call to add one later. A process can add one through `context.env`, as [Add Resources Mid-run](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/modelling/dynamic-topology/index.md) shows.
- **`advance()` needs a started run.** It raises `RuntimeError` before `start()`, after `close()` and after the run's own end, and `ValueError` for a time that is not after `now`. [Run in Segments](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/run-length/#run-in-segments) shows it.
- **`strict` defaults to False here.** [Strict Pacing](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/clocks-and-pacing/#strict-pacing) gives what it does and its default in each API.
- **`environment=` takes a subclass of `DynamicRealtimeEnvironment`.** The context builds it in `start()` with the same arguments it would give its own environment, so its `__init__` takes `**kwargs` and passes them on.
- **A subscribe refuses a processed event.** `context.subscribe(event)` raises `RuntimeError` when the event has already happened, or when it is called outside a process.

______________________________________________________________________

## Example

Full script

The complete file, which the documentation tests run:

```python
"""The Builder API page: a whole simulation in one Python file, step by step.

Run it with `python builder.py`: it runs unpaced for 2 simulation minutes and prints
every record to the terminal.
"""

import logging
from datetime import datetime

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, LocalIngress, SimulationContext

app = SimulationContext(
    sim_id="Shop",
    factor=0.0,  # 0.0 unpaced, 1.0 real time
    random_seed=42,  # the same draws on every run
    logical_start_time=datetime(2026, 10, 1, 9, 0),  # what simulation time 0 is
)

app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=2, max_cap=5)  # 2 packers now, room for 5
app.add_container("boxes", current_cap=200, max_cap=200, level=100)  # an amount
app.add_store("parcels", current_cap=20, max_cap=50)  # items, waiting for a courier
app.add_variable("conveyor_speed", 1.5)  # any other live value

app.add_service("packing", dist="triangular", low=1, mode=2, high=4)
app.add_service("labelling", dist="constant", value=0.5)


@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    get={"container": "boxes", "amount": 1},  # one box, once it has a packer
    next="print_label",  # the task that follows
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    # The value of the finished event: exactly this dictionary
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.task(service_id="labelling", put={"store": "parcels"})  # a timed step
def print_label(task_id: int, upstream):
    # upstream is what pack_order handed on; the payload becomes the parcel
    return {"event_type": "label_printed", "packed_by": upstream.task_id}


@app.task(get={"store": "parcels"})
def collect(task_id: int, item):
    return {"event_type": "parcel_collected", "label": item["event_type"]}


# An order every 2 s on average, keyed orders-1, ..., each starting pack_order
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5, spawn="pack_order")
app.add_arrival("couriers", dist="constant", value=10, spawn="collect")  # every 10 s

app.with_stats("typical", interval=30)  # readings, counts, waits, every 30 s


def speed_drift(context: SimulationContext, step: float):
    """Raises the conveyor speed a little every 10 simulation seconds."""
    path = "Shop.variables.conveyor_speed"
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(10.0)
        speed = context.env.registry.get(path).value
        context.env.registry.update(path, speed + step)


app.add_process(speed_drift, step=0.1)

app.add_ingress(LocalIngress(schedule=[(5.0, "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 3)]))
app.add_egress(ConsoleEgress(), batch_size=100, flush_interval=1.0)
app.with_batching(batch_size=1_000, flush_interval=5.0)  # defaults for other sinks

paths = app.compile_parameters()  # the SimParameter that run() registers

if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    app.run(until="2 min")
```

[Low-level API](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/low-level-api/index.md) writes the same kind of model by hand. A blueprint makes the same builder calls from a file, as [YAML Blueprints](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/blueprints/index.md) describes.

# Low-level API

This page writes a simulation with SimPy and the environment directly: a packing team with a stock of boxes and a store of packed orders, every step written by hand. It builds on [SimPy and desflow](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/simpy/index.md), which describes the SimPy constructs, and on [Builder API](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/builder-api/index.md), which writes the same kind of model for you.

______________________________________________________________________

## What It Is

Use the low-level API when you need what the builder does not do: events and interactions of your own shape, such as a resource created while the run goes on in [Add Resources Mid-run](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/modelling/dynamic-topology/index.md). A builder or blueprint model can also start a low-level process with `add_process`, as [Tasks and Processes](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/tasks-and-processes/processes/#how-it-works) shows.

A low-level script takes these steps, in this order:

______________________________________________________________________

## How to Use It

### Create the Environment

```python
import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    ContainerConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicContainer,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    DynamicStore,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
    time_to_seconds,
)
```

```python
env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)  # unpaced; 1.0 follows the wall clock
```

`factor` sets the pacing: `1.0` follows the wall clock, and `0.0` runs as fast as possible. `logical_start_time` and `go_live_at` work as [Time and Pacing](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/index.md) describes.

### Register the Parameters

```python
env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        # An order every 2 s on average (rate 0.5)
        arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
        service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=1.5, std=0.3)},
        resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=3)},
        containers={"boxes": ContainerConfig(current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=100)},
        stores={"finished": CapacityConfig(current_cap=50, max_cap=50)},
        variables={"boxes_per_order": 1.0},
    )
)
```

One `SimParameter` holds every parameter of one simulation under its `sim_id`. Registering it gives each value a path, such as `Shop.arrival.orders.rate`, and only the registered paths exist. [Live Parameters](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/live-parameters/index.md) lists the paths.

### Attach the Connectors

```python
env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])  # starts the egress thread
# env.setup_ingress([KafkaIngress(...)]) would start the ingress thread
env.setup_stats("Shop", "basic", interval=60)  # readings and counts every minute
```

`setup_egress` starts the egress thread, which writes every record the processes publish. `setup_ingress` starts the ingress thread for parameter changes from outside, and `setup_stats` switches on the built-in statistics. [Egress](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/egress/index.md) lists the arguments of `setup_egress`, including a [warm-up](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#one-run-starts-empty) and labels sinks.

### Create Resources, Containers and Stores

```python
packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")  # reads Shop.resources.packers.*
boxes = DynamicContainer(env, "Shop", "boxes")  # starts at its level, 100
finished = DynamicStore(env, "Shop", "finished")
sampler = Sampler(seed=42)  # a random stream per distribution, from one seed
```

Each one reads its capacity from the registry when it is created, so the parameters must be registered first. Each one also adds itself to the statistics. `Sampler(seed=42)` gives each registered distribution a random stream of its own, so a run repeats exactly, as [Arrivals and Services](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/arrivals-and-services/#seeding) describes.

### Write the Processes

A process is a SimPy generator: it `yield`s to wait, and publishes records as it goes. This one does what `@app.task` does in the builder, with a box from stock and a store for the result. It publishes each event with the entity key, the task's name and its instance id, and reports each step to the statistics:

```python
def order(env, key, task_id):
    """One order: queue for a packer, take a box, pack, then store the result."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)  # what @app.task reports for you
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        count = env.registry.get("Shop.variables.boxes_per_order").value
        yield boxes.get(count)  # waits if the stock is too low
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        yield finished.put({"order": key})
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished("orders")
```

The service time is drawn once the order has a packer and a box, from the configuration the registry holds at that moment, so a change made while it waited still applies to it.

The arrival loop keeps the configuration object rather than a copy of the rate. The registry changes that object in place when a new rate arrives, so the next draw uses the current rate. It gives each order its key, `orders-1`, `orders-2`:

```python
def arrivals(env):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")  # the live config object
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))  # each draw reads the current rate
        env.process(order(env, f"orders-{task_id + 1}", task_id))  # the entity key
        task_id += 1
```

A reading of your own is a process that publishes at an interval. `publish_telemetry` uses the name exactly as given:

```python
def telemetry(env):
    """A reading of your own, beside the built-in statistics."""
    while True:
        env.publish_telemetry("Shop.boxes_per_packer", boxes.level / packers.capacity)
        yield env.timeout(10.0)
```

A process can also change the simulation itself, through the registry, as a connector or a scenario would:

```python
def refill_and_rush(env):
    """Refills boxes every minute, and doubles arrivals after five minutes."""
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(60.0)
        missing = boxes.capacity - boxes.level
        if missing > 0:  # SimPy refuses a put of 0
            yield boxes.put(missing)
        if env.now >= 300 and env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.rate").value < 1.0:
            env.registry.update("Shop.arrival.orders.rate", 1.0)
            env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 2)
```

### Start the Processes and Run

```python
env.process(arrivals(env))
env.process(telemetry(env))
env.process(refill_and_rush(env))
```

```python
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)
try:
    env.run(until=time_to_seconds("10 min"))  # until is in simulation seconds
finally:
    env.teardown()  # flushes the buffers and stops the threads
```

`ConsoleEgress` writes each record as a log line at INFO level, so logging is switched on first. `env.run` is SimPy's, so `until` is a number of simulation seconds. `time_to_seconds` converts a duration such as `"10 min"`. `teardown` in `finally` publishes the last statistics, flushes the last records and stops both threads, even when the run stops with Ctrl+C or an error.

A script can run the model in segments by calling `env.run(until=...)` again, as in SimPy. `env.schedule(event, priority, delay)` is SimPy's own: `simpy.events.URGENT` puts an event before the `NORMAL` ones at its time. [Run Length](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/run-length/#run-in-segments) covers segments, `strict`, `sync()` and `env.resume_pacing()`.

An environment subclass is plain Python: `class Traced(DynamicRealtimeEnvironment)`, whose `__init__` takes `**kwargs` and passes them on, and whose `step` or `schedule` calls `super()`. Inside `run()`, `step` runs once per event, desflow's own events included.

______________________________________________________________________

## How It Works

The environment does little for you. It paces the clock, holds the registry, writes records on the egress thread and keeps the statistics that `setup_stats` switches on. Everything else is your code. [Builder API](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/builder-api/#how-it-works) lists what `SimulationContext.run()` writes for you on top of the same steps.

The environment runs on three threads: the SimPy thread runs your processes, the ingress thread runs the sources and the egress thread runs the sinks. Alongside your processes, the environment starts processes of its own on the SimPy thread:

- The ingress monitor applies the sources' changes to the registry every 0.1 simulation seconds.
- Each sink has a process that flushes its buffer on the sink's interval.
- The lag monitor measures how far the clock is behind the wall clock once the run is live.
- The statistics timer publishes the statistics every interval.
- One process ends the warm-up.

`env.step()` and `env.peek()` do not count these processes. [Time and Pacing](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/#how-it-works) shows the threads and the switch to real time.

______________________________________________________________________

## Stability and Limits

Nothing is checked before the run as a whole. Each call checks only what it reads, when it runs:

- **An unregistered path raises `KeyError`** when a resource, a process or a `registry.get` asks for it, so register the parameters before creating anything that reads them.
- **A record without egress is dropped.** Until `setup_egress` runs, `publish_event` and `publish_telemetry` do nothing, without an error.
- **A `Sampler()` with no seed draws nothing at random,** as [Arrivals and Services](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/arrivals-and-services/#how-it-works) explains, so give it a seed.
- **A paced run is strict by default.** [Strict Pacing](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/clocks-and-pacing/#strict-pacing) gives what it does and its default in each API.
- **An unhandled failure stops the run under `stop`.** `DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(on_unhandled_failure=...)` is `stop` by default, as a plain SimPy environment is. Under `stop`, a one-shot `Signal` failure that nobody waits for raises `SignalFailed`, and the run stops. Pass `"continue"` to defuse such a failure and let the run go on. A re-arming signal's failure is always defused. An exception raised in a process stops the run under both settings. The keyword must be `stop` or `continue`.

Beyond those, a process can do anything SimPy can model.

______________________________________________________________________

## Example

Full script

The complete file, which the documentation tests run:

```python
"""A complete low-level simulation, as the Low-level API page explains it step by step.

One packing team with a stock of boxes and a store of packed orders. Run it with
`python low_level.py`: it runs unpaced for 10 simulation minutes and prints every record
to the terminal.
"""

import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    ContainerConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicContainer,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    DynamicStore,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
    time_to_seconds,
)

env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)  # unpaced; 1.0 follows the wall clock

env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        # An order every 2 s on average (rate 0.5)
        arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
        service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=1.5, std=0.3)},
        resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=3)},
        containers={"boxes": ContainerConfig(current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=100)},
        stores={"finished": CapacityConfig(current_cap=50, max_cap=50)},
        variables={"boxes_per_order": 1.0},
    )
)

env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])  # starts the egress thread
# env.setup_ingress([KafkaIngress(...)]) would start the ingress thread
env.setup_stats("Shop", "basic", interval=60)  # readings and counts every minute

packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")  # reads Shop.resources.packers.*
boxes = DynamicContainer(env, "Shop", "boxes")  # starts at its level, 100
finished = DynamicStore(env, "Shop", "finished")
sampler = Sampler(seed=42)  # a random stream per distribution, from one seed


def order(env, key, task_id):
    """One order: queue for a packer, take a box, pack, then store the result."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)  # what @app.task reports for you
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        count = env.registry.get("Shop.variables.boxes_per_order").value
        yield boxes.get(count)  # waits if the stock is too low
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        yield finished.put({"order": key})
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished("orders")


def arrivals(env):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")  # the live config object
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))  # each draw reads the current rate
        env.process(order(env, f"orders-{task_id + 1}", task_id))  # the entity key
        task_id += 1


def telemetry(env):
    """A reading of your own, beside the built-in statistics."""
    while True:
        env.publish_telemetry("Shop.boxes_per_packer", boxes.level / packers.capacity)
        yield env.timeout(10.0)


def refill_and_rush(env):
    """Refills boxes every minute, and doubles arrivals after five minutes."""
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(60.0)
        missing = boxes.capacity - boxes.level
        if missing > 0:  # SimPy refuses a put of 0
            yield boxes.put(missing)
        if env.now >= 300 and env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.rate").value < 1.0:
            env.registry.update("Shop.arrival.orders.rate", 1.0)
            env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 2)


env.process(arrivals(env))
env.process(telemetry(env))
env.process(refill_and_rush(env))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    try:
        env.run(until=time_to_seconds("10 min"))  # until is in simulation seconds
    finally:
        env.teardown()  # flushes the buffers and stops the threads
    assert (
        packers.capacity == 2
        and env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.rate").value == 1.0
    )
    assert len(finished.items) > 0
```

# Model Parts

A model is made of a few kinds of parts. This page is the map: which block models what, and what it is called in each way of writing. Each block has a page of its own.

______________________________________________________________________

## What It Is

An **entity** is the thing that flows through a model: an order, a visitor, a support call. It enters through an arrival and does the work its task describes. While it works, it holds a resource, and it may take from or add to a store or container. Then it goes on to the next task. [What Is DES?](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/what-is-des/index.md) explains discrete-event simulation, the kind of simulation these blocks build. Look at how the blocks connect:

| Block      | What it models                                                    | YAML                        | Builder                            | Low-level                                     | Page                                                                                                               |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Arrival    | how often an entity enters, and what it starts with               | `arrivals`                  | `add_arrival`, `@app.arrival_loop` | a process that waits for a drawn gap          | [Arrivals and Services](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/arrivals-and-services/index.md)  |
| Service    | how long a piece of work takes                                    | `services`                  | `add_service`                      | a `DistributionConfig` drawn with a `Sampler` | [Arrivals and Services](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/arrivals-and-services/index.md)  |
| Task       | what one entity does, with its events                             | `tasks`                     | `@app.task`                        | a SimPy process                               | [Tasks and Processes](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/tasks-and-processes/index.md)                  |
| Resource   | packers, benches, lanes: whole units held by a task               | `resources`                 | `add_resource`                     | `DynamicResource`                             | [Resources](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/resources/index.md)                                      |
| Container  | an amount, such as a stock of boxes, that tasks take and add      | `containers`                | `add_container`                    | `DynamicContainer`                            | [Stores and Containers](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/stores-and-containers/index.md)  |
| Store      | items, such as parcels on a shelf, that tasks put and get         | `stores`                    | `add_store`                        | `DynamicStore`                                | [Stores and Containers](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/stores-and-containers/index.md)  |
| Task flow  | the task that follows a finished one, and what the entity carries | `next`, `attributes`, `set` | `next=`, `attributes=`, `set=`     | `Router`, `Entity`                            | [Task Flow](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/task-flow/index.md)                          |
