| Process    | anything else that runs over time: a break, a drift, a schedule   | `processes`                 | `add_process`                      | `env.process`                                 | [Tasks and Processes](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/tasks-and-processes/index.md)                  |
| Statistics | what the run measures about itself                                | `stats`                     | `with_stats`                       | `env.setup_stats`, `env.stats`                | [Statistics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/statistics/index.md)                            |
| Variable   | any other live value, such as a speed                             | `variables`                 | `add_variable`                     | `SimParameter(variables=...)`                 | [Live Parameters](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/live-parameters/index.md) |

The [shop tutorial](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/first-simulation/index.md), in the Learn section, puts them together one at a time, in a small shop.

______________________________________________________________________

## How to Use It

A model declares its blocks, and its tasks use them by name. A task names its service and its resource, and an arrival names the task it starts. The table above gives each block's YAML key, builder call and low-level class. [Writing a Model](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/index.md) shows a whole model in each form.

______________________________________________________________________

## How It Works

When the run starts, `run()` builds the environment, registers every block's parameters in the registry, builds the resources, stores and containers, and starts the arrivals and processes. [What `run()` Does](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/tasks-and-processes/#what-run-does) lists the steps in order. From then on, each block reads its live values from the registry: a distribution reads its parameters at each draw, and a resource follows its capacity path.

# Arrivals and Services: `Sampler` and the Distributions

Two building blocks set the timing of every simulation. An **arrival** decides how often a new entity enters the model: an order, a visitor, a support call. A **service** decides how long a piece of work takes: packing an order, answering a call. Both are distributions of time, and each time one is needed, a value is drawn from the distribution with its current parameters.

______________________________________________________________________

## What It Is

| Block   | Answers                                | Used by                                            | Example                            |
| ------- | -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Arrival | How long until the next entity?        | the arrival loop, which starts a task for each one | an order every 2 s on average      |
| Service | How long does this piece of work take? | a task, while it holds its resource                | 3 s of packing, give or take 0.5 s |

An arrival draws each gap afresh from its distribution, so the gaps differ and entities arrive at uneven times. Look at the first five orders of the shop in [First Simulation](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/first-simulation/index.md):

______________________________________________________________________

## How to Use It

Every distribution is a family, `dist`, and the parameters that family takes. There are ten families. A parameter outside its range, a missing one, or one the family does not take is refused when the model is built, with the YAML line when it comes from a blueprint. [Reference, Distributions](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/distributions/index.md) lists every family with its parameters, rules, mean and variance. On this page, the table below names each family, the list under it gives each family's rules, and one example shows the form.

| Family                                                                                             | Use it for                                                                                                                                       | Parameters                                        |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- |
| [`exponential`](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/distributions/#exponential)           | Gaps between arrivals that happen independently of each other: orders, calls, visits. Many short gaps and a few long ones, with mean `1 / rate`. | `rate`                                            |
| [`normal`](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/distributions/#normal)                     | Work with a typical time and a small, symmetric spread.                                                                                          | `mean`, `std`                                     |
| [`truncated_normal`](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/distributions/#truncated_normal) | Work with a typical time and a hard minimum.                                                                                                     | `mean`, `std`, `low`                              |
| [`lognormal`](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/distributions/#lognormal)               | Times that are never negative and now and then much longer: repairs, support calls.                                                              | `mean`, `std`                                     |
| [`constant`](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/distributions/#constant)                 | Fixed times: a conveyor, a setup, a step that takes no time.                                                                                     | `value`                                           |
| [`uniform`](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/distributions/#uniform)                   | Any time in a range, all equally likely, when only the range is known.                                                                           | `low`, `high`                                     |
| [`triangular`](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/distributions/#triangular)             | An expert's estimate: the shortest, the most likely and the longest time.                                                                        | `low`, `mode`, `high`                             |
| [`gamma`](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/distributions/#gamma)                       | Times less variable than exponential. A whole-number shape is the Erlang distribution: that many exponential steps in a row.                     | `shape`, `scale`                                  |
| [`weibull`](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/distributions/#weibull)                   | Time to failure: a shape below 1 fails early, a shape above 1 wears out.                                                                         | `shape`, `scale`                                  |
| [`empirical`](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/distributions/#empirical)               | Times taken from real data, when no family fits.                                                                                                 | `values` with `weights`, or `edges` with `counts` |

The rules for each family's parameters:

- `exponential`: `rate` above 0, in events per second: 0.5 is one every 2 seconds on average, 2.0 is two a second. It is the one parameter that is not a time, so it takes no duration.
- `normal`: `mean`, and `std` 0 or more (0 when left out). A `std` of 0 gives the mean every time. A draw can be negative, and every time is raised to at least 0.00001 seconds. In a wide normal, these raised draws raise the mean, so use `truncated_normal` instead.
- `truncated_normal`: `mean`, `std` 0 or more, and `low`, 0 when left out. With `std` 0, `mean` must be at least `low`. A draw below `low` is thrown away and drawn again, so no draws pile up at the limit. The mean is therefore the truncated distribution's own: 1.29 seconds for `mean: 1, std: 1, low: 0`. The higher `low` is above the mean, the fewer plain draws are kept. So when `low` is more than half a standard deviation above the mean, `truncated_normal` draws from an exponential proposal instead (Robert, 1995), which stays exact and fast for any `low`.
- `lognormal`: `mean` above 0 and `std` 0 or more (0 when left out). Both describe the times you get, not the underlying normal. desflow converts them.
- `constant`: `value` 0 or more. It uses no random number at all.
- `uniform`: `low` and `high`, with `low < high`. The mean is halfway between them.
- `triangular`: `low`, `mode` and `high`, all required, with `low <= mode <= high` and `low < high`. The mean is (low + mode + high) ÷ 3.
- `gamma`: `shape` and `scale`, both above 0. The mean is shape × scale and the variance shape × scale². From a mean and a standard deviation: shape = (mean ÷ std)² and scale = std² ÷ mean, so a mean of 1.5 seconds with a std of 0.5 is shape 9 and scale 0.1667.
- `weibull`: `shape` and `scale`, both above 0. The mean is scale × gamma(1 + 1 ÷ shape), where gamma is the gamma function.
- `empirical`: either `values`, each equally likely unless the optional `weights` give one weight per value; or a histogram of `edges` and `counts`, with one count per bin. A histogram draw picks a bin in proportion to its count, then any time inside the bin, all equally likely. Weights and counts are 0 or more and add up to more than 0, and edges increase. The lists are taken when the model is loaded, so an `empirical` distribution has no registry path and does not change while the run goes on.

`desflow dist` lists the families, and `desflow dist <family>` prints one family's parameters and rules. With `--mean` and `--std` it converts them to the family's parameters, so the gamma above needs no arithmetic:

```bash
desflow dist gamma --mean 1.5 --std 0.5
```

```text
parameters: shape 9, scale 0.166667
YAML: {dist: gamma, shape: 9, scale: 0.166667}
Python: dist="gamma", shape=9, scale=0.166667
```

The last two lines are the service in a blueprint and in the builder. [Command Line](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/cli/#convert-parameters) shows the other conversions.

Three of these families in a blueprint: a labelling time of at least 0.2 seconds, a station that fails more often as it wears, a histogram of measured packing times with three bins, and a scanning time of 0.5 seconds four times in five and 2 seconds otherwise:

```yaml
# under services: a hard minimum, a time to failure, a histogram of data, and
# weighted values
labelling: {dist: truncated_normal, mean: 1 s, std: 1 s, low: 0.2 s}
station_failure: {dist: weibull, shape: 1.5, scale: 10 min}
measured_packing: {dist: empirical, edges: [1 s, 2 s, 3 s, 4 s], counts: [5, 3, 2]}
scanning: {dist: empirical, values: [0.5 s, 2 s], weights: [4, 1]}
```

```python
# A hard minimum, a time to failure, a histogram of data, and weighted values
app.add_service("labelling", dist="truncated_normal", mean=1.0, std=1.0, low=0.2)
app.add_service("station_failure", dist="weibull", shape=1.5, scale=600)
app.add_service(
    "measured_packing", dist="empirical", edges=[1, 2, 3, 4], counts=[5, 3, 2]
)
app.add_service("scanning", dist="empirical", values=[0.5, 2], weights=[4, 1])
```

Each is a `DistributionConfig` with the same parameters in seconds, such as `DistributionConfig(dist="weibull", shape=1.5, scale=600)`.

An arrival or a service takes the same form for every family: `dist`, and the parameters in that family's row of the table. An exponential arrival, in the three ways to write it:

```yaml
# under arrivals: an order every 2 seconds on average
orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack}
```

```python
# An order every 2 s on average, each starting the task pack
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5, spawn="pack")
```

```python
gap = DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)  # an order every 2 s on average
```

An arrival draws its gap from data in the same way. Here a batch arrives 1 second after the last one three times in four, and 5 seconds after it otherwise:

```yaml
# under arrivals: a gap of 1 second three times in four, and 5 seconds otherwise
batches: {dist: empirical, values: [1 s, 5 s], weights: [3, 1], spawn: pack}
```

```python
# A gap of 1 s three times in four, and 5 s otherwise
app.add_arrival(
    "batches", dist="empirical", values=[1, 5], weights=[3, 1], spawn="pack"
)
```

`DistributionConfig(dist="empirical", values=[1, 5], weights=[3, 1])` is the gap.

### Durations

In a blueprint, every time-valued parameter takes a duration as well as a number of seconds: `mean`, `std`, `low`, `mode`, `high`, `scale` and `value`, and the `values` and `edges` of an `empirical`. A plain number is seconds. `rate` stays a number per second.

```yaml
# under services: every time-valued parameter takes a duration
support_call: {dist: lognormal, mean: 5 min, std: 3 min}
```

The builder takes seconds: `app.add_service("support_call", dist="lognormal", mean=300, std=180)`.

The low-level API takes seconds: `DistributionConfig(dist="lognormal", mean=300, std=180)`.

### Seeding

A seed makes every draw the same on every run:

```yaml
# The same draws on every run; leave it out to draw a seed and log it
random_seed: 42
```

`desflow run arrivals_services.yaml --seed 7` overrides it without editing the file.

```python
# The same draws on every run; leave it out to draw a seed and log it
app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0, random_seed=42)
```

```python
sampler = Sampler(seed=42)  # the same draws on every run
```

In the low-level API you draw yourself, from the current values:

```python
seconds = sampler.sample(packing)  # one draw, in seconds, from the current values
```

A run without a seed draws one and logs it, so it can be repeated: `desflow run` logs the command with `--seed`, and a builder run logs the value to pass as `random_seed`:

```text
No random_seed was given, so this run uses 3166812249. Pass random_seed=3166812249 to repeat it.
```

A low-level `Sampler()` with no seed draws nothing at random, as [How It Works](#how-it-works) explains. [Randomness and Seeds](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/randomness-and-seeds/index.md) shows seeds in use.

### Replay

An arrival can take its times from recorded rows instead of a distribution. Each row of a CSV or Parquet file, or of a list of dicts, becomes one entity at the row's time. The fields named in `fields` become the entity's attributes. Here each row of `local_replay_orders.csv` is an order, at its time in seconds from the start of the run:

```yaml
arrivals:
  orders:
    replay:
      # A CSV or Parquet file, relative to this blueprint
      path: ../local_replay_orders.csv
      time: time
      unit: s
      fields: [order_id, items]
    spawn: pack
```

```python
# A CSV or Parquet file, or a list of dicts
.add_arrival_replay(
    "orders", TRACE, time="time", unit="s", fields=["order_id", "items"]
)
```

`add_arrival_replay` takes `spawn=` as `add_arrival` does, which starts the named task for each row. This example writes an `@app.arrival_loop` of its own instead, where `wait_for_arrival("orders")` waits for the next row.

```python
def replay(env, sampler, packers):
    """Starts one order at each row's time, carrying the row's fields."""
    rows = read_trace(TRACE, time="time", unit="s", fields=["order_id", "items"])
    for number, row in enumerate(rows, start=1):
        yield env.timeout(row.time - env.now)
        key = f"orders-{number}"
        env.process(pack(env, sampler, packers, key, number - 1, row.fields))
```

`read_trace` reads and checks the rows, and returns each with its simulation `time`, row `number` and `fields`.

`unit` is `ms`, `s`, `min` or `h` from the start of the run, or `timestamp` for a date and time, placed on the run's clock from `logical_start_time`. The rows must be in time order, and the arrival follows these rules:

- Rows at equal times arrive at that time, in the order of the file.
- A row before the start stops the run, and rows at or after `until` never arrive.
- A row without a valid time stops the run, unless `on_invalid` is `skip`, which leaves it out with a warning.
- After the last row, the arrival stops and logs one INFO line.

A Parquet file needs the `parquet` extra. A replayed arrival has no registry path. [Local Replay](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/local-replay/index.md) compares a recorded morning with a model of it.

______________________________________________________________________

## How It Works

**One registry of distributions.** Every family is declared once, in `desflow.core.distributions.DISTRIBUTIONS`, with its parameters, its range rules, how to draw from it, its mean and variance, and what it gives with no random generator. The YAML models, the builder, `DistributionConfig`, the `Sampler` and the registry's live paths all read it, so they accept the same families and parameters. These are 200,000 draws from each family:

**A draw reads the live configuration.** A `DistributionConfig` holds the family and its parameters. `Sampler.sample(config)` reads the parameters at the moment it is called, so a change made while the run goes on applies from the next draw. A task draws its service time once it has its resource and has published `started`. The arrival loop draws the next gap when it starts waiting. Every value is raised to at least 0.00001 seconds, so a time is never 0 or negative.

**One random stream per distribution.** A seeded `Sampler` makes one generator for each name: NumPy's `SeedSequence(seed, spawn_key=(CRC32 of the name,))`. When the registry registers a distribution, it names it by its path without the sim id, such as `arrival.orders` or `service.packing`, and every draw from that distribution comes from that stream. Probability routing draws from `route.<task>` in the same way, as [Task Flow](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/task-flow/index.md) describes. Each stream depends only on the seed and the distribution's name. Adding a distribution therefore leaves every other one's draws unchanged. The name leaves out the sim id, so renaming the simulation does not change them either:

In the low-level API, a `DistributionConfig` that was never registered draws from the `Sampler`'s main generator instead. Your own code can take a stream of its own with `sampler.generator("<name>")`:

A blueprint and a builder model register every distribution, so each draws from its own stream. Code of your own takes a stream from `context.sampler.generator("<name>")` once the run is built.

A blueprint and a builder model register every distribution, so each draws from its own stream. Code of your own takes a stream from `context.sampler.generator("<name>")` once the run is built.

```python
# Each registered distribution draws from the stream named by its path without
# the sim id; register the parameters, and sample() picks the stream
registry = SimulationRegistry(simpy.Environment())
registry.register_sim_parameter(SimParameter(sim_id="Shop", arrival={"orders": gap}))
assert gap.stream == "arrival.orders"
stream = Sampler(seed=42).generator("arrival.orders")  # the same seed, the same name
assert stream is not None and sampler.sample(gap) == stream.exponential(2.0)
```

`Sampler(rng=np.random.default_rng(42))` draws the same numbers as `Sampler(seed=42)`, because the streams come from the generator's seed.

**No random generator.** A `Sampler()` with neither a seed nor a generator draws nothing at random: every sample is the distribution's mean, or a constant's value. A run then uses the mean of every input and gives the same output each time, which suits a test. That output is not the model's average result: [variation lengthens waits](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/#variation-lengthens-waits), so a run on mean inputs gives shorter waits than random runs give on average. A `truncated_normal` gives its `mean` or its `low`, whichever is higher.

A blueprint and a builder model always have a random generator: the `random_seed`, or a seed drawn and logged at the start. Draws at the mean are for a low-level test.

A blueprint and a builder model always have a random generator: the `random_seed`, or a seed drawn and logged at the start. Draws at the mean are for a low-level test.

```python
fixed = Sampler()  # no random generator: every draw is the mean, or the value
assert fixed.sample(packing) == 3.0 and fixed.sample(gap) == 2.0
assert fixed.sample(checking) == 1.5  # shape × scale
```

**SimPy and desflow.** SimPy has no distributions: a SimPy model draws its own times, usually with `random.expovariate(0.5)` for a gap of 2 seconds on average, and writes `yield env.timeout(...)` with the result. Nothing checks the parameters, a negative draw makes `timeout` raise, and the parameters are ordinary variables. desflow names each distribution and its parameters once, checks them, keeps them in the registry, and gives each a stream of its own. [SimPy and desflow](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/simpy/index.md) compares the two.

______________________________________________________________________

## Under Live Changes

Each scalar parameter a family takes has a path in the registry: `<sim_id>.arrival.<name>.rate` for an exponential arrival, `<sim_id>.service.<name>.mean` and `.std` for a normal service, `.low`, `.mode` and `.high` for a triangular, `.shape` and `.scale` for a gamma or weibull, `.value` for a constant. A scenario, an ingress message or a process changes it while the run goes on, as [Live Parameters](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/live-parameters/index.md) explains:

- The next draw uses the new value. An order already being packed keeps the time it drew, and the arrival already being waited for keeps its gap.
- An update is checked on a copy of the configuration, by the same rules as at build. A value outside the range is refused with an error log line, and the old value stays:

A scenario step or an ingress message with an out-of-range value is refused in the same way, with the same error log line.

A scenario step or an ingress message with an out-of-range value is refused in the same way, with the same error log line.

```python
packing_path = "Shop.service.packing.std"
registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(sim_id="Shop", service={"packing": packing})
)
registry.update(packing_path, -1.0)  # refused with an error log line
assert registry.get(packing_path).value == 0.5  # the old value stays
```

```text
Invalid value for 'Shop.service.packing.std': normal std must be 0 or more, got -1.0. Update ignored.
```

- The family is fixed when the model is built. There is no path that turns a `normal` into an `exponential`. An update to a parameter the family does not have, such as `.rate` on a normal, is refused as an unknown path, with a warning.
- An `empirical` distribution has no paths: its lists are taken at load.

______________________________________________________________________

## Stability and Limits

- **Refused at build.** The same checks refuse a bad distribution when the model is built. These three are an out-of-range `std`, a parameter `normal` does not take, and a `mode` above `high`:

  `desflow run` and `SimulationContext.from_yaml` refuse the same parameters, with the file, the line and the same message: `shop.yaml:3: services.packing: Value error, normal std must be 0 or more, got -1.0`.

  `app.add_service` and `app.add_arrival` raise the same `ValueError`, such as `normal std must be 0 or more, got -1.0`.

  ```python
  refused: List[Dict[str, Any]] = [
      {"dist": "normal", "mean": 3.0, "std": -1.0},  # out of range
      {"dist": "normal", "mean": 3.0, "rate": 2.0},  # a parameter normal does not take
      {"dist": "triangular", "low": 1.0, "mode": 3.0, "high": 2.0},  # mode above high
  ]
  for parameters in refused:
      try:
          DistributionConfig(**parameters)
      except ValueError as error:
          print(error)
  ```

  ```text
  normal std must be 0 or more, got -1.0
  normal does not take rate; it takes mean, std
  triangular needs low <= mode <= high, got low 1.0, mode 3.0, high 2.0
  ```

- **A wide `normal`.** When `std` is half of `mean`, 2.3% of draws fall below 0 and are raised to the floor. When `std` equals `mean`, 15.9% are. The raised draws push the average time up: the 200,000 draws of the normal panel in the chart above, with mean 1 and std 1, average 1.08, not 1. Use `truncated_normal`.

- **Rate against mean.** `exponential` takes a `rate` per second, not a mean gap: an order every 30 seconds is `rate: 0.0333`, not `30`.

- **A seed and the timestamps.** A seed fixes the draws and so the simulation times, but each record's `timestamp` also depends on when the run started, unless `logical_start_time` is set, as [Time and Pacing](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/index.md) explains.

- **Spread lengthens queues.** Two models with the same mean times but a different spread have different queues: more spread means longer waits, as [Queues and Capacity](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/queues-and-capacity/index.md) and [Choosing Inputs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/choosing-inputs/index.md) measure.

______________________________________________________________________

## Example: Local Replay

The `local-replay` example has one packer and the 40 orders of a recorded morning, which it replays from a CSV file at their times. The last order arrives at 73 seconds. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own after 120 simulation seconds.

The tutorial page [Local Replay](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/local-replay/index.md) teaches these features step by step.

**Quick Start**

`desflow examples get` downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

```bash
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get local-replay --api yaml
cd local-replay/yaml

# 3. Run it
desflow run local_replay.yaml
```

```bash
# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get local-replay --api yaml
cd local-replay/yaml

# 3. Run it
desflow run local_replay.yaml
```

# Input Fitting

A model's distributions should come from data where data exists. Input fitting takes a column of measured times and fits every distribution family desflow has. It checks each result, and also offers the data itself as an empirical distribution. It writes the chosen settings in a form a model loads. This page describes the command and the Python call, every option, each outcome and how to deal with it, and how the fitting is done.

______________________________________________________________________

## What It Is

`desflow fit` and `fit_column` fit the families of [Arrivals and Services](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/arrivals-and-services/index.md) to service durations or to the gaps between arrivals, by maximum likelihood with scipy. Maximum likelihood chooses the parameters under which the measured values are most probable. Each family's fit becomes one row of a table, with its parameters in seconds and its diagnostics, and the best is marked. [Fitting the Inputs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/fit-the-inputs/index.md) fits the shop's 40 packing times and shows why the best by the numbers still needs checking against the model's answer. [Fit a Distribution](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/analysis/fit-a-distribution/index.md) fits the gaps of an order log.

Fitting needs the `fit` extra, which installs scipy and matplotlib: `pip install "desflow[fit]"`. A base install runs without the extra: desflow imports scipy and matplotlib only when a fit runs.

______________________________________________________________________

## How to Use It

### Fit a Column

```bash
# Fit the packing times, write the best fit and plot every candidate
desflow fit packing_times.csv --column packing_seconds --unit s --lower 0 --out packing_fit.yaml --plot fit.png
```

The command prints the table, writes the best candidate's settings to `--out` and the plot to `--plot`. It exits with status 1 when no candidate is usable, and with status 2 when the input is invalid.

```python
times = read_column(DATA, "packing_seconds")
result = fit_column(times, unit="s", lower=0)
print(result.text())  # every candidate, its status and diagnostics
```

```python
result = fit_column(read_column(DATA, "packing_seconds"), unit="s", lower=0)
print(result.text())  # every candidate, its status and diagnostics
PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    # An order every 1.25 s on average (rate 0.8)
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.8)},
    # The best candidate's settings, such as dist="triangular", low=0.546332
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(**result.settings())},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=2, max_cap=4)},
)
```

`read_column(path, column)`, imported with `from desflow.analysis.fit import read_column`, reads one CSV column as text. `fit_column` takes any list of numbers or text, where an empty cell or None is a missing value.

### Options

| Command option       | `fit_column` argument | What it sets                                                                                                             | Default               |
| -------------------- | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------- |
| `--column`           |                       | the CSV column to fit                                                                                                    | required              |
| `--unit`             | `unit`                | the data's unit: `ms`, `s`, `min` or `h`; the settings are always in seconds                                             | `s`                   |
| `--candidates`       | `candidates`          | the families to try, such as `gamma,lognormal`; an unknown name is refused                                               | every family          |
| `--lower`, `--upper` | `lower`, `upper`      | the plausible range, in the data's unit: a value outside it is invalid, and a family that can draw outside it is flagged | none                  |
| `--bins`             | `bins`                | offer the empirical distribution as a histogram with this many bins                                                      | the values themselves |
| `--min-count`        | `min_count`           | the fewest values a family is fitted to                                                                                  | 20                    |
| `--tolerance`        | `tolerance`           | how far a fitted mean and standard deviation may be from the data's, as a share of the data's                            | 0.25                  |
| `--drop-invalid`     | `drop_invalid`        | leave invalid values out, counted, rather than stopping                                                                  | off                   |
| `--out`              | `result.yaml()`       | write the best candidate's settings as YAML                                                                              |                       |
| `--plot`             | `result.plot(path)`   | draw the data against the best candidate                                                                                 |                       |

A value is invalid when it is not a number, is not finite, or lies outside `--lower` and `--upper`. The table's first line counts the rows, and the values used, missing and invalid.

### Read the Result

`fit_column` returns a `FitResult`:

- **`table`:** one row per candidate, with `family`, `status`, `reason`, `parameters`, `log_likelihood`, `aic`, `ks_statistic`, `ks_p_value`, `bounds` and `best`. `aic` is the [AIC](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/a-simulation-study/#aic-and-the-ks-test), where lower is better.
- **`best`:** the best candidate's family.
- **`settings(kind=None)`:** the settings of the best, or of the family `kind`, for `add_service(name, **settings)`. A family that is not usable is refused, and the error names those that are.
- **`text()`:** the table as the command prints it.
- **`yaml(kind=None)`:** the settings as the YAML file `--out` writes.
- **`plot(path, kind=None)`:** the PNG `--plot` draws: the data's histogram over values generated from the candidate, and a Q-Q plot, which puts each sorted data value against the generated value at the same quantile. Points on the diagonal mean that the two agree.

The settings have six significant digits, the same numbers the YAML file holds, so a script and a blueprint that load one fit draw the same values.

### How the Best Is Chosen

The best is the fitted family with the lowest [AIC](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/a-simulation-study/#aic-and-the-ks-test) among those that cannot draw outside `--lower` and `--upper`. When every value is the same, it is `constant`. When no family within the bounds fitted, it is `empirical`, which never draws outside the data's range. Only when there is no empirical candidate is a fitted family that can draw outside the bounds chosen. A family that is rejected, did not fit or was skipped is never chosen.

When two families' AIC are too close to tell them apart, as [AIC and the KS Test](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/a-simulation-study/#aic-and-the-ks-test) explains, check what the choice changes in the model's answer, as [Fitting the Inputs](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/inputs/fit-the-inputs/#does-the-choice-matter) does.

### Outcomes

Each candidate ends with one status. Every one but `fitted` has a reason, and none stops the fit:

| Status                      | Cause                                                                                        | What to do                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `skipped`                   | fewer values than `--min-count`                                                              | collect more data, or use the `empirical` candidate, which is still offered; lower `--min-count` only if the values are known to be typical                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `skipped`                   | a value of 0 or below, for `gamma`, `weibull` or `lognormal`, which are defined above 0 only | find out what the zeros are: rounding (record finer times), a different kind of event (remove it from the data), or real zero durations (use a family with no positive-only support, such as `exponential` or `truncated_normal`)                                                                                                                                                          |
| `skipped`                   | every value is the same, so only `constant` and `empirical` are fitted                       | use `constant`, or check that the column is the one meant                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `skipped`                   | a value below `low`, for `truncated_normal`, whose `low` is `--lower`, or 0                  | set `--lower` to the true lower bound                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `did not fit`               | scipy's fit raised an error or its search did not settle; the reason is scipy's message      | the data is far from that family's shape: choose another family; more data can help                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `rejected`                  | a fitted parameter is not finite or is out of the family's range                             | as for `did not fit`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `rejected`                  | the fitted mean or standard deviation is more than `--tolerance` from the data's             | look for outliers: correct or remove a value that is a recording error, and keep one that is real. `--upper` leaves out values above it only with `--drop-invalid`; without it, such a value stops the fit with status 2. With `--upper`, only the families bounded above, `uniform` and `triangular`, can be chosen as best, then `empirical`. Or use `--bins` for an empirical histogram |
| `rejected`                  | a value lies where the family cannot draw                                                    | as for the zeros above                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `fitted` with a bounds note | the family can draw below `--lower` or above `--upper`, such as `normal` below 0             | it is chosen only when nothing within the bounds fits; prefer a family with the right support                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

The command fails only when no candidate is usable, `empirical` included. `empirical` is unusable only when there are no values, or when `--candidates` leaves it out.

### Load the Settings

`!include` reads a mapping from another file, relative to the blueprint, so the file `--out` wrote is loaded and checked as if it were written in place:

```yaml
services:
  # The fitted distribution, read from the file desflow fit wrote
  packing: !include packing_fit.yaml
```

An arrival also needs its `spawn`, so the include names the file and adds keys to it: `orders: !include {file: fitted/orders.yaml, spawn: pack}`. A YAML syntax error in the included file, or a file that is not a mapping, names that file and its line. A wrong key or value in it is reported at the blueprint's `!include` line, and so is a missing file. A file that includes itself, directly or through another, is refused at the `!include` that closes the loop.

```python
# The best candidate's settings, such as dist="triangular", low=0.546332
.add_service("packing", **result.settings())
```

`DistributionConfig(**result.settings())`, as the `fit` section above shows.

______________________________________________________________________

## How It Works

**Data first.** The values are read, and missing ones are counted and left out. Invalid ones are refused or, with `--drop-invalid`, counted and left out. They are converted to seconds. Then each family is checked against the data before it is fitted: enough values, positive values where the family needs them, and not a constant column.

**Maximum likelihood, location at 0.** desflow's families have no location parameter: a gamma or a Weibull starts at 0. scipy can also fit a location, which moves the start of the distribution to wherever the data suggests. For the tutorials' 40 packing times plus one outlier of 120 seconds, a free location puts a gamma's start at 0.70 seconds, the smallest value, with a shape of 0.21 and a scale of 81. desflow has no parameter for that start. So the location of `exponential`, `gamma`, `weibull` and `lognormal` is fixed at 0, and each fit is converted to desflow's parameters:

| Family             | Fitted with                                                                                        | desflow's parameters                                                      |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `exponential`      | `scipy.stats.expon.fit(x, floc=0)`                                                                 | `rate` = 1 ÷ scale                                                        |
| `normal`           | `scipy.stats.norm.fit(x)`                                                                          | `mean`, `std`                                                             |
| `lognormal`        | `scipy.stats.lognorm.fit(x, floc=0)`                                                               | the variable's `mean` = scale × e^(s²/2) and `std` = mean × √(e^(s²) − 1) |
| `truncated_normal` | the likelihood of `scipy.stats.truncnorm` with `low` fixed, maximised by `scipy.optimize.minimize` | `mean`, `std`, `low`                                                      |
| `uniform`          | `scipy.stats.uniform.fit(x)`                                                                       | `low`, `high`                                                             |
| `triangular`       | `scipy.stats.triang.fit(x)`                                                                        | `low`, `mode`, `high`                                                     |
| `gamma`            | `scipy.stats.gamma.fit(x, floc=0)`                                                                 | `shape`, `scale`                                                          |
| `weibull`          | `scipy.stats.weibull_min.fit(x, floc=0)`                                                           | `shape`, `scale`                                                          |
| `constant`         | every value is the same                                                                            | `value`                                                                   |
| `empirical`        | the values, or `numpy.histogram` with `--bins`                                                     | `values`, or `edges` and `counts`                                         |

Each fit runs on its own, so one that fails is a row, not a crash.

**Checks.** Every fitted result is checked before it can be chosen. Each parameter must be finite and within the family's rules, the same rules a blueprint's distribution is checked against. The family's mean and standard deviation, from desflow's own formulas, must be within `--tolerance` of the data's. A result that fails is `rejected` with the reason. Some bad fits still pass these checks. Fitted to a gamma, the three values 1.0, 1.0000001 and 1.0000002 give a shape of 1.4 × 10¹⁴ and a scale of 7.1 × 10⁻¹⁵, with the right mean and spread. `--min-count` guards against such fits: no family is fitted to fewer values than `--min-count`.

**Diagnostics.** For each fitted family, the table gives the log-likelihood of the data and the AIC. The k in the AIC counts only the fitted parameters: a fixed location does not count. The table also gives the [Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/a-simulation-study/#aic-and-the-ks-test) and p-value from `scipy.stats.kstest`. The p-value assumes the parameters were known in advance. They were estimated from the same data, so the p-value is approximate and tends to be too high. `empirical` has no AIC.

**Plot.** The generated values are drawn through desflow's `Sampler`, seeded, with the same smallest delay a run applies, so the plot shows what a run draws and repeats exactly.

______________________________________________________________________

## Stability and Limits

- **Size of the extra.** These sizes were measured in new Python 3.12 environments on macOS. scipy 1.18.1 takes about 70 MB installed with uv, and about 100 MB with pip, which also compiles bytecode. Its download is 20 to 37 MB, depending on the platform. matplotlib and its dependencies, beyond the NumPy desflow already needs, add about 55 MB with uv and about 70 MB with pip. Fitting is not in the base install because of these sizes.
- **Local files only.** The command reads a CSV file. Reading from a database or an object store, and automated selection beyond the lowest AIC, come later.
- **A fit is not a validation.** A family that fits the data well can still change the model's answer, and a model whose inputs fit can still answer the question badly. Compare the model's output with the real system's, as [Experiment Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/experiment-results/#compare-with-observed-values) does.
- **One column at a time.** Each column is fitted on its own, so a dependence between two inputs, such as larger orders taking longer to pack, is not captured.

______________________________________________________________________

# Task Flow: the Next Task by Condition or Probability

An entity rarely leaves after completing just one task. An order is checked, perhaps wrapped as a gift, packed, sometimes packed again, and shipped. This page shows how a finished task chooses the next one, and what the entity carries from task to task.

______________________________________________________________________

## What It Is

A **flow** is the sequence of tasks one entity passes through. Each task names what follows it: always the same task, the first of several rules whose condition holds, or a task drawn at random by weight. A rule can send the entity back to a task it has passed, for **rework**. A task that names nothing ends the flow. The entity keeps its key and its **attributes** through the whole flow, and every task can read them.

[A Flow of Tasks](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/shop-logic/flow-of-tasks/index.md) builds a pick, pack and ship flow step by step.

______________________________________________________________________

## How to Use It

### Choose the Next Task

`next` takes one of these forms:

- **A task name**, `next: pack_order`: always that task.
- **Rules**, `when` with an optional `default`: each rule is a condition and a task. Rules are tried in order. The first matching rule wins, and `default` applies if none matches. With no default and no matching rule, the flow ends.
- **Weights**, below.
- **In the builder, a function** that takes the `Upstream` and returns a task name or `None`.

```yaml
check_order:
  payload: {total: 80}
  # Rules are tried in order; the first match wins. Otherwise, use the default.
  next:
    when:
      - {condition: "level.stock == 0", task: backorder}
      - {condition: "payload.total >= 100 or attr.gift == 1", task: wrap_gift}
    default: pack_order
```

```python
# Rules are tried in order; the first match wins. Otherwise, use the default.
@app.task(
    next={
        "when": [
            {"condition": "level.stock == 0", "task": "backorder"},
            {
                "condition": "payload.total >= 100 or attr.gift == 1",
                "task": "wrap_gift",
            },
        ],
        "default": "pack_order",
    }
)
def check_order(task_id: int):
    return {"total": 80}
```

```python
# The same rules as next, as a Router; choose() returns the next task's name
route = Router(
    {
        "when": [{"condition": "attr.gift == 1", "task": "wrap_gift"}],
        "default": "pack_order",
    }
)
order = Entity("orders-1", "orders", {"gift": 0})  # key, arrival, attributes
finished = Upstream(0, order.key, order.attributes, {"total": 80})
assert route.choose(finished, env=None) == "pack_order"
```

A `Router` takes the same rules as `next`. When a task finishes, its process builds the `Upstream`, asks `route.choose(upstream, env, levels=...)` for the next task's name, and starts that task with the same entity. `env` lets a condition read `registry[...]` and `t`. `levels`, a mapping from store and container names to the objects, lets it read `level.<name>`.

The condition is evaluated when the task finishes, after its `set`. `payload.` reads the payload of the task that just finished, `attr.` the entity's attributes, `level.` a store's or container's level, and `registry["..."]` a live parameter. [How It Works](#how-it-works) lists everything a condition can use.

### Weights

`weights` maps task names to numbers, and the next task is drawn in proportion to them. The draw comes from a random stream of the routing task's own, `route.<task>`, so a seeded run repeats it and it changes no other draw:

```yaml
pack_order:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  get: {container: stock, amount: 1}
  payload: {event_type: order_packed}
  # A task drawn in proportion to its weight: one in ten is packed again
  next:
    weights: {ship_order: 9, pack_order: 1}
```

```python
# A task drawn in proportion to its weight: one in ten is packed again
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    get={"container": "stock", "amount": 1},
    next={"weights": {"ship_order": 9, "pack_order": 1}},
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}
```

```python
# Weights draw from a generator: the routing task's own stream, as the builder's do
rework = Router({"weights": {"ship_order": 9, "pack_order": 1}})
rework.rng = Sampler(seed=42).generator("route.pack_order")
choices = [rework.choose(finished) for _ in range(1000)]
```

### Attributes

An arrival gives each new entity its starting `attributes`, and a task's `set` changes them when the task finishes. Each entity gets its own copy. Attributes are not published: a condition reads them as `attr.<name>`, and a payload includes them only when it asks.

```yaml
arrivals:
  # Each order starts with these attributes, read as attr.gift
  # An order every 2 s on average (rate 0.5)
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: check_order, attributes: {gift: 0}}
  # A gift order every 10 s on average (rate 0.1)
  gifts: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.1, spawn: check_order, attributes: {gift: 1}}
```

```yaml
# Applied to the order's attributes when the task finishes
set: {backordered: 1}
```

A task's `attributes` list adds the named attributes to a mapping payload, as `ship_order` does in the full blueprint, [`task_flow.yaml`](https://github.com/jaehyeon-kim/desflow/blob/v0.27.0/docs/snippets/yaml/task_flow.yaml).

```python
# Each order starts with these attributes, read as attr.gift
# An order every 2 s on average (rate 0.5)
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5, attributes={"gift": 0})
# A gift order every 10 s on average (rate 0.1)
app.add_arrival("gifts", dist="exponential", rate=0.1, attributes={"gift": 1})
```

```python
# `set` is applied to the order's attributes when the task finishes
@app.task(service_id="supplying", set={"backordered": 1}, next="check_order")
def backorder(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_backordered"}
```

An `Entity(key, arrival, attributes)` carries them. The process updates `entity.attributes` itself after a task, as the low-level tab of [A Flow of Tasks](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/shop-logic/flow-of-tasks/index.md) shows.

### Entity Key

Each arrival starts a new entity, keyed by the arrival's name and a counter from 1: `orders-1`, `orders-2`. Every event of every task in its flow carries that key as its record key, so a sink can follow one order through the whole flow. Kafka sends records with the same key to one partition, so it keeps one order's events in order. The builder can replace the key with a function of the counter:

A blueprint uses the default key.

```python
# Keys ret-00001, ret-00002 instead of returns-1, from the counter, which starts at 1
# A return every 20 s on average (rate 0.05)
app.add_arrival("returns", dist="exponential", rate=0.05, key=lambda n: f"ret-{n:05d}")
```

The process that creates each `Entity` gives it its key.

Below are the finished events of `gifts-5` in [`task_flow.yaml`](https://github.com/jaehyeon-kim/desflow/blob/v0.27.0/docs/snippets/yaml/task_flow.yaml), the blueprint whose parts this page shows. The gift order is checked while the shelf is empty, backordered, checked again, wrapped, packed and shipped, all under one key:

```text
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 19.216, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'check_order', 'instance': 13, 'value': {'total': 80}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 49.216, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'backorder', 'instance': 1, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_backordered'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 49.216, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'check_order', 'instance': 34, 'value': {'total': 80}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 52.216, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'wrap_gift', 'instance': 7, 'value': {'event_type': 'gift_wrapped'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 54.362, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 29, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 54.362, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'ship_order', 'instance': 27, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_shipped', 'gift': 1, 'backordered': 1}}
```

### Upstream

A task started by `next` receives what the task before it handed on, the `Upstream`: the finished task's instance id, the entity's key and attributes, and the finished task's payload. A builder function gets it by declaring a parameter called `upstream`, and gets the entity by declaring `entity`. A function that declares neither is called without them. The first task of a flow gets `upstream=None`.

A blueprint task has no function to declare `upstream`. Its `payload` names the attributes it carries, and its `next` conditions read the finished task's payload as `payload.<field>` and the entity's attributes as `attr.<name>`.

```python
# A function declaring `upstream` receives what the previous task handed on,
# and `entity` the order itself; a payload includes attributes only when it asks
@app.task()
def ship_order(task_id: int, upstream, entity):
    return {
        "event_type": "order_shipped",
        "packed_by": upstream.task_id,  # the instance of pack_order before it
        "gift": entity.attributes.get("gift"),
        "backordered": entity.attributes.get("backordered"),
    }


# A rule can also be a function of the Upstream, returning a task name or None
@app.task(next=lambda upstream: "check_order" if upstream.payload["ok"] else None)
def inspect_return(task_id: int):
    return {"ok": False}
```

The low-level API has no `Upstream`: a process holds the order and its attributes itself, and decides the next step in Python.

______________________________________________________________________

## How It Works

**Conditions.** A condition is a Python expression, parsed with Python's `ast` module and checked against a list of what is allowed before it is ever evaluated. Nothing goes through `eval`. It may use:

- numbers, `True` and `False`, and the arithmetic `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `//` and `%`;
- the comparisons `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `==` and `!=`, strings compared with `==` or `!=`, and `in` and `not in` with `items(<store>)` on the right;
- `and`, `or`, `not`, and the conditional form `a if c else b`;
- names with their source as a prefix:
  - `payload.<field>`, `attr.<name>` and `level.<name>`;
  - `users.<name>`, how many units of a resource are held, and `queue.<name>`, how many requests wait for it ([Resources](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/resources/#read-the-queue-and-users));
  - `putters.<name>` and `getters.<name>`, how many puts and gets wait at a store or container;
  - `count(<store>)` and `items(<store>)`, how many items a store holds and the list of them ([Stores and Containers](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/stores-and-containers/#registry-paths-readings-and-conditions));
  - `item.<field>`, the item the task's store `get` took ([Stores and Containers](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/model-parts/stores-and-containers/#pick-an-item-or-give-up-waiting));
  - `wait.<branch>.done`, `.ok` and `.value`, the task's wait, and `signal.<name>.count`, `.ok` and `.value` ([Signals and Waiting](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/tasks-and-processes/signals-and-waiting/#wait-signals-and-child-flows));
  - `process.<name>`, `.instance` and `.target` ([Tasks and Processes](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/tasks-and-processes/processes/#how-it-works));
  - `registry["<path>"]`;
- `t`, the simulation time in seconds.

A name carries its source, so adding a payload field cannot change what an attribute of the same name means. The `registry[...]` form lets a registry path, which contains dots, be written whole. Anything else is refused with a message that names it:

A blueprint condition that uses anything else is refused when the blueprint is built, with the same message.

```python
for text in ("payload.total ** 2", "x > 1", "open('orders.csv')"):
    try:
        Expression(text)
    except ValueError as error:
        print(error)
```

The low-level API has no conditions: a process decides in Python.

```text
'payload.total ** 2' uses the operator Pow, which an expression cannot
'x > 1' uses the name 'x' (write payload.<field>, attr.<name>, level.<name>, users.<name>, queue.<name>, putters.<name>, getters.<name>, item.<field>, count(<store>), items(<store>), wait.<branch>.<part>, signal.<name>.<part>, process.<name>, registry["<path>"] or t), which an expression cannot
'open('orders.csv')' uses a Call other than count(<store>) or items(<store>), which an expression cannot
```

A blueprint is checked when it loads, and each error names its YAML line. Every condition must parse, and every task a rule names must exist. Every `level.<name>` must name a store or container, every `users.<name>` and `queue.<name>` a resource, every `putters.<name>` and `getters.<name>` a store or container, and every `count(...)` and `items(...)` a store. Every `registry["..."]` must be a path of the model. The builder makes the same checks when `run()` starts. A name that is missing when a condition is evaluated, such as a payload field, raises an error naming the expression.

**Weights.** The weights are turned into cumulative shares once. Each choice draws one uniform number from the routing task's stream and picks the task whose share it falls in.

**Starting the Next Task.** When a task finishes, it applies `set`, builds the `Upstream` and asks its rules for the next task. It starts that task as a new SimPy process, with the same entity and the next instance id from the task's counter. An arrival that spawns the task uses the same counter, so no two runs of a task share an id. In SimPy terms, one process starting the next is the whole mechanism. [SimPy and desflow](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/simpy/index.md) describes processes.

______________________________________________________________________

## Stability and Limits

- **Flow balance.** The rate into each task follows from the rates into the tasks before it and the routing shares. With weights of 9 to ship and 1 back to packing, one packing in ten sends the order back to be packed again. Every order is packed once, one in ten a second time, one in a hundred a third time, and so on. An order is therefore packed 1 + 0.1 + 0.01 + ... = 1 ÷ 0.9 = 1.11 times on average, so the packers see 11% more work than there are orders.
- **Rework raises utilisation.** Work the load out with the rework included, as [Queues and Capacity](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/queues-and-capacity/index.md) does, or a rework loop can push a resource past full use. [Queueing Basics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/queueing-basics/#utilisation) explains utilisation.
- **Refused expressions.** `**`, function calls, indexing other than `registry["..."]`, list and dictionary literals, and bare names other than `t` are refused.
- **One entity, one flow.** A task leads to at most one next task. Splitting one order into several, or joining several into one, comes after 1.0.
- **`decide` is kept free.** The task key `decide` is kept for decisions sent from outside for one entity, planned after 1.0. Today it is refused like any unknown key.

______________________________________________________________________

## Example: A Flow of Tasks

In the `flow` example, orders are picked, gift orders are wrapped, one parcel in ten is packed again, and every order is shipped. Wrapping and shipping are timed steps. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

The tutorial page [A Flow of Tasks](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/shop-logic/flow-of-tasks/index.md) teaches these features step by step.

**Quick Start**


```bash

cd flow/yaml

# 3. Find the bottleneck, with no run

# 4. Run it
```

```yaml
tasks:
  pick:
    service: picking
    resource: pickers
    payload: {event_type: order_picked}
    # The first rule that holds wins; default catches the rest.
    next:
      when:
        - {condition: "attr.gift == 1", task: wrap}
      default: pack
  wrap:
    # A timed step: a service and no resource, so no queued event and no wait.
    service: wrapping
    payload: {event_type: gift_wrapped}
    # Applied to the entity's attributes when the task finishes.
    set: {wrapped: 1}
    next: pack
  pack:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
    # Drawn from this task's own random sequence: one parcel in ten is packed again.
    next:
      weights: {ship: 9, pack: 1}
```

The whole file is [`examples/yaml/flow.yaml`](https://github.com/jaehyeon-kim/desflow/blob/v0.27.0/examples/yaml/flow.yaml).

```python
@app.task(
```
