# Custom Resource Types

A [resource](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/resources/index.md) can grant its units by a rule of your own. This page shows how to write one.

______________________________________________________________________

## What It Is

Some shops grant their units by a rule of their own, such as sharing a packer between customer classes by weight. A custom resource type replaces the rule by which a resource grants its units, and keeps the capacity that follows the registry.

______________________________________________________________________

## How to Use It

To change how a resource grants units, subclass `ResourceBase` and name the class in `type`. `ResourceBase` is built on the hooks of SimPy's `BaseResource`, as a subclass of SimPy's `Resource` is. A subclass can change these:

- Override `_do_put(request)` to decide when a request is granted, and `_do_get(release)` to decide what a release gives back.
- Set `PutQueue` to the class of the waiting line. It can be SimPy's `SortedQueue`, written `staticmethod(functools.partial(SortedQueue, maxlen=2))`.
- Set `request` to `BoundClass(MyRequest)`, for a request class that subclasses `DynamicResourceRequest`, or set `release` the same way, for a release class that subclasses `DynamicRelease`. Both base classes are in `desflow.resources.resource`.

This resource keeps how long each request waited:

```yaml
resources:
  # A subclass of ResourceBase that keeps how long each request waited
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4, type: !python shop_logic.LoggedPackers}
```

The class is in `shop_logic.py`, beside the blueprint:

```python
class LoggedPackers(ResourceBase):
    """A resource that keeps how long each request waited before it was granted."""

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.waits = []

    def _do_put(self, request):
        super()._do_put(request)
        if request.triggered:  # the request was granted just now
            self.waits.append(self.env.now - request.time)
```

```python
app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0)
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, type=LoggedPackers)
```

The class is the one the Low-level tab shows.

```python
class LoggedPackers(ResourceBase):
    """A resource that keeps how long each request waited before it was granted."""

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.waits = []

    def _do_put(self, request):
        super()._do_put(request)
        if request.triggered:  # the request was granted just now
            self.waits.append(self.env.now - request.time)
```

```python
env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop", resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=4)}
    )
)
packers = LoggedPackers(env, "Shop", "packers")


def order(env):
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        yield env.timeout(2.0)
```

______________________________________________________________________

## How It Works

`DynamicResource` is `ResourceBase` with nothing changed. The constructor is `DynamicResource`'s, because the resource reads its capacity from the registry. A subclass that defines `__init__` therefore takes `*args, **kwargs` and passes them on. A `PutQueue` of your own sets its own order and length, so it takes no `queue_limit`. The tests run each of these beside the same SimPy subclass in all three APIs.

______________________________________________________________________

## Stability and Limits

The limits of this page are listed with those of the whole section, in [Stability and Limits](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/resources/#stability-and-limits) on the Resources page.

# Time and Pacing

A run has two clocks of its own, simulation time and logical time. A run can follow the wall clock, ignore it, or ignore it at first and follow it later. This page shows how to read the current time and which parts of the environment run on each thread. [Clocks and Pacing](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/clocks-and-pacing/index.md) shows the clock settings, and [Run Length](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/run-length/index.md) shows the [warm-up](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#one-run-starts-empty) and how long a run lasts.

______________________________________________________________________

## What It Is

**Simulation time** is the number of seconds SimPy has advanced, starting at `initial_time`, 0 by default. Every record carries it as `sim_ts`. **Logical time** is the date and time a record carries as `timestamp`: `logical_start_time` plus the simulation time. `factor` sets how simulation time relates to the wall clock, and `go_live_at` switches that relation once during a run. One hour of simulation time is one hour of logical time, and takes as long on the wall clock as `factor` says:

The settings are the same on `DynamicRealtimeEnvironment`, on `SimulationContext` and in the `simulation` section of a blueprint.

______________________________________________________________________

## Pages in This Section

- [Clocks and Pacing](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/clocks-and-pacing/index.md): the logical start time, the time zone, the factor, going live, the lag and strict pacing.
- [Run Length](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/run-length/index.md): the warm-up, the initial time, how long a run lasts, stopping early, draining, stepping and running in segments.

______________________________________________________________________

## How to Use It

### Read the Current Time

`t` is the simulation clock in a condition or an expression, the value of `context.env.now` in the builder and `env.now` in the low-level API. A route or a balk can depend on it, such as `next: {when: [{condition: "t < 110", task: early}], default: late}`. A `wait: {condition: ...}` that reads `t` is not a timer. A condition is checked again only after a change of state, not as time passes. To wait for a time, use a `timeout` branch.

______________________________________________________________________

## How It Works

**What the environment holds.** A `DynamicRealtimeEnvironment` is SimPy's `RealtimeEnvironment` with four additions: the registry at `env.registry`, the ingress connectors, the egress connectors with their buffers, and the statistics at `env.stats`.

**Threads.** A run uses three threads, with queues between them. Records flow from the processes to the sinks, and parameter changes flow from the sources to the registry:

- **SimPy thread:** runs the model. When a process publishes a record, the record goes into a buffer for each sink, and a full buffer is handed to that sink's queue.
- **Egress thread:** runs the sinks' asyncio code, which drains the queues and writes to Kafka, files or databases, so network waits never stall a simulation step.
- **Ingress thread:** runs the sources, which put `(path, value)` pairs on a queue.

**Two kinds of queue.** The word queue means two different things in desflow:

- **A waiting line in the model** holds entities, such as orders waiting for a packer. A resource keeps its line in `queue`, ordered `fifo`, `lifo` or by `priority`, and a request past its `queue_limit` raises `QueueFull`. Stores and containers have lines of puts and gets that wait. These lines are what a study measures: their lengths and waits are in the records and the statistics.
- **A hand-off queue** holds data on its way between the threads above. The ingress queue has no limit, and the ingress monitor applies it. Each sink has its own queue of at most `max_queued_batches` batches. When a sink's queue is full, the simulation waits, so a slow sink slows the run instead of building a backlog. When it stays full for `drain_stall_seconds`, the run stops rather than lose records. These queues change how fast the records arrive, never what they hold.

**Processes it starts.** Besides your own processes, the environment starts these, as events of its own that `step()` and `peek()` do not count:

- an ingress monitor, which applies queued changes every 0.1 simulation seconds;
- a lag monitor, which publishes `system.simulation.lag_seconds` every `lag_interval`, at a `factor` above 0 or after going live;
- a timed flush per sink, at a `factor` above 0;
- the statistics timer;
- the warm-up reset.

They share SimPy's one event queue with the model's events, so `run()` processes them in order with the model's events. A script that steps the model never sees them. `advance()` and `finish()` run them in the same way. An environment subclass that overrides `step()` sees every event inside `run()`, desflow's own included, and only the model's events when a script steps outside `run()`.

[Clocks and Pacing](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/clocks-and-pacing/#how-it-works) describes how the pacing switches during a run, and [Run Length](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/run-length/#how-it-works) how the model and the run end.

**SimPy and desflow.** SimPy's `RealtimeEnvironment` takes one `factor` for the whole run. With `strict=True`, it raises an error when the model falls behind the wall clock. desflow runs without waiting at `factor: 0`, switches to real time at `go_live_at`, and stamps every record with a logical time. By default it reports falling behind as telemetry, and with `strict=True` it raises, as SimPy's does. [SimPy and desflow](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/simpy/index.md) compares the two.

______________________________________________________________________

## Stability and Limits

- **A run with a sink or ingress needs `until`**, or Ctrl+C, as [Run Length](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/run-length/#run-length_1) explains.
- **At `factor: 0`** no timed flush runs, so records leave a buffer when it reaches `batch_size` and at teardown, as [Egress](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/egress/index.md) explains. `LocalIngress` follows the wall clock, so its changes can land after an unpaced run has ended. A scenario follows the simulation clock. No `system.simulation.lag_seconds` is published unless `lag_interval` is set, and it reports 0 while the run is ahead of the wall clock.
- **`warmup` drops, `go_live_at` routes.** Records before a warm-up are gone. Records before `go_live_at` go to the sinks that take history.
- **A model slower than the wall clock** falls behind at `factor: 1.0` and does not catch up by skipping events. `lag_seconds` shows by how much.

# Clocks and Pacing

This page shows the clock settings of a run, described in [Time and Pacing](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/index.md): the logical start time, the time zone, the factor, going live, the lag and strict pacing.

______________________________________________________________________

## What It Is

A run's records carry dates and times, as the events of a real shop would. The logical start time and the time zone set those dates. The factor sets how fast the run goes against the wall clock: a backfill of last week runs without waiting, and a live demo runs in step with the wall clock. Going live switches from the first to the second within one run.

______________________________________________________________________

## How to Use It

### Logical Start Time

`logical_start_time` is the date and time that simulation time 0 maps to. Without it, the run uses the moment the environment is created. A run with a backdated start writes history:

`logical_start_time` under `simulation` takes `now`, a signed duration or an ISO datetime. This blueprint starts a day before the file is loaded:

```yaml
# Read against the moment the file is loaded: a day of history up to now
logical_start_time: -1d
```

```python
app = SimulationContext(
    sim_id="Shop",
    factor=0.0,
    logical_start_time=datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(days=7),  # a week
)
```

`DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(logical_start_time=...)` takes the same datetime.

A datetime without an offset is read in the run's time zone, described next. In a blueprint it takes `now`, a signed duration such as `-7d`, or an ISO datetime, as [YAML Blueprints](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/writing-a-model/blueprints/#times-and-durations) describes.

### Time Zone

`timezone` names the zone that record timestamps are written in, as an IANA name such as `Australia/Melbourne`. Every `timestamp` carries the offset of its moment, such as `2026-10-03T12:00:00.000+10:00`, or `+00:00` in UTC. By default the zone is that of `logical_start_time` when it has one, and UTC otherwise. A `logical_start_time` or `go_live_at` without an offset, `now`, and the default start are read in that zone:

```yaml
# Under simulation: timestamps written in Melbourne time, with its offset; the
# start and now are read in it. UTC by default
timezone: ${SIM_TIMEZONE:-Australia/Melbourne}
```

```python
# Timestamps in Melbourne time, with their offset: 2026-10-03T12:00:00.000+10:00
melbourne = SimulationContext(
    sim_id="Shop",
    factor=0.0,
    timezone="Australia/Melbourne",
    logical_start_time=datetime(2026, 10, 3, 12, 0),  # read in Melbourne time
)
```

```python
zoned = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(
    factor=0.0,
    timezone="Australia/Melbourne",
    logical_start_time=datetime(2026, 10, 3, 12, 0),
)
print(zoned.start_datetime)  # 2026-10-03 12:00:00+10:00
```

The clock runs in UTC, so a daylight-saving change in the zone never adds or drops simulation time. In Melbourne, the clocks went forward an hour on 4 October 2026. A run of 24 simulation hours from 12:00 on 3 October therefore ends at 13:00 on 4 October, `2026-10-04T13:00:00.000+11:00`. A replayed timestamp without an offset is read in the zone too.

### Factor

The wall-clock duration of a stretch of the run is its simulation duration times `factor`:

`factor` under `simulation`, here read from an environment variable:

```yaml
# An unquoted value is read after the replacement, so this is the number 0
factor: ${SIM_FACTOR:-0}
```

`SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0)` takes the same number.

```python
live = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=1.0)  # 1 simulated second takes 1 real second
twice_as_fast = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.5)  # takes half a real second
unpaced = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)  # takes no real time at all
```

- `factor: 1.0` follows the wall clock: a process that waits 5 simulation seconds waits 5 real seconds. It suits a live twin feeding a dashboard.
- `factor: 0` does not wait at all: the run goes as fast as the machine allows. It suits history, tests and experiments. At `factor: 0` each event is processed by SimPy's own `Environment.step`, without the real-time arithmetic. `strict` is not checked, because there is no wall clock to fall behind. A pending `go_live_at` is still checked before each event, and pacing starts at it.

### Go Live

`factor` applies until the logical clock reaches `go_live_at`, and from that instant the run is paced at one simulation second per real second. With a backdated `logical_start_time` and `factor: 0`, one run writes the history as fast as it can, then keeps going in real time:

```yaml
# A day of history at factor 0, then 1 simulated second per real second from now;
# when: history and when: live split the records at this instant
logical_start_time: -1d
go_live_at: now
```

`SimulationContext(factor=0.0, logical_start_time=..., go_live_at=...)` takes the same two times as datetimes.

```python
go_live_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(
    factor=0.0,  # until go_live_at
    logical_start_time=go_live_at - timedelta(days=7),
    go_live_at=go_live_at,  # from here, 1 simulated second per real second
)
```

A sink with `when: history` receives the records stamped before `go_live_at`, and one with `when: live` the rest, so the two halves can go to different places:

**Why one run rather than two.** A demo of a data lake beside a live stream usually needs two datasets: a backdated history sitting in a lake, and a live stream arriving now. They have to be the same shop, with the same packers, the same distributions and the same task ids, or the join between them is meaningless.

Producing them needs two values of `factor` that conflict. History needs `factor=0.0`, so that a week of events is generated as fast as the machine allows. A live tail needs `factor=1.0`, so that events arrive at one simulated second per real second.

Without `go_live_at`, the only way to get both is to start two processes with the same `random_seed` and the same `logical_start_time`, one fast-forwarding into Parquet and one pacing into Kafka. That costs:

- A second full execution of the same simulation, so the history is generated twice.
- The seed and the start instant are written in two places, which have to be edited together. If one changes and the other does not, the two halves stop being the same shop, with no error.
- Nothing makes the two halves meet. Each process decides on its own where its half ends, so the two halves can overlap or leave a gap.

`go_live_at` replaces both processes with one. The run generates history unpaced up to that logical instant, then switches to real-time pacing and keeps going. There is one seed, one start instant and one instant where history ends and the live tail begins.

**Three settings.** Three separate settings make up the feature, and each answers a different question.

| Setting              | Question it answers                                                             |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `logical_start_time` | Where does the logical clock start? Set it in the past to backdate the history. |
| `go_live_at`         | At which logical instant does pacing stop being `factor` and become real time?  |
| `when` on a sink     | Which sink receives each record?                                                |

They are independent. `go_live_at` changes pacing only. It never routes a record. `when` routes records only. It never changes pacing. Used together, they give the history and the live stream from one run. In a blueprint, `when: history` and `when: live` compare each record's timestamp with `go_live_at` themselves. A Python predicate has to compare with the same instant. Otherwise the records switch sinks at a different instant from the one where the pacing switches.

On a `DynamicRealtimeEnvironment`, `env.factor` reports the run's `factor`, such as `0.0`, until the logical clock reaches `go_live_at`, and `1.0` afterwards.

[Parquet History, Kafka Live](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/examples/backfill-live/index.md) builds such a run.

### Lag

At a `factor` above 0 the run follows the wall clock, and `system.simulation.lag_seconds` says how many seconds it is behind, as telemetry. `lag_interval` sets how often it is published, in simulation seconds or a duration. By default, it is published every simulation second at a `factor` above 0. At `factor: 0` it is off, because such a run is meant to be ahead of the wall clock. A run at `factor: 0` that goes live starts publishing it at the go-live instant. A `lag_interval` of 0 turns it off:

```yaml
# Under simulation: how far the run is behind the wall clock, every 10 s; by
# default off at factor 0 and every second otherwise, and 0 turns it off
lag_interval: 10 s
```

```python
# system.simulation.lag_seconds every 10 simulation seconds; 0 turns it off
paced = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, lag_interval="10 s")
```

```python
# The low-level API sets it with the sinks; the default "auto" is off at factor 0
# env.setup_egress(sinks, lag_monitor_interval=10)
```

### Strict Pacing

A paced step that starts more than `factor` real seconds late has fallen behind the wall clock. By default the run goes on and `system.simulation.lag_seconds` reports the delay. With `strict` on, the run raises `RuntimeError` (`Simulation too slow for real time (1.500s).`) instead, as SimPy's `RealtimeEnvironment` does. The setting has a different default in each API:

- **Low-level API:** `strict=True`, SimPy's default. A live script with a sink that can block passes `strict=False`.
- **Builder:** `SimulationContext(strict=False)`, the default, so that a live run with a sink goes on when the sink is slow.
- **YAML:** `simulation.strict`, default `false`.

```yaml
# Under simulation: raise RuntimeError when a paced step is more than factor
# seconds behind the wall clock; false by default, and never checked at factor 0
strict: true
```

```python
# A paced step more than factor seconds behind the wall clock raises RuntimeError;
# the builder's default is False
checked = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, strict=True)
```

```python
# The low-level API is strict unless you pass strict=False, as SimPy's is
raising = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=1.0)
tolerant = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=1.0, strict=False)
```

`strict` is never checked at `factor: 0`, including before `go_live_at`: an unpaced run has no wall clock to fall behind, and SimPy's check would raise on the first step of every unpaced script. After a pause, SimPy's `env.sync()` moves only the wall-clock anchor to now. The next event would then wait `factor` seconds for each simulation second since `env_start`. `env_start` is the start of the run, the go-live instant once the run has gone live, or the last `resume_pacing()`. `env.resume_pacing()` moves both anchors, so the next event waits `factor` seconds for each simulation second after `now`:

A context from `SimulationContext.from_yaml` runs in segments as the builder does, and resumes pacing with `app.env.resume_pacing()` in the same way.

The builder's environment is `app.env`. Call `app.env.resume_pacing()` before the next `advance()` of a run in segments, as [Run in Segments](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/run-length/#run-in-segments) describes.

```python
paused = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.01, strict=False)  # 1.0 follows the clock
paused.run(until=10)
# ... a pause, such as a stop in a debugger: the wall clock is now ahead of the run
paused.resume_pacing()  # from here, factor real seconds per simulation second
paused.run(until=20)
```

______________________________________________________________________

## How It Works

**Pacing and the switch.** Before each event, the environment checks the logical clock. At the first event at or after `go_live_at`, it sets the factor to 1.0 and moves its two anchors, `env_start` and `real_start`, so that the go-live instant counts as now. Without this move, the first paced event would wait on the wall clock for the whole backfill. The switch happens once, and always sets the factor to 1.0. A `go_live_at` at or before `logical_start_time` paces the whole run, with a warning. A run that ends before its `go_live_at` stays unpaced. A `go_live_at` or `logical_start_time` without an offset is read in the run's time zone, so the two can be compared whichever way each is written.

______________________________________________________________________

## Stability and Limits

The limits of this page are listed with those of the whole section, in [Stability and Limits](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/#stability-and-limits) on the Time and Pacing page.

# Run Length

This page shows how a run starts and ends, described in [Time and Pacing](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/index.md): the [warm-up](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#one-run-starts-empty), the initial time, the run length, stopping early, draining, stepping and running in segments.

______________________________________________________________________

## What It Is

A study decides how long to watch the shop: a working day that ends at closing time, or a long run that leaves out its empty start. These settings decide when a run starts measuring, when it stops, and what happens to the orders still in the shop at the end.

______________________________________________________________________

## How to Use It

### Warm-up

`warmup` leaves the start of a run out of what it reports. It is one time per run, in simulation seconds or a duration. No sink receives a record or telemetry stamped before it, and the built-in statistics are reset once at that moment, so they describe the rest of the run. A run without it sends everything, which is what a data generator usually wants.

```yaml
# Records and statistics start after the first 2 minutes; 0 keeps everything
warmup: ${WARMUP:-2 min}
```

```python
# No sink receives a record stamped before 10 minutes, and the statistics restart then
measured = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0, warmup="10 min")
# In the low-level API, the warm-up is set with the sinks:
# env.setup_egress(sinks, warmup=600)
```

The warm-up is an argument of the sinks, because it is the sinks that leave records out: `env.setup_egress(sinks, warmup=600)`. A run with no sink has no records to leave out. When the warm-up is set through the builder, the statistics are also reset at it.

The warm-up drops early records. `go_live_at` drops nothing, and only decides which sink gets each record. [Trusting Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/trusting-results/index.md) shows how to choose a warm-up length.

### Initial Time

`initial_time` is the reading of the simulation clock when the run starts, 0 when left out, in seconds or as a duration. A model of a shift that starts at 8 in the morning can start its clock at 8 hours. Every event time, every record's `sim_ts` and `until` then read that clock. A record's `timestamp` is still `logical_start_time` plus `sim_ts`, to within 1 millisecond, because `sim_ts` is rounded and `timestamp` is truncated:

```yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  # The clock starts at 8 h, so the first order at 8 h 10 min is at sim_ts 29400
  initial_time: 8 h
```

```python
# The clock starts at 8 hours: event times, sim_ts and until all read it
shift = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0, initial_time="8 h")
```

```python
# The clock starts at 8 hours, in seconds, as in SimPy's Environment(initial_time=)
morning = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0, initial_time=8 * 3600)
```

`until` is a clock reading too, so a run with `initial_time: 8 h` and `until: 16 h` lasts 8 hours. A scenario step's `at` and the `warmup` are different: they are lengths of time from the start of the run. Look at where each falls on the clock of that run:

With `initial_time: 8 h`, a step at `30 min` applies at 8.5 hours, and a warm-up of `10 min` ends at 8 hours 10 minutes.

The state the run starts with holds from the initial time, before the first arrival: a resource's `current_cap`, a container's `level`, a store's `items` and an arrival's `attributes`. The tests check each against plain SimPy ([SimPy Compatibility](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/simpy/compatibility/index.md)).

### Run Length

`until` is in simulation seconds. `run()` and a blueprint's `run.until` also take a duration such as `"10 min"`, `"8 hours"` or `"1 week"`. A month counts as 30 days and a year as 365.

`desflow run FILE --until TIME` overrides `run.until` for one run, without editing the file: `desflow run shop.yaml --until "10 min"` runs `shop.yaml` for 10 simulation minutes, whatever its `run.until` says.

```yaml
run:
  # A duration, such as 1 week, or a number of seconds
  until: ${RUN_FOR:-1 hour}
```

```python
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
app.run(until="1 week")  # 604,800 simulation seconds; a number is seconds too
```

`env.run(until=604800)` takes seconds only, as SimPy's `run` does.

The run stops at `until` before any event due at exactly that time, as SimPy's `run(until=...)` does: an order due at the horizon never arrives, and a task due to finish there stays unfinished. Statistics published at teardown read the model at `until`.

Events due at the same time run by priority, and then in the order they were scheduled (SimPy 4.1.2, `core.py`: `schedule` and `run`; `URGENT` and `NORMAL` in `events.py`). `run(until=...)` schedules its stop at urgent priority, so the stop comes before the ordinary events due at that time. How a scenario step or a change from an ingress connector ranks among them is in [Live Parameters](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/live-runs-and-connectors/live-parameters/#script-an-experiment). Here two orders are packed at 5 seconds, and one is due at the horizon of 10 seconds:

The order of events due at the same time belongs to the environment, so it is the same in every form. The Low-level tab shows it with three processes on one environment.

The order of events due at the same time belongs to the environment, so it is the same in every form. The Low-level tab shows it with three processes on one environment.

```python
ties = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
packed = []


def pack(name, seconds):
    yield ties.timeout(seconds)
    packed.append(name)


ties.process(pack("first", 5))
ties.process(pack("second", 5))  # due at the same time: runs after "first"
ties.process(pack("at the horizon", 10))
ties.run(until=10)
print(packed)  # ['first', 'second']: nothing due at 10 runs
```

Without `until`, SimPy runs until no events remain, and a run with an arrival never runs out of events. Neither does any run with a sink or an ingress connector, even when its own work is done. The environment's own processes repeat for as long as the run lasts. Give such a run an `until`, a `stop` or a drain, or stop it with Ctrl+C.

### Stop Early

`stop` ends the run before `until` when something happens. It takes these forms:

- `{signal: name}` ends the run at the next firing of a signal.
- `{condition: ...}` ends it at the first moment a condition holds. The condition is checked after every change of a level, a capacity, a registry value or a signal, and after every finished task.
- In the builder, `run(stop=...)` also takes a signal's name, or a function of the context that returns any SimPy event, such as `lambda context: context.env.timeout(30)`. The function is called once the run is built.
- In the low-level API, the same is SimPy's `env.run(until=event)`.

The run ends at whichever comes first, `stop` or `until`, and no other event at that moment runs after it. When both fall at the same moment, `until` ends the run, as SimPy's own `until` would.

`run()` and `finish()` return what SimPy's `env.run(until=event)` returns: the value of the event that ended the run:

| What ended the run                                           | Value returned                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A `stop` on a signal                                         | the signal's value, such as the finished payload of the task that fired it |
| A `stop` on a condition                                      | `True`                                                                     |
| A `stop` on a function's event                               | the event's own value                                                      |
| `until`, a drain, or `until` and the stop at the same moment | `None`                                                                     |

If the signal fails, the run still closes, and the sinks receive their records. Then `run()` raises the `SignalFailed` the signal failed with, as SimPy raises the exception of a failed event. `desflow run` reports it and exits with an error.

### Drain

A fixed horizon cuts the run at `until` with orders still in the shop. A **drain** stops the arrivals at `until` and keeps running until every entity in the model has left. Set it with `drain: true`, or with `drain: {limit: 1 h}` to stop at the latest 1 hour after `until`. `desflow run --drain` sets it from the command line. The environment's own processes, such as the statistics timer, never hold a drain open. The `end-conditions` example closes the shop at 120 seconds, drains for at most a minute, and stops at once if the boxes run out:

```yaml
run:
  # No new orders after closing time.
  until: 120
  # Then pack the orders in the shop, for at most 60 seconds.
  drain: {limit: 60}
  # Stop at once when the last box is taken.
  stop: {condition: level.boxes == 0}
```

```python
app.run(
    # No new orders after closing time
    until=120,
    # Then pack the orders in the shop, for at most 60 seconds
    drain={"limit": 60},
    # Stop at once when the last box is taken
    stop={"condition": "level.boxes == 0"},
)
```

`context.stop_arrivals()` stops the arrival loops by hand, as a drain does at `until`.

```python
def run_to_end(env, shop, source):
    """Runs to closing time, then drains for at most 60 s, or until no boxes are left."""
    out_of_boxes = env.event()

    def check():
        if shop["boxes"].level == 0 and not out_of_boxes.triggered:
            out_of_boxes.succeed()

    env.watch_changes(check)
    # Closing time, unless the boxes run out first, which ends the run at once
    env.run(until=env.timeout(120) | out_of_boxes)
    if out_of_boxes.triggered:
        return
    source.interrupt()  # no new orders after closing time
    packed = env.all_of([p for p in shop["orders"] if p.is_alive])
    env.run(until=packed | env.timeout(60) | out_of_boxes)
```

The low-level API writes a drain as SimPy does: interrupt the source process, then run until all the admitted processes end.

With statistics at `basic` or above, `flows.<arrival>.started`, `finished` and `in_system` say how many entities entered, left and are still in the model. From `minimal`, `tasks.<task>.in_progress` says how many instances of each task are queued or being served. [End Conditions](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/end-conditions/index.md) compares a fixed horizon with a drain.

### Step and Peek

`start()` builds everything `run()` builds and starts every process, with the clock still at its start. Two methods then move through the model one event at a time, as SimPy's `env.step()` and `env.peek()` do:

- `step()` processes the next event of the model.
- `peek()` gives the time of the next event, or infinity when none is left.

Both count only the model's events, so a script steps the model as it would in SimPy. The events desflow adds do not count: the statistics timer, the flush timers, the lag and ingress monitors, and a resource's capacity watcher. `peek()` skips them, and `step()` runs those due before the model's next event in the same call. When only desflow's events are left, `step()` raises `EmptySchedule` and `peek()` gives infinity. `finish()` and `run()` still process them.

`finish()` runs a started run on to the end that `run()` would reach (`until`, the `stop` or the end of the drain), then closes it. `run()` is `start()` followed by `finish()`. After `advance()` or `step()`, `finish()` closes the run as follows:

- When the clock has reached `until` or passed it, and there is no `stop` or `drain`, `finish()` closes the run at once, as a run that ended at `until` does.
- When `step()` brought the clock to exactly `until`, the records hold the run's records, which end with the final statistics. They also hold the records of the events at `until` that `step()` processed, as in SimPy. A statistics reading due at `until` is not published again, and the close adds only the values that changed after it.
- After steps past `until`, the run closes where the steps stopped, with the final statistics at that time.

`close()` ends the run where it is. A context from `from_yaml` steps the same way:

`SimulationContext.from_yaml("shop.yaml")` returns a context with the same `start()`, `peek()`, `step()` and `close()`, as the Builder tab shows.

```python
def every_ten(context):
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(10)


stepped = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0).add_process(every_ten)
stepped.start()  # builds everything run() builds; the clock is still at 0
while stepped.peek() < 30:  # the time of the next event
    stepped.step()  # processes the next model event, after desflow's own events due before it
print(f"stopped before {stepped.peek()} at {stepped.env.now}")
stepped.close()  # the teardown run() does at its end
```

`env.peek()` and `env.step()` on a `DynamicRealtimeEnvironment` skip desflow's own events in the same way, and `env.run(until=...)` runs on from where the steps stopped.

It prints `stopped before 30 at 20`. Stepping does not stop at `until`: compare `peek()` with the time you want to stop at.

### Run in Segments

`advance(until)` runs a started run up to a time and returns with the run still open, so a script can read the model, change it with `context.env`, or wait, then run the next segment. `finish()` runs on to the end, as it does after `start()`:

A context from `SimulationContext.from_yaml("shop.yaml")` has the same `start()`, `advance()` and `finish()`, as the Builder tab shows.

```python
def pulse(context):
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(10)


segmented = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0).add_process(pulse)
segmented.start(until=60)
segmented.advance(25)  # runs the model to 25; the events at 25 wait for the next call
segmented.advance("40 s")  # a duration is seconds from the start, not from now
print(f"paused at {segmented.env.now}")
segmented.finish()  # on to start()'s until, 60, and closes
```

Call `env.run(until=...)` again for each segment, as in SimPy. The records are the same as those of one run.

It prints `paused at 40.0`. A run in segments gives the same records as one `run()`, the telemetry and statistics included, because nothing is flushed at a segment boundary. The same holds for a script that calls `env.run(until=...)` again on a low-level environment, as in SimPy. A few rules:

- `until` is a reading of the simulation clock after `now`, in seconds or as a duration such as `"10 min"`. It can also be an event, as the third rule in this list describes. A time that is not after `now` raises `ValueError`, as SimPy does. `advance()` before `start()` or after `close()` raises `RuntimeError`.
- The run stops at the earlier of `until` and its own end: `start()`'s `until`, the `stop` or the end of a drain. A later `advance()` raises `RuntimeError`, so call `finish()` or `close()`. `finish()` returns the end's value: `None` for `until` or a drain, and the stop's value for a stop. For a failed stop, it raises the stop's exception again.
- `until` may be an event, such as `context.signal("gate").wait()`: the run stops where the event fires and returns its value, and the next `advance()` goes on, as SimPy's `env.run(until=event)` does.
- The event that ends a segment stays in the queue: `peek()` gives the segment's time and `step()` processes it.
- `advance()` does not move the wall-clock anchor. A paced run that waited between segments is behind when it goes on, so call `env.resume_pacing()` first.

______________________________________________________________________

## How It Works

**The end of the model and the end of the run.** The model ends when the clock stops: at `until`, at a `stop`, or when a drain empties the model. The run ends after that, at `close()`, which `run()` calls in a `finally` block. `close()` publishes the last statistics, still stamped at the time the model ended. It then flushes and stops the egress connectors, and then stops the ingress connectors. A sink may take a while to drain its queue, but no record it receives is later than the model's end.

# Results

A run publishes records, and it can also measure itself. One run gives one sample, many runs give an interval, and several designs give a comparison. The pages of this section go from one run to a whole study.

______________________________________________________________________

## What It Is

- **Statistics** are collected during one run: how busy each resource was, how long tasks waited, how many entities finished. A warm-up period can be left out.
- **Replications** run the same model with many seeds and give each statistic a mean and a 95% interval.
- **Experiments** run replications of several designs, compare the designs seed by seed, check them against bounds and observed values, and write the results and a report to files.

______________________________________________________________________

## Pages in This Section

- [Built-in Statistics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/statistics/index.md): how to switch the statistics on, what each level publishes and costs, how each value is computed, and how to add readings of your own.
- [Replications](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/replications/index.md): how to run replications from the command line and from Python, what they return and send to the sinks, and how the seeds and intervals are made.
- [Experiments](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/experiments/index.md): the experiment file, the Python call and every setting.
- [Experiment Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/experiment-results/index.md): what an experiment compares, checks and writes, and its report.

______________________________________________________________________

## How to Use It

- For one run, switch the statistics on with `stats` in YAML or `with_stats` in the builder.
- For an interval, run replications with `desflow run --replications`.
- To compare designs, run an experiment with `desflow experiment`.

______________________________________________________________________

## How It Works

Each layer uses the one below it. The statistics measure one run while it goes on. Replications build the model again for each seed, run it unpaced with no ingress and no egress, read the statistics at the end of each run, and give a Student t interval over the runs. An experiment runs replications for each design and compares the designs seed by seed.

# Built-in Statistics

A run can measure itself: how busy each resource was, how long tasks waited, how many entities finished. This page shows how to switch the statistics on, what each level publishes and costs, how each value is computed, and how to add readings of your own.

______________________________________________________________________

## What It Is

The built-in statistics are measures that desflow keeps while the run goes on and publishes as telemetry, under fixed names such as `Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean`. They need no code of yours in the builder or YAML, and they reach every sink like any other telemetry. They are off by default, because most runs only generate data. [Measuring a Run](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/measuring-a-run/index.md) reads them on the shop.

______________________________________________________________________

## How to Use It

### Choose a Level

A level switches them on. Each level publishes what the levels before it publish, and answers one more question:

| Level     | Question                                | Adds                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| --------- | --------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `none`    |                                         | nothing; the default                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `minimal` | What is happening now?                  | resources: `capacity`, `in_use`, `queue_length`, `utilization`, and `down` for one that breaks down; stores and containers: `capacity`, `level`, `getters_waiting`, `putters_waiting`; tasks: `in_progress`                                                                                                                        |
| `basic`   | How much got done, and how busy was it? | tasks and flows: `finished`; flows: `started` and `in_system`; tasks: `balked`, `reneged`, `failed`, `interrupted`, `preempted` and `resumed`, and flows: `failed`, once one happens; resources: `utilization_avg`, `queue_length_avg`, and `downtime` and `failures` for one that breaks down; stores and containers: `level_avg` |
| `typical` | How long did tasks take?                | tasks: `wait_mean`, `wait_max`, `service_mean`, `service_max`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `all`     | How long did the slowest take?          | tasks: `wait_p50`, `wait_p95`, `wait_p99`, `service_p50`, `service_p95`, `service_p99`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

They are published every `interval` of simulation time, 10 seconds when it is not given. The first publication comes one interval after the start, and one more comes at the end of the run. When the timer has already published at the end's time, the end publishes only the values that changed since:

```yaml
# none (the default), minimal, basic, typical or all, each adding to the one before;
# published every interval of simulation time and once at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 1 min}
```

`stats: typical` is the short form, with the 10-second interval. The interval takes seconds or a duration.

```python
# none (the default), minimal, basic, typical or all, each adding to the one before;
# published every interval of simulation seconds and once at the end
app.with_stats("typical", interval=60)
```

```python
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=60)  # before or after the resources
```

Resources, stores and containers add themselves to `env.stats` when they are built. Tasks are your own processes, so each reports its steps:

```python
# A low-level task reports its own steps to the statistics
env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
with packers.request() as request:
    yield request
    env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
    yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
env.stats.flow_finished("orders")  # the order leaves the shop
```

### Read the Names

Every statistic is published as telemetry named `<sim_id>.stats.<kind>.<name>.<statistic>`, where the kind is `resources`, `stores`, `containers`, `tasks` or `flows`. A flow is named by the arrival that started its entities: `Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished` counts the orders that left the model. [Reference, Statistics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/statistics/index.md) lists every name with what it measures. Below are the statistics that [`statistics.yaml`](https://github.com/jaehyeon-kim/desflow/blob/v0.27.0/docs/snippets/yaml/statistics.yaml), the blueprint whose `levels` part is shown above, publishes at the end of its two-minute run:

```text
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 2}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.in_use', 'value': 2}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length', 'value': 6}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization', 'value': 100.0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization_avg', 'value': 90.79208653095155}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length_avg', 'value': 1.9083531344309013}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.in_progress', 'value': 8}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.finished', 'value': 70}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean', 'value': 2.7959715976263215}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_max', 'value': 11.22214686679115}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.service_mean', 'value': 3.0335617388528364}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.service_max', 'value': 6.357944038555676}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished', 'value': 70}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.flows.orders.started', 'value': 78}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.flows.orders.in_system', 'value': 8}
```

The same values can be read by name, during or after the run:

`desflow run --stdout` prints the same values as telemetry records, as above.

`app.env.stats.readings()` gives the same values, by name, during or after the run.

```python
# Every statistic the level publishes, by its published name
readings = env.stats.readings()
print(f"mean wait {readings['Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean']:.2f} s")
```

### Which Entities a Count Covers

When the statistics are read, every entity that has arrived belongs to one population. Each population has its own counts, published from `basic` unless the table says otherwise. A mean wait or service time covers only the instances that reached that step, so report the counts beside it:

| Population       | Which entities                                                                                     | Counts                                                                                                                                                      |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| completed        | left the model after their last task                                                               | `flows.<arrival>.finished`; `tasks.<task>.finished` per task                                                                                                |
| still present    | started and not yet ended when the statistics are read                                             | `flows.<arrival>.in_system`; `tasks.<task>.in_progress`, the instances queued or started, from `minimal`                                                    |
| rejected         | refused to join a queue, as their `balk` held                                                      | `tasks.<task>.balked`                                                                                                                                       |
| abandoned        | left a queue when their `patience` ran out, or ended by an interrupt under `on_interrupt: abandon` | `tasks.<task>.reneged`; an abandoned flow leaves `in_system` without adding to `finished` or `failed`, and `tasks.<task>.interrupted` counts the interrupts |
| failed           | ended in a failure that no `on_fail` handled                                                       | `flows.<arrival>.failed`; `tasks.<task>.failed` counts failed instances                                                                                     |
| warm-up-crossing | started before the warm-up ended and ended after it                                                | in `finished`, and in the wait and service times with their whole wait, but not in `started`                                                                |

An entity a task spawns ([Start a Flow Without Waiting](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/tasks-and-processes/signals-and-waiting/#start-a-flow-without-waiting)) counts as a flow of its own under the spawned task's name. So `flows.<task>.*` and `tasks.<task>.*` cover it as they cover any arrival's flow. The spawning entity's key is in `attr.parent`.

Without a [warm-up](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#one-run-starts-empty), `started` is `finished` plus `in_system` plus the entities that balked, reneged, failed or were abandoned. A warm-up starts `started`, `finished`, `failed` and the outcome counts again from zero, and leaves `in_system` and `in_progress` as they are. After a warm-up, `finished` also counts the warm-up-crossing entities, which `started` leaves out, so `finished` can be larger than `started`. [End Conditions](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/end-conditions/index.md) counts each population of a run.

### Add Readings of Your Own

Anything else is a custom reading: a function called at an interval of simulation time, which publishes with `context.publish(name, value)` as `<sim_id>.<name>`. It can read resources, stores, containers or any registry value.

```yaml
telemetry:
  # Readings of your own: called as packers_report(context) every 30 seconds
  - interval: 30
    function: !python shop_logic.packers_report
```

The function is in `shop_logic.py`, beside the blueprint:

```python
def packers_report(context):
    """A custom reading: orders waiting per packer, and the live arrival rate."""
    packers = context.get_resource("packers")
    waiting = len(packers.queue)
    context.publish("waiting_per_packer", waiting / max(packers.capacity, 1))
    rate = context.env.registry.get(f"{context.sim_id}.arrival.orders.rate").value
    context.publish("arrival_rate", rate)  # as Shop.arrival_rate
```

```python
@app.telemetry_loop(interval=30.0)
def packers_report(context: SimulationContext):
    """Readings of your own: orders waiting per packer, and the live arrival rate."""
    packers = context.get_resource("packers")
    waiting = len(packers.queue)
    context.publish("waiting_per_packer", waiting / max(packers.capacity, 1))
    rate = context.env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.rate").value
    context.publish("arrival_rate", rate)  # as Shop.arrival_rate
```

A process that loops, publishes with `env.publish_telemetry(name, value)` and waits with `env.timeout(interval)` does the same.

______________________________________________________________________

## How It Works

The environment keeps one `Statistics` object, `env.stats`, which collects nothing until a level above `none` is set. Its timer publishes every value at each interval, and the teardown publishes them once more. When the timer has already published at the teardown's time, the teardown publishes only the values that changed since.

**Readings now.** `capacity`, `in_use`, `queue_length` and `level` are read from the object at the moment of publishing. `in_use` counts the units held by tasks, and a capacity drop does not take busy units away. After a drop, `in_use` can therefore be above `capacity`, and `utilization` (`in_use ÷ capacity × 100`) can be above 100%. A resource with no limit (`current_cap: .inf`) publishes `capacity` as `null` and a `utilization` of 0. A store or container with no limit publishes its `capacity` as `null` too.

**Breakdowns.** A resource with a `breakdown` reads `down` now: 1 while it is down, 0 otherwise. `downtime` adds the length of each down period, and of one still going on. `failures` adds one at each failure. [Model Breakdowns](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/how-to/modelling/breakdowns/index.md) checks both against the events.

**Averages over time.** `utilization_avg`, `queue_length_avg` and `level_avg` weigh each value by how long it lasted. Each resource, store and container reports every change, and the statistics add the area under the value since the last change, so the average is exact at any moment rather than sampled:

**Counts.** `finished` adds one when a task instance finishes, and a flow's `finished` adds one when an entity's last task has no next task. A flow's `started` adds one when an entity's first task instance begins, before its balk check and its queue, whether or not it is then served. An entity that the `spawn` key or an `on:` spawn action starts is counted at the spawn when the spawn has no `after`. With an `after`, it is counted when the spawned task starts, after the delay. `in_system` is the number of the flow's entities in the model now: started, and not yet finished, failed or gone. [Which Entities a Count Covers](#which-entities-a-count-covers) shows how `started` adds up. A task's `in_progress` is the number of its instances queued or started and not yet ended, now. A low-level process reports an entity's start with `env.stats.flow_started(arrival)`. It reports an entity that leaves without finishing or failing with `env.stats.flow_ended(arrival)`. A task's `balked` adds one when an instance refuses to join its queue, `reneged` when one leaves the queue after its patience, and `failed` when one fails ([Failures](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/tasks-and-processes/failures/#failures)). A flow's `failed` adds one when an entity's flow ends in a failure no `on_fail` handles. `interrupted` and `preempted` add one for each interrupt or preemption an instance receives, and `resumed` when it is served again. Each is published once it is above 0. A balked, reneged or failed instance adds no wait or service time. An interrupted instance that resumes adds one wait, the sum of all its waits, and one service time, the time it was served. A low-level process counts them with `env.stats.task_balked(task, instance)`, `env.stats.task_reneged(task, instance)`, `env.stats.task_failed(task, instance)`, `env.stats.flow_failed(arrival)`, `env.stats.task_interrupted(task, instance, preempted=...)` and `env.stats.task_resumed(task, instance)`.

**Wait and service.** The wait of a task instance runs from its `queued` step to its `started` step, and its service from `started` to finished. A task that never queues, such as a timed step, waits 0. `typical` keeps only a count, a total and a maximum of each, so the memory they use does not grow with the run. `all` keeps every observation and computes the percentiles exactly with NumPy's `percentile` at each publication, so its memory grows with the number of tasks.

**Warm-up.** A run's `warmup` resets every statistic once, at that time: the averages start again from zero area, and the counts and observations from zero. An instance that was queued before the reset and starts after it counts with its whole wait. [Time and Pacing](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/time-and-pacing/index.md) describes the warm-up.

______________________________________________________________________

## Stability and Limits

- **Cost.** `minimal` reads a few values at each publication. `basic` adds a little work at every change of a resource, store or container. `typical` adds a little at every task step. `all` keeps every wait and service time in memory for the whole run. Use it for runs of thousands of tasks, not for a generator that runs for days.
- **One way to get resource readings.** Before 0.21.0, a `telemetry` entry could publish `<resource>.<reading>` by name. That shortcut is gone: `stats: minimal` publishes the same readings, under `Shop.stats.resources.<name>.<reading>`. `telemetry` now takes only a function, for readings of your own.
- **One run is one sample.** The statistics describe one run with one seed. Values from the same run are not independent of each other, and another seed gives other values. [Replications](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#replications) give independent values. [Trusting Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/trusting-results/index.md) shows what that means for a result, and [Replications](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/replications/index.md) run a model with many seeds.
- **A task appears once it has run.** At `typical` and `all`, a task's statistics are published from the first time it starts. At `basic`, they are published from the first time it finishes.

______________________________________________________________________

## Example: Measuring a Run

The `measuring` example publishes every statistic of the packers and the pack task every 5 minutes of simulation time, and leaves out a 3-minute warm-up. When packing slows down, it sends a ground-truth record to a sink of its own. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

The tutorial page [Measuring a Run](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/measuring-a-run/index.md) teaches these features step by step.


```bash

```

```yaml

scenario:
```


```python
def slow_packing(context):
    """Packing slows from 4 to 4.8 seconds on average at 12 minutes, with its label."""
    yield context.env.timeout(720)
    path = "Shop.service.packing.scale"
    registry = context.env.registry
    old = registry.get(path).value
    registry.update(path, 1.2)
    context.env.publish_label(
        {"fault": "slow_packing", "cause": "new packing material"},
        path=path,
        old=old,
        new=registry.get(path).value,
    )


app.add_process(slow_packing)
```

The whole file is [`examples/builder/measuring_example.py`](https://github.com/jaehyeon-kim/desflow/blob/v0.27.0/examples/builder/measuring_example.py).

# Replications

One run of a model is one sample: another seed draws other times and gives other values. [Replications](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#replications) run the same model with many seeds and summarise each built-in statistic with a mean and a [95% interval](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#interval-and-half-width). This page shows how to run them from the command line and from Python, in each of the three ways to write a model, what they return and send to the sinks, and how the seeds and intervals are made.

______________________________________________________________________

## What It Is

A replication is one run of the model with a seed of its own. N replications give N independent values of each [built-in statistic](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/statistics/index.md), such as the mean wait of a task. Their mean is the estimate, and the **half-width** of its 95% interval says how precise it is: with 95% confidence, the true value lies within the mean plus or minus the half-width. [Trusting Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/trusting-results/index.md) shows on the shop why one run is not an answer and how to choose the number of replications.

______________________________________________________________________

## How to Use It

### Run Replications

Give the model, the number of replications, the seed they are spawned from and the time the arrivals stop:

```bash
desflow run replications.yaml --replications 20 --measure tasks.pack.wait_mean
```

`--seed` overrides `simulation.random_seed`, and `--until` overrides `run.until`, as for one run. `--level` sets the confidence level (0.95 when it is not given), `--workers` sets how many replications run at once, each in its own process, and `--drain` drains every replication, as `run.drain: true` does. The command prints the summary, the seed of each replication and the command that repeats one. The blueprint's own `warmup` applies to every replication:

```yaml
# The replications' seeds are spawned from this one; --seed overrides it
random_seed: 42
warmup: 3 min
```

```python
# shop is a function returning a new SimulationContext, called once per run
result = replicate(shop, 3, seed=42, until="1 h", warmup="3 min", measures=MEASURES)
```

`shop` is a function with no arguments that returns a new `SimulationContext`, such as [the example's](https://github.com/jaehyeon-kim/desflow/blob/v0.27.0/examples/builder/replications_example.py), because each replication starts from a new context. A blueprint path works here too.

```python
def model(env, sampler):
    """Builds the shop in the environment it is given, drawing from sampler."""
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.process(orders(env, sampler, DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")))


def low_level():
    shop = LowLevelModel(model, sim_id="Shop")
    return replicate(shop, 3, seed=42, until=3600, warmup=180, measures=MEASURES)
```

`LowLevelModel` takes a function that builds the model, given an environment and a sampler, and the `sim_id` that the model's statistics are published under. The function registers the parameters, builds the resources and starts the processes. It sets up no statistics, because `replicate` does, and it sets up no sinks. Its tasks report their steps to `env.stats`, as [Statistics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/statistics/index.md) shows.

`replicate` takes these options:

| Option      | What it sets                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | Default                                                     |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `n`         | how many replications, 2 or more                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |                                                             |
| `seed`      | the seed the replications' seeds are spawned from; None draws one and logs it                                                                                                                                                                                                 |                                                             |
| `until`     | where each replication's arrivals stop, in seconds or a duration such as `"1 h"`; the replication ends there unless `stop` ends it earlier or `drain` runs on                                                                                                                 | a blueprint's `run.until`                                   |
| `stop`      | ends each replication when it happens, as for `run()`: `{"signal": name}`, a signal's name, or `{"condition": "..."}`; for a `LowLevelModel`, a function of the environment that returns the event                                                                            | a blueprint's `run.stop`                                    |
| `drain`     | at `until`, stop the arrivals and run each replication on until no entity is left: `True`, or `{"limit": "1 h"}`; a `LowLevelModel` is drained when its function returns its arrival processes and reports its entities with `env.stats.flow_started` and `flow_finished`     | a blueprint's `run.drain`                                   |
| `warmup`    | the end of each replication's warm-up                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | the model's own                                             |
| `measures`  | the statistics to summarise                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | every statistic the run publishes, at least up to `typical` |
| `level`     | the confidence level of the half-widths                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | 0.95                                                        |
| `workers`   | how many replications run at once, each in its own process                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | 1                                                           |
| `overrides` | registry paths and the values every replication starts with, such as `{"Shop.resources.packers.current_cap": 3}`, set in the order given; a value the registry would refuse or clamp is refused, so a `max_cap` below the current `current_cap` needs `current_cap` set first | none                                                        |

### Choose the Measures

A measure is a statistic's published name without the sim id and `stats`, such as `tasks.pack.wait_mean` for `Shop.stats.tasks.pack.wait_mean`. [Reference, Statistics](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/statistics/index.md) lists them. Each replication keeps the statistics level its measures need, whatever level the model sets: `basic` for counts and time averages, `typical` for means and maxima of waits and services, and `all` for percentiles. A higher level the model sets stays.

A name that no replication publishes is refused, with the names the model does publish. A count that is published only once it is above 0, such as `reneged`, is 0 in a replication without one. A mean with no observation in a replication, such as the wait of a task that never started, is refused with the replication's number rather than left out.

### Read the Result

`replicate`, imported with `from desflow import replicate`, returns a `Replications`. Its `summary` has one row per measure: a mapping with `measure`, `n`, `mean`, `half_width` and `level`. The interval runs from `mean - half_width` to `mean + half_width`. Its `table` has one row per replication and measure, with the replication's number and seed, and `seeds` lists the seeds in order:

```python
print(result.summary_text())  # each measure's n, mean and half-width
for row in result.summary:  # measure, n, mean, half_width and level
    low, high = row["mean"] - row["half_width"], row["mean"] + row["half_width"]
    print(f"{row['measure']}: {low:.2f} to {high:.2f} ({row['level']:.0%})")
print(result.seeds)  # replication i ran with seeds[i - 1]
for row in result.table:  # one row per replication and measure
    print(row["replication"], row["seed"], row["measure"], row["value"])
```

The summary of the three replications above:

```text
measure                               n          mean    half-width (95%)
tasks.pack.wait_mean                  3          4.16                2.22
resources.packers.utilization_avg     3         78.51               4.363
```

Three replications give a wide interval. [Trusting Results](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/studies/trusting-results/#choose-the-precision) shows how to choose enough.

### Repeat One Replication

Each replication's seed is a plain integer, recorded in `seeds` and in every row of the table. Any replication can therefore be repeated on its own, with the same end time, drain and [warm-up](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#one-run-starts-empty): `desflow run shop.yaml --seed <its seed>`, `random_seed` in a builder context, or `Sampler(seed=...)` in the low-level API. That run publishes its event records, which replications do not.

### What the Sinks Receive

When the model has sinks, a blueprint's `egress` or a builder's `add_egress`, they receive the result once, as telemetry stamped at the end time: each replication's value, then each measure's mean, half-width and count. A low-level model has no sinks of its own. Below are the records a Console sink receives from the three replications above:

```text
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack.wait_mean.replication.1', 'value': 3.1279921040674012}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack.wait_mean.replication.2', 'value': 4.692163115004602}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack.wait_mean.replication.3', 'value': 4.6595156392512935}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization_avg.replication.1', 'value': 77.72020813552408}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization_avg.replication.2', 'value': 77.2928455841536}
```

[Records and Telemetry](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/reference/records-and-telemetry/#telemetry-names) lists the names.

______________________________________________________________________

## How It Works

**Seeds.** The replications' seeds are `numpy.random.SeedSequence(seed).spawn(n)`, each turned into one plain integer. The same seed gives the same list, and a longer list starts with the shorter one, so 40 replications begin with the 10 that `n=10` runs. Within a replication each distribution draws from a random sequence of its own, as in any run ([Randomness and Seeds](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/first-model/randomness-and-seeds/index.md)).

**One replication.** Each replication builds the model again: it reads the blueprint, calls the factory, or calls the low-level function with a new environment and sampler. It runs unpaced, at `factor` 0, with no ingress, no egress and no statistics timer. It applies the warm-up and the `overrides` before the clock starts, and reads `env.stats.readings()` at its end. A blueprint's `run.before` functions run once per replication, and once more when the model has sinks, for the build that sends them the result.

**Intervals.** The half-width is t × s ÷ √n. Here s is the sample standard deviation of the n values, and t is the Student t quantile at (1 + level) ÷ 2 with n − 1 degrees of freedom. desflow computes the quantile itself, by bisection on the t distribution's cumulative probability, so replications need nothing beyond a base install. The tests check it against a published table.

**Workers.** With `workers` above 1, replications run in a pool of that many processes. Each process imports the model. The model must therefore be a blueprint path or a function defined at the top of a module. A lambda, or a function defined inside another function, is refused with that reason. The values are the same as with one worker.

**Sinks.** When the model has sinks, it is built once more after the last replication, with its sinks, without its ingress, and with the clock at the end time. This build is not run. Its own statistics are switched off, so the sinks receive only the result. A model without sinks is not built again.

______________________________________________________________________

## Stability and Limits

- **No event records.** Replications send no event records: the orders of twenty replications, each with its own seed, would mix in one sink and could not be told apart. Repeat one replication with its seed to get its records.
- **Independent seeds only.** Every replication of one call has its own seed. Comparing two designs with the same seeds, and checking that their random streams line up, is an experiment's job ([Experiments](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/user-guide/results/experiments/index.md)).
- **Same model each time.** A builder factory must return a new context on every call. A context that has run keeps its entity counters and is not a new replication.
- **Built-in statistics only.** A replication summarises the built-in statistics at its end. Readings of your own, published with `context.publish`, are not summarised.
- **Steady state and terminating runs.** The warm-up applies to each replication. A run with a natural start and end, such as a shop day, keeps its empty start and needs no warm-up. [Output Analysis](https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/learn/concepts/output-analysis/#terminating-or-steady-state) explains the two kinds of run.

______________________________________________________________________
